source_data.original_text: i.e. descendants of Lugaidh Cal, Ca. 318; ¶ the posterity of Lugaidh Cal branched into 7 septs, viz.—the Calraighe of Brí Leith, al. C. an Chalaidh; ¶ C. Innse Nisc, desc. fr. Fraechar, son of Lugaidh; ¶ C. Tre Maige, fr. Cobhthach; ¶ C. of Breaghmhaine, fr. Ailill; ¶ C. Luirg, fr. Lughaidh, son of Lughaidh (O'Drean its hereditary chieftain); ¶ C. of Corann, fr. Aenghus, son of Lughaidh, are C. Luirg and C. of Corann (O'h Innreachtaigh is the hereditary ch. of C. of Corann); ¶ C. of Cuil Cearna are of the race of Aenghus (O'Scingin is their hereditary ch.); ¶ fr. Eochaidh, son of Aenghus, son of Lughaidh [Cal], come C. of L. Gile and the Dartraighe; ¶ the 4 chief septs of Dartraighe and C. are Meg Fhlannchaidh (their kings), Meg Crunnluachra (their dynasts), Tealach Churnain (their poets), Ui Finn (their Brughadha, farmers); ¶ the septs of C. are Tealach Crunnluachra, Tealach Curnain, Tealach Critain, Tealach Treabhaire, Tealach Uaruisce, and Tealach Cairnean; ¶ the C. of Muirisc in Tir Ua nAmhalghadha come fr. Cael, son of Lughaidh Cal, al. C. of Magh hEileag, O'Mailfhina its hereditary chieftain; ¶ they became extinct but a few and Ui Gaibhtheacháin and Ui Floinn took the l., so that they are the most powerful therein and these also are of the race of Aenghus, son of Amhalghaidh; ¶ Cuil Cearnadha is called Calraighe Cuil fr. being in the angle of Fith Gathlaidh; ¶ and, if the learned say truly, it should be called C. Innse Nisc; ¶ its hereditary tribes are Ua Cuinn, Ua Iarnain and Ua Finain and O Rothlain is its chief; ¶ (the references were, alas! omitted in transcription for press, but many of them will appear under the various Calraigi); ¶ Lughaidh Cal mac Ithe is uaid Dartraidhe na C., Hz. 16, Sa. 63 b 2; ¶ C. Luirc, C. an Challaigh, C. Insi Nisc, and C. Muighi Muirisc come fr. Lughaidh Mal, Lec. 242; ¶ i.e., Treb ol C., W. of L. Erne; ¶ the Corco Laigi and the Corco Orchten in Mun; ¶ one of the 46 Aicme of the Aitechaigh, Bb. 96 b, 140 a. c.; ¶ al. C. Droma Cliab, al. C. Locha Gile; ¶ exiit ad regiones Callrigi Tre Maige et fecit æcclessiam juxta Druim Leas, et erexit ad Campum Ailmaige et fundavit ibi Domnach Ailmaige, a edocht du manchuib Drommo Lías ocus du maithib Callrigi, A. 15 a a, 17 a b; ¶ "veniens in finem Calrigi, babtitzavit filium Cairthin .... Druimm Daro .i. Druim Lias," A. 17 a b; ¶ luid P. hi crích Callraigi do Druim Dara bali itá indiu Druim Lias, Tl. 144; ¶ this sept occupied Drumlease in c. Leit., and all the obscure place-names of A. 17 a b must be at or nr. Drumlease and Domnach Ailmaige; ¶ v. Calrige Aelmaige; ¶ comprising the N. of c. Sli. and part of c. Leit., p. Drumlease, c. Leit., was in it; ¶ also the p. Calry, in b. Carbury, c. Sli., Tp., Fm. vi. 2010, Ar. 134; ¶ al. C. Locha Gile, N. 262.

Located in a raised terraced area in the W half of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL011-011001-), known as ‘The Cashel’.
A lintelled creepway or souterrain-like feature extends from the area before Teach Molaise (SL001-001005-) towards the south-west angle of Templenatinny (SL001-001011-). This is not a souterrain proper (i.e. tunnelled below ground level), but is built within the raised terrace that forms the western subdivision of the Cashel.  The feature was not surveyed in detail as inspection of the interior indicated that the roof lintels – large flat stone slabs – are in danger of collapse.

The above description is derived from a survey of the archaeological remains undertaken in 1998-99 and published in J. O’Sullivan and T. Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
This clochan, traditionally known as ‘Toorybrennel’ or ‘the schoolhouse’, is located in the W half of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL011-011001-) known as ‘The Cashel’. It abuts the S side of Templenatinny church (SL001001011-).
Clochan or beehive cell of drystone construction, subcircular on plan, internally and externally, with walls of coursed small and medium rubble rising to a slab-built corbelled roof (internally). The structure is set within a terraced area in the north-west of the Cashel where it is conjoined to a smaller corbelled cell (SL001-001084-) on the south and on the north abuts Templenatinny (SL001-001011-). Access is via a narrow alley leading through the terrace revetment from the cemetery (SL001-001029-). The doorway is in the north and is formed by massive single-stone jambs. There is a wall bench at the west or right-hand side (entering) and, opposite the door, a narrow, deep window. There are two low aumbries - at ground level - in the south and east. The external wall face is thicker at the base, stepping in to form a level scarcement around the full circuit of the wall at shoulder level. The floor is currently spread with modern gravel. 
The clochan has been substantially rebuilt in restoration works.

The above description is derived from the survey of the archaeological remains undertaken in 1998-99 and published in J. O’Sullivan and T. Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 15 June 2012

source_data.original_text:
This clochan, traditionally known as ‘Trahanacorresh’, is located in an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL011-011001-) known as ‘The Cashel’.
A large, drystone cell or clochan lies within the extreme north-east arc of the Cashel wall, immediately adjacent to the north-east entrance. Access is via a short, narrow, sunken passageway from the cemetery (SL001-001-029-)  leading to a few shallow steps which descend into the doorway. This passes between a low stone retaining wall on one side and the outer face wall of the building on the other. An arrangement of slabs and rubble forms a small bay or stall within one side of the passage. The building itself is subrectangular on plan, with rounded outer corners, and rises to a roughly domed or beehive roof. As at Toorybrennel (SL001-001003-), a broad scarcement is carried around the exterior at shoulder level. In this case, however, it is a less regular feature: at the outer or north-east face it is formed by the surface of the Cashel wall and it is absent on the west front, over the doorway. Internally, the building is divided into three chambers. The principal chamber rises to a corbelled roof formed by large slabs. Access to a small, low chamber to the south is via a low doorway or creepway. Immediately above this is a second small chamber set below the corbelled roof. Access between these smaller chambers is via an opening in the slabbed ceiling of the lower one.

The above description is derived from the survey of the archaeological remains undertaken in 1998-99 and published in J. O’Sullivan and T. Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 15 June 2012

source_data.original_text:
Located in an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL011-011001-), known as ‘The Cashel’.
This tiny church, known as Teach Molaise or St. Molaise's Chapel, is traditionally identified as the tomb chapel or shrine chapel of St Molaise, the island’s patron saint, and housed the secondary relics of the saint until modern times. It is set close to the Cashel wall in the north-west part of the interior. Here, the building stands parallel to the enclosure wall, on an orientation of 64°30’ that is considerably at variance with the standard liturgical east/west alignment and, indeed, considerably at variance with the more orthodox alignment of Templemolaise (SL001-001009-). 
The building is 2.7 m long by (max.) 2.8 m wide, within walls about 0.5 m thick. Thus it is slightly wider than it is long, with proportions of about 1:1. It is also trapezoidal in plan, widening slightly towards the east end. The walls are of mortared rubble, roughly coursed. There is a west doorway, slightly off centre, with a simple Greek cross inscribed on the lintel. The east wall is pierced by a small round-headed window and by several putlog holes (partly blocked) on the interior and exterior. The roof is of mortared stone, now grass clad. It is asymetrical and of very low pitch. The building is generally sound and bears only light vegetation on the roof. It is closed by a padlocked, metal, barred gate set in the doorway. 
The atypical dimensions, the low, irregular roof, and visible changes in the masonry (described below) are most certainly due to very extensive rebuilding – especially of the side walls and roof. The overall effect was to widen the building by about 0.6 m and it can be deduced that the overall external dimensions of the primary building were about 3.8 m long by.2.7 m wide, giving proportions of about 1.4:1.
Internally, most of the floor area is taken up by features abutting the side walls and east gable. A layer of loosely laid large flags lies along the foot of the north wall, internally. The east end is internally spanned from wall to wall by an altar (SL001-001007-), formed by a high, narrow stone bench. A broader, lower stone bench extends along the south wall and this is known as Leaba Molaise (St Molaise’s bed) (SL001-001006-). Externally, there is also a low stone bench with a surface of loose flags spanning the entire length of the south wall and this appears to have been keyed to the masonry of that wall. 
The west doorway is trabeate in form (i.e. with a flat lintel). It is about 1.4 m high and the jambs batter from a width of 0.54 m at the base to 0.51 m at the top. The jambs are of large, moderately well-squared, but not well-fitted, sandstone blocks. Most of these span the thickness of wall. The lowest jamb stone on the south side projects 0.1 m from the internal wall face. Directly below this is a pivot stone for an upright door-post, with a hole 0.05m wide by 0.01m deep on its upper surface. The north side of the projecting jamb stone is shaped to accommodate the post. Midway along its external face the lintel (H: 0.19 m, W: 1.03 m) is inscribed with a simple Greek cross (c. 0.15 m across) with slightly expanded terminals, and there is also a vertical groove, 0.06 m long, midway along its interior face. 
Much of the exterior of the round-headed east window has been reset. The ope currently measures 0.4 m high by 0.25 m wide. Its monolithic, inward-splaying lintel is neatly rebated at the exterior, and behind this a deep hole – 0.03 m wide by 0.08 m deep – pierces both the north and south sides of its soffit. Of the exterior jamb stones only one at the north is definitely original. Along the reveal of this stone, and directly below the hole in the soffit of the lintel, is a vertical groove, 0.01 m deep. These features probably accommodated a pivoting shutter that could only have opened to the exterior. A small niche in the exterior of the north and south jamb bases may have accommodated a piece of wood, pierced with a hole, on which this shutter could pivot. Alternatively, these niches may be late features. The soffit of the lintel features another groove behind the two holes, which may have accommodated an inner wooden frame covered with thin, stretched hide or some other translucent material. The exterior shutter would have protected this from weathering. Despite the fact that it may be rebuilt, the embrasure is of well-cut, well-fitted stone, descending in three steps internally. It measures 1.17 m high by 0.52 –0.38 m wide. Its base is considerably lower internally than the base of the opening. 
The substantial rebuilding of this church is attested by its odd dimensions, irregular roof and also by changes in its fabric. The side walls were certainly rebuilt and also the upper parts of the end walls, probably at the same time that the stone roof was added. Where it survives in situ – in parts of the end walls – the original masonry is roughly coursed, squared rubble of mainly medium to large blocks, quite well fitted. There are relatively few spalls and only moderate visible mortar. In contrast, the rebuilt side walls are of random rubble of less regular, poorer fitting blocks, with more spalls and more visible mortar. In both gables there are irregular vertical joints where the secondary masonry abuts the primary work. No scars or tusking stones of the original side walls are apparent on the end walls internally, and it may be that parts of the internal faces of the end walls were also rebuilt. Changes in masonry style also indicate that the exterior east wall was rebuilt, from about height of the window ledge, and even less of the exterior west wall appears to be original. It is possible that some of the original coins – medium to large, well-squared blocks – survive in situ in the east gable, especially at the north-east angle. The unusually short proportions of the church support the possibility that these are the original quoins, now merely the tell-tales in the rebuilt end walls of a somewhat narrower original building. If so then, unlike most shrine chapels, this building had no antae in its primary phase.
Two putlog holes occur at a high level, internally, in each of the end walls, but are almost certainly late. Three occur in the exterior east wall. The lowest of these is set in the surviving remnant of primary masonry and thus is itself an early feature.
The structure of the irregular stone roof is partly obscured by vegetation at the exterior and mortar at the interior, but it is clearly a late medieval or post-medieval feature. It was raised on formwork built with long narrow laths and the impressions of these survive in the mortar that thickly covers the internal surface. Some of the upper stones in the rebuilt end walls are probably coping stones from the original gables. None of these is in situ but their form suggests that the original roof was very steeply pitched. It may have been wooden with a thatch or shingle cladding.
A charcoal-bearing mortar sample from the E wall of the building yielded a calibrated radiocarbon date of AD 724–836 at one sigma probability (Berger 1992, 884) and AD 690–980 at two sigma (Berger 1995, 172). As the east wall was substantially rebuilt, probably in the later medieval period, the dated mortar may not have been in a primary context when sampled.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 16 January 2018

Located in a church (SL001-001005-), known as Teach Molaise.
A stone altar spans the entire east end of Teach Molaise, internally. This is a high narrow bench – raised almost to the window sill – formed of small and medium angular slabs. Wakeman (1893, 42) describes a fortuitous discovery here; ‘While removing some of the accumulation in search of carved or lettered stones, my companion ... was rewarded by the discovery of a cist-like hollow within the centre of the altar ... no doubt, intended as a secret receptacle for some very sacred relic. We found within it a piece of decayed yew ... this we returned to the cist, over which we replaced the stones’.
 
A wooden stature (SL001-001008-), traditionally said to represent St. Molaise, formerly stood on this altar.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
This church, traditionally known as ‘Templemolaise’ or ‘Teampall na bFear’ (the men’s church), is located in the E half of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL011-011001-), known as ‘The Cashel’. 
The principal church within the Cashel occupies the large open space in which the cemetery (001-001-029-) (north of the church) and freestanding leachta (SL001-001013-; SL001-001019-; SL001-001021-) are also found. It is a single-cell pre-Romanesque church with antae at the east end (i.e. squared pilasters on the angles formed by an extension of the side walls past the end gable), a single west doorway and a round-headed east window. The building measures 7.73 m long by 3.55 m wide, within walls about 0.7 m thick. The building is oriented at 93 degrees. The interior is level and bare, with modern gravel throughout.
The masonry is mortared random rubble of mainly small to large and a few massive sandstone blocks (maximum 1.68 m by 0.37 m), with different sizes often mixed indiscriminately. Rough coursing is evident in places. Some blocks are quite well fitted, with moderate spalls, and very little visible mortar. The blocks are slightly smaller, on average, at the interior, and there is a line of uprights visible at the base of the interior. 
The doorway in the west gable is of trabeate form (i.e.with a flat lintel). It is 1.56 m high with jambs that batter from 0.64 m wide at the base to 0.54 m at the top. The jamb stones are mainly large sandstone blocks, moderately well fitted, and rough punch dressing is visible in places. In each jamb one block spans the thickness of the wall. On the north side this block features a small semi-circular hole in its east side.
The round-headed east window was probably rebuilt by the Board of Works in 1880. It has three monolithic lintels and there is a stone setting between two of these. The lintels splay unevenly to the interior, and the exterior one, which is of coarser stone than the rest, also splays outwards slightly near its exterior edge. It is not clear whether the jambs were battered originally, but the ope now measures 0.64 m by 0.39 m. There are three steps in the embrasure and quite rough punch-dressing is visible on many of the surround stones. On the soffit of the outer lintel is a deep hole – 0.025 m wide and 0.02m deep – for hanging a shutter on its north side. There is a corresponding hollow on its south side – 0.05 m wide and 0.04 m deep. The soffit is rebated exterior to the hole, suggesting that the shutter opened inwards. Poor refitting means that the stump of a metal rivet is visible on the underside of the lintel. It probably served to secure the shutter to the south jamb. 
The antae survive only at the east end. The southern one is.0.7 m wide by 0.2 m deep. The northern one is deeper, irregular in plan, and its blocks are not as well fitted. It was probably entirely rebuilt by the Board of Works in 1880, but note that no antae are shown at the west end in a drawing made in the 1790s by Angelo Bigari in the course of his sketching tour of Connaught with Gabriel Beranger.
There is a variety of evidence that the church was extended westwards: the absence of antae at this end, the slightly off-centre position of the doorway, and the unusually long proportions of the building (2:1). 
A mortar sample from the building yielded a radiocarbon date of cal AD 800–1150 at two sigma probability (Berger 1992, 884) and cal AD 660–980 at one sigma (Berger 1995, 172). As the sample was taken from the west wall, the date may relate to the second phase of the building. 
A stone trough (SL001-001010-), two cross-inscribed pillars (SL001-001023-; SL001-001026-), an inscribed pillar (SL001-001024-) and a bullaun stone (SL001-001034-) are located adjacent to the W end of the church, and there is a leacht (SL001-001021-) a few meters to E of the church.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
This church, traditionally named ‘Templenatinny’ or ‘Teampall na Teine’, is located in the W half of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL011-011001-), known as ‘The Cashel’. 
A clochan (SL001-001003-), named Torybrennel, abuts it at S. This large rectilinear building is orientated NE/SW and measures 5.1 m long by 3.4 m wide, within walls 0.65 m thick. The walls are of mortared rubble, roughly brought to course. Putlog holes at the wall head, internally, indicate positions of wooden roof joists. A shallow plinth – possibly remnants of the original wall footings or possibly an earlier building on the same stance – extends from the base of the building on the east, north and west wall faces. There is a plain doorway midway in the south wall, with a broad internal splay. The lintel bears a cross and may be a reused cross slab (SL001-001033-). Opposite this is a large window of similar form (the external ground level rises to the sill). The east gable is pierced by a narrow window, with a wide internal splay. Immediately below this is a small aumbry slightly offset to the north. The most distinctive feature of the building is the ‘hearth’ (SL001-001012-), a group of flat stones edge-set within the floor to form a square kerb, roughly 1 m wide. There is a millstone lying within the south-west corner. The floor is now overspread with gravel.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Located S of centre in the interior of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL011-011001-), known as ‘The Cashel’. 
This well-built leacht measures 2 m east/west by 1.8 m north/south and is 0.9 m high. The base is partly formed by flat slabs, edge-set (cist-like); over these the sides are raised in small and medium flat stones, evenly coursed and generally fair-faced. On the surface is a very diverse mass of stones including: numerous undecorated beach cobbles; several cross-inscribed beach cobbles, known as the 'Clocha Breaca' or cursing stones (SL001-001015-), a group of three plano-convex stones, one having a disc-shaped ‘stopper’ which rotates in a cavity on its top; and a tall, oblong block (SL001-001016-), on a tapered foot, which also has a ‘stopper’ on top, as well as cross-inscribed sides. In addition, the fragments of a cross slab with flabellum (SL001-001018-) were recorded by Wakeman on this leacht.

source_data.original_text:
This record refers to fifteen cross-carved, rounded stones or cobbles known as the ‘cursing stones’ or ‘clocha breacha’ (speckled stones). They are associated with a leacht (SL001-001013-) in an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL011-011001-), known as ‘The Cashel’ on Inishmurray Island. Eight are in situ on the island, four are in the National Museum together with a possible fifth (DU018-409----), one is in Alnwick Castle, and the location of one other is unknown. The spherical cobbles vary in size (diam. 0.12-0.41m) and bear a variety of incised designs; the more elaborate examples may date stylistically to between the period between the late 9th and 11th centuries.  
Use of cursing stones is recorded in an annotation on an early 17th-century map of Inishmurray, and reads as follows: ‘In this islande there dwelleth a holye man called Scanlon of whom the countrie people holde a superstitious opinion that if he be angry with any one and do turne the speckled stones upon them which he kepeth for that use they shall dye within that yeare.’  (Captain John Baxter’s ‘Map of the North-West Parte of Ireland’ (1603), in The Admiralty Library, Greenwich. Quoted in O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 23, plate 13). 

For a detailed description of these stones and associated rituals see:
Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.
pp. 105-110, 335-41.

source_data.original_text:
Located on top of a leacht (Sl001-001013-), in association with cross-carved cobbles, known as the ‘cursing stones’ or ‘clocha breacha’(SL001-001015-).
Cross-inscribed upright oblong block with tapering stem (H: 0.595 m, W: 0.255>0.07 m, Th: 0.125 m) and a hollow 0.11 m in diameter in its upper surface. A stone disc with a diameter of 0.24 m has a hemispherical projection on the underside that is fitted into this hollow. The south face is filled with an incised shafted cross (c.0.27 m by 0.2 m) with a lozenge-shaped expansion at the crossing, whose upper arms terminate in large concave-sided squares. Each of the upper quadrants is decorated with a diagonally disposed cross, while each of the lower quadrants is decorated with a vertically-disposed cross with cusped serif terminals whose lower arms turn inwards at their base, apparently to join the shaft of the principal cross. At the base of the lower left quadrant is a linear stepped border. Each of the narrow sides is filled with an incised shafted cross (0.19 m by 0.1 m) with cusped serif terminals and a false-relief hollowed boss at the crossing.

source_data.original_text:
Located within an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL001-001001-), 4m N of Templemolaise church (SL001-001009-).
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership. Pillar stone (H: <1.32 m, W: 0.34 m, Th: 0.126 m) inscribed on its west face with a shafted cross (0.732 m by 0.246 m). It is formed from a primary incised cross with serifed terminals in the upper arms, encapsulated within an outline cross, with which it fuses at the terminals. The upper arms terminate in outward curling flourishes while the shaft terminates in a simpler expansion bisected by an incised vertical element. Midway along the shaft of the outline cross is a very worn expansion. In each of the narrow sides, at roughly the height of the cross arms, is a vertically orientated oblong hole (c. 0.12 m by 0.25 m and 0.06 m deep). These are linked with two smaller holes (c. 25 mm in diameter) incised into the back of the pillar. In recent times, the holes were the focus of rituals relating to child-bearing and fertility (Wakeman 1886; 1893; Mountbatten 1972; McGowan 1998). Originally, however, the holes in the narrow sides probably held wooden arms secured with nails driven through the smaller holes at the back of the pillar.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
In an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL001-001001-) known as ‘the Cashel’. The graveyard extends across the central and eastern part of the cashel, and is bounded to N, W and S by walls which form internal subdivisions within the Cashel. It is traditionally known as ‘the Men’s Cemetery’.
Grave markers occur throughout the open area surrounding Templemolaise (SL001-001009-). There are 180–200 visible grave markers (it is impossible to say how many of the smaller prone slabs were originally erected as headstones). These take various forms, including several early carved slabs and pillars (with crosses or memorial inscriptions), cist-like arrangements of edge-set slabs or ceallunach graves, modern plinthed crosses with memorial inscriptions and, most commonly, low, rough, unmarked sandstone headstones set upright in the turf. Most of these grave markers occur in the open area between Templemolaise (SL001-001009-) and the much smaller church known as Teach Molaise (SL001-001005-). The importance of the latter – the purported founder’s tomb shrine – is indicated by the concentration of early inscribed stones and cross slabs lying immediately adjacent to it. Other notable, though smaller concentrations occur by the south wall of Templemolaise and around the Clocha Breaca leacht (SL001-001013-). Both the early slabs by Teach Molaise and the many plain, low headstones form rows on a north/south alignment (indicating west/east grave orientation). Thus, in broad terms, the orientation and limits of the cemetery accord with the north/south boundary formed by the western enclosure [subdivision] and the east/west boundary formed by the northern enclosure [subdivision]. In contrast, grave markers peter out towards the southern enclosure [subdivision]. Significantly, perhaps, this was probably reserved for burials of the Waters family (Mountbatten 1972, 50) and may be an entirely modern construction.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 16 January 2018

source_data.original_text:
This holy well, named ‘Tober Molaise’ on the 1912 OS 6-inch map, is located immediately to E of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL001-001001-) known as the ‘Cashel’.
The well today is as described by Wakeman (1893, 124): ‘There are two holy wells on Inishmurray – one of which stands outside the Cashel, near the Water-gate, to which portal it probably gives its name. It is dedicated to St Molaise, and is covered by a stone-roofed, bee-hive-shaped, mortarless structure, measuring, internally, seven feet by six [2.1m by 1.8m]. The doorway, a truly Cyclopean work, is six feet [1.8m] in height, three [0.9m] in breadth at the lintel, and four [1.2m] at the base. Five stone steps lead from this ope to the water, which is neither abundant nor palatable.’ Although the entrance is clear, much of this feature is heavily overgrown and partly obscured by abutting field walls and associated spreads of small rubble.

source_data.original_text:
Located in the ecclesiastical enclosure/cashel (SL001-001001-), to SE of Teach Molaise (SL001-001005-).
Rectangular recumbent slab (H: 1.26 m, W: 0.748 m, Th: 0.06 m) whose surface is filled with a plain rectangular outline border frame (W: 0.064<0.08 m), defined by two thin incised lines. At the central point of the base, this frame is decorated with a small skeuomorphic spike, tapering into a bulbous terminal (0.052 m across). The taper is formed from incised lines and is decorated with an incised outline triangle. The terminal is embellished with an upward-facing C-scroll-in false relief. The outer left-hand line of the frame does not extend to the edge of the slab, indicating that this corner was already missing when the design was carved. The inner line of the frame is broken briefly at the midpoint of the lower side. The frame surrounds a single-strand incised shafted cross (0.864 m by 0.476 m) decorated with an incised outline circle at the crossing which the arms abut. Each arm terminates in a semi-circle that abut the frame. The whole cross is embellished with an outline cross with arms 0.056<0.068 m wide.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
Brought to the Schoolhouse/OPW conservation store from Teach Molaise (SL001-001005-) in the Cashel (SL001-001001-) in 1989.
Small slab (H: 0.55 m, W: 0.245 m, Th: 0.025) with damaged motif, probably a cross, filling its upper two-thirds. The middle third has a thin incised border running along the edges of the slab. At their lowest point these lines both turn inwards and upwards at c. 45º until they meet on the slab axis. From this point two slightly irregular lines rise, diverging slowly until they reach the upper third of the slab, where a roughly horizontal line runs from the left of the two and joins with the slab border. These lines probably represent the shaft and left arm of a cross but above this the sculpture comprises a number of randomly placed irregular shapes and a few sub-circular hollows. There is an intermittent border along the top of the slab.
It would appear that this slab was rejected before it was finished, for a number of areas in the upper third which are flush with the surface of the slab would seem to preclude the possibility that the partial cross motif in the middle third was once complete.

source_data.original_text:
Brought to the Schoolhouse/OPW conservation store from Teach Molaise (SL001-001005-) in the Cashel (SL001-001001-) in 1989.
Slab (H: 0.89 m, W: 0.25 m, Th: 0.03 m) comprising two re-joined fragments. Its surface is filled with a shafted cross in false relief. This element divides into pairs of strands just before the crossing which intersect one another before passing into opposite flanking cross arms. The false relief also divides into strands at the terminals which, in the case of the horizontal arms, comprise simple Stafford knots. The upper and lower terminals are worn but were more complex. At the base the strands each loop twice around an independent element in the shape of a downward-facing ‘D’, before joining again and tapering to a point suggestive of a skeumorphic spike. In the upper right-hand quadrant is a short inscription: 
T[U/A][R] A [I/L/N/M] [  ].
One possible reading is ‘tarais’, an abbreviation of taraisse meaning trustworthy, faithful, worthy of confidence (DIL), though on balance the second letter is more likely to be ‘u’ than ‘a’.

Slab (H: 0.665 m, W: 0.465 m, Th: 0.06 m) with false relief ringed cross filling its upper two thirds. Slab (H: 0.49 m, W: 0.49 m, Th: 0.07 m) with cross whose shaft is formed from a wide false relief band from which two strands emerge forming a Y shape. It is decorated with an incised shafted cross (0.10 m by 0.04 m) with cusped serifs, which stands on its base. Brought to the Schoolhouse/OPW conservation store from Teach Molaise (SL001-001005-) in the Cashel (SL001-001001-) in 1989.
Slab (H: 0.676 m, W: 0.258 m, Th: 0.036 m) with cross filling upper portion of both faces.  On one side is a slightly shafted incised cross with expanded serifs that terminate in a pair of mirrored backed spirals. The upper terminal features an extra pair of spirals above these. The base of the shaft develops, below the spirals, into an incised skeuomorphic tapering spike that bisects an axially positioned rectilinear motif with a break at its base. This incised cross is embellished with an outline cross formed from pairs of false relief twisting strands (two turns in each vertical, a single in the horizontals) with Stafford knot terminals and a simple interweave at the crossing. In each quadrant is an incised circular pit. On the other face is a slightly shafted irregular incised cross with cusped serifs on the horizontal arms, a serif with mirrored downward facing loops on the upper arm and, near the base, a bulbous swelling that surrounds a false-relief dimpled boss before developing into a skeuomorphic spike. In each quadrant is an incised crosslet with cusped terminals.
The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

source_data.original_text:
This clochan is built into a raised terraced area in the NW quadrant of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL011-011001-), known as ‘The Cashel’. It abuts the E side of a clochan, named Torybrennel (SL001001003-).
This small cell is conjoined to the south face of the much larger Toorybrenell, but there is no direct access between them. It forms part of the terraced area. Internally, it is oblong on plan, with an east/west axis, rounded angles to the walls at the west end and square angles at the east end. The entrance is from the north, via a narrow passage running from the main passage through the terrace. An edge-set slab forms a sill stone; a large orthostat forms the right-hand door jamb (entering).  The walls are of drystone rubble and small slabs, well coursed to form vertical faces, though corbelled towards the roof, which is closed by large flat slabs. The internal dimensions are 1.7 m east/west by 1.1 m north/south; the roof slabs are 1.4 m over the floor. The doorway is less than 1 m high and 0.5 m wide. 
The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
Located within the W sector of the enclosing wall of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL011-011001-), known as ‘The Cashel’.
Within the western enclosure or subdivision of the Cashel, a low creepway gives access to large mural chamber built within the Cashel wall on the west side. The creepway is built with drystone rubble side walls, spanned by large lintel slabs. The narrow entrance is flanked by small orthostats, forming jambs. The creepway is over 3 m long; it expands to 0.9 m at its mid point, but narrows again to pass between two more orthostatic jambs giving access to a large, well-made chamber. This is rectangular on plan, with vertical walls formed by massive edge-set slabs and a corbelled roof, closed by large slabs. The chamber measures 1.5 m long by 1.3 m (east/west); the roof rises to 1.3 m over a floor of humic earth.

source_data.original_text:
This church, which is named ‘Templemurray or Templenaman’ (Mary’s Church or the Women’s Church, respectively) on the 1837 and 1912 OS 6-inch maps, is located 25m N of the shoreline on the SE side of Inishmurray island, and 85m SE of an early medieval ecclesiastical enclosure (SL001-001001-). The church stands within the N end of an oblong enclosure (SL001-002002-), which also encloses a graveyard (SL001-002007-). There are an inscribed stone (SL001-002005-) and a cross-slab (SL001-0020012-) within the church, and a bullaun stone (SL001-002004-) immediately outside the door.
This large rectilinear building is orientated east/west and measures 8.6 m long by 4 m wide, within walls 0.7 m thick. The walls are of mortared rubble construction, with large blocks roughly coursed. There is a plain doorway, internally splayed, midway in the south wall (this is now closed by a new barred & padlocked gate). An older doorway in the west gable is indicated by a large panel of secondary or inserted masonry. The east gable is pierced by a single window, broadly splayed, with external mouldings. This is flanked by narrow, plain, splayed windows – set directly over aumbries – in the east ends of the north and south walls. The footings of a stone altar can be seen against the east gable, beneath the window. There are four small grave markers – undecorated rough slabs – set upright within the floor. Otherwise, this is overspread with modern gravel. A cross-slab (SL001-002012-) rests against the north wall. 
The building now stands almost entire to the wall heads, but has clearly been substantially rebuilt and is heavily pointed throughout.  A mortar sample from the building yielded a calibrated radiocarbon date of AD 1320–1640 at two sigma probability (Berger 1995, 172).
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 16 January 2018

source_data.original_text:
Located on the shoreline on the SE side of Inishmurray island, 85m SE of an early medieval ecclesiastical enclosure (SL001-001001-). 
A well-made wall of mortared random rubble encloses the church (SL001-002001-), cemetery (SL001-002007-) and leacht (SL001-003001-) at Templenaman. The wall is 0.8 m wide and, variously, 0.9–1.3 m high. It is capped by a coping of roughly squared flat slabs. The enclosure thus formed is oblong on plan – 40 m long by 15 m wide – rounded in the north, but truncated in the south by cliff erosion (a low rubble wall of secondary build spans part of the cliff-edge, but even this is partly eroded). Thus, the enclosure was certainly longer once, but is receding before marine erosion at its south end. There is a gateway on the west side, with a large flat orthostat forming one jamb (SL001-002011-), and a rough stile at either side of the enclosure towards the south end. The wall appears on the first edition of the Ordnance Survey (1837) more or less as on later editions; despite this, it is probably of relatively modern construction.
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
This cross-inscribed pillar stands immediately outside the SW side of an enclosure (SL001-002002-), which contains Templenaman church (SL001-002001-) and a graveyard (SL001-002007-).
Pillar (H: <1.45 m, W: 0.29 m, Th: 0.11 m). W face has incised cross (0.52 m by 0.23 m) the lower arms of which terminate in wide triangular serifs while the serif of the upper arm terminates in three points separated by cusps. Beneath the lower arm the shaft extends a further 0.175 m before terminating with a triangular serif. In each of the lower quadrants is a small hole that links with a larger, vertically oriented oblong hole in each of the narrow sides (0.11 m by 0.06 m by 0.07 m). There is another small hole on the upper surface of the pillar. Below the cross on the W face are remnants of an inscription on two or possibly three vertical lines (0.69 m by 0.21 m). There appears to have been another shorter vertical inscription low down on the north side. High on the east face is an equal armed incised cross (0.195 m by 0.017 m) with wide triangular serifs. The holes in the narrow sides probably held wooden arms secured with nails driven through the smaller holes in the W face.
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
Located in an enclosure (SL001-002002-) on the SE shoreline of Inishmurray island, and 85m SE of an early medieval ecclesiastical enclosure (SL001-001001-). This graveyard is traditionally known as ‘The Women’s Cemetery’, and is associated with Templenaman, The women’s church (SL001-002001-). There is a leacht (SL001-003001-) within the S end of the graveyard.
Within the enclosure (SL001-002002-) grave markers occur throughout the area south of the women’s church (SL001-002001-), but particularly in the south and east of the enclosure. These take various forms, including several modern plinthed crosses, at least three cross slabs or cross-inscribed pillars (SL001-002008-; SL001-002012- & SL001-002013-), and an early inscribed memorial stone (SL001-002005-); but the commonest form is the unmarked, rough, sandstone slab erected to form a low headstone. There are at least 60 of these, including four within the church. They generally face east/west and are roughly aligned in rows (though this is less pronounced than in the Men’s Cemetery (SL001-001029-), at the Cashel (SL001-001001-)). There is a notable concentration of these towards the southern end of the cemetery and especially around the Crossatemple leacht (SL001-003001-).
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
Located close to an eroding shoreline cliff edge, at the SE end of the enclosure (SL001-002002-) which surrounds Templenaman church (SL001-002001-) and graveyard (SL001-002007-). 
This leacht is named ‘Crossatemple’ on the 1837 and 1912 OS 6-inch maps. It is a well-made rectilinear cairn of flat slabs and small rubble, measuring 2.4 m north/south by 1.6 m east/west and 0.8 m high. It is surmounted by an ornate cross slab (SL001-003002-) and also by several beach rolled cobbles, possibly ‘cursing stones’ (these are not decorated). Several small unmarked grave stones (sandstone slabs) cluster about the foot of the leacht on the south and east and some flat slabs lying within the turf on the south side may be a remnant of paving.
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.

source_data.original_text:
Located on Crossatemple leacht (SL001-003001-).
First recorded by Wood-Martin (1882, 150, no.5) and Wakeman (1886, 274–5, fig.49) in the men’s cemetery (SL001-001029-). By 1901 it had been moved to the Clocha Breaca leacht (SL001-001013-) where it was photographed (Heraughty 1982, 30). The date and circumstances of its removal to its present position are unknown.
Slab (H: <0.834 m, W: 0.396 m, Th: 0.064) whose upper two-thirds are filled with an incised slightly shafted central cross (0.495 m by 0.342 m) with a false relief dimpled boss at the crossing, and broad forked terminals. The tips of the lower terminal curve into an incised rectangular frame that surrounds the whole motif. In each quadrant is a crosslet similar to the main cross though lacking a boss and, between the crosslet and cross, a circular pit. In the case of the lower crosslets, the forked terminal tips of their outer arms join with the frame.
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
Recorded by Wakeman (1886, 317, fig. 75; 1893, 143, fig. 75) as mounted on the leacht (SL001-003001-) at Crossatemple (Station of Mary) but clearly not the slab (SL001-003002-) presently positioned there. Wakeman’s general sketch of the leacht suggests the slab protruded 0.6 m from the surface, was 0.3 m in width, and 0.05m thick. He says it has been 'sculpted with two crosses, but the carving on one side has become almost entirely obliterated by time and the growth of lichen - so much so that it is impossible to trace the design with any degree of certainty.' This implies that the cross on one face may have been reasonably well preserved, but he gives no details of its design. The whereabouts of this cross-slab are unknown.

source_data.original_text:
Located within the W half of an enclosure (SL001-004001-), on an eroding cliff face on the SE shoreline of Inishmurray Island.
This leacht is part of a complex of monuments, named ‘Relickoran’ on the 1837 and 1912 OS 6-inch maps, a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership. Subject to severe marine erosion, these monuments were archaeologically excavated (99E0381) over two seasons in 1999 and 2000; the results are described in detail in O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin (2008, 251-298). 
Prior to excavation, the leacht was intact on its north side and stood to four or five drystone courses (H c. 0.7m) of well-laid small rubble, but the southern half had largely collapsed. The uppermost part appeared to have been rebuilt in the modern era, but the excavation uncovered the original, square basal outline (1.9m N−S; 1.8m E−W) of the structure, which was faced with large, flat stones on the E and S, and with thinner, edge-set stones on the W and N. On the W side, the edge-set stones were incorporated into the kerb of a paved path, which formed a circuit of the enclosure (SL001-004001-); this suggests that the leacht and path were of a single build. The enclosure, leacht and paving were constructed on the site of an active burial ground, and burials continued within the enclosure for several centuries, with a particular concentration in the immediate vicinity of the leacht. Radiocarbon dating of the skeletal remains indicate that the leacht and its enclosure, as well as the adjoining enclosure (SL001-004007-), were built sometime between the early 8th century and the 12th century. (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 251-298).
Two cross slabs (SL001-004004-; SL001-004008-) once stood on this leacht; they are now in the Schoolhouse/OPW conservation storehouse. Following excavation, the leacht was reconstructed in its original position by the OPW in 2001.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 8 March 2018

source_data.original_text:
Located in an enclosure (SL001-004001-), on an eroding cliff face on the SE shoreline of Inishmurray Island. This burial ground is part of a complex of monuments, comprising two conjoined enclosures (SL001-004001-; SL001-004007-), two leachts (SL001-004002-; SL001-004006-), four cross-slabs (SL001-004004-; SL001-004008-; SL001-004009-; SL001-004010-) and a cross-inscribed pillar (SL001-004005-); it is named ‘Relickoran’ on the 1837 and 1912 OS 6-inch maps, and is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership. Subject to severe marine erosion, these monuments were archaeologically excavated (99E0381) over two seasons in 1999 and 2000; the results are described in detail in O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin (2008, 251-298). 
Prior to excavation, there was little evidence, other than the placename, ‘Relickoran’ (Reilig Ódhráin or Ódran’s cemetery), to indicate the presence of a burial ground. However, the excavation revealed that the burial ground was in fact the primary monument here, pre-dating the construction of the conjoined enclosures and their respective leachts.
The earliest graves, c. 20 in all, were oriented NE−SW. They underlay the E part of the larger enclosure (SL001-004001-), and extended to NE beyond the walls, indicating that they predated the construction of the enclosures. Although grave cuts were found, no skeletal remains survived, with the result that this earliest burial phase could not be dated precisely, but it may be contemporary with the earliest phase of monastic settlement on the island (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 293)
Later burials, c. 40 in total, were all oriented E−W. Skeletal remains were present, but poorly preserved. This reorganisation of the burial ground on an E−W orientation appears to have begun before the construction of the enclosures, as some E−W burials underlay the enclosure walls, leachts and paving. Radiocarbon dates, derived from skeletal material, suggest that the two enclosures, the leachts and the paved path in the larger enclosure were all constructed, in a single formal design, sometime after the early 8th century and before the 12th century. If the evidence of cross-slab style is taken into account, it may be possible to refine that estimate to the period between the late 9th to 11th centuries (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 297). After the burial ground was enclosed, it continued in use for several centuries. The burials were mostly confined to the larger enclosure (MA001-004001-), with a particular concentration focused on the leacht (SL001-004002-). Graves were laid out in well-ordered rows, though many of the early burials were disturbed or truncated by later insertions. The latest burials dated from the late 15th to early 17th centuries. 
There was little evidence for coffins or shrouds, but several white quartzite pebbles were recovered, which appeared to have been deliberately deposited in the graves. Some of the graves grouped around the leacht (SL001-004002-) were edged with cist-like stone settings, and had flat cover stones. Two small cross-slabs (SL001-004009-; SL001-004010-) found close to the leacht were probably grave markers.
The skeletal remains were fragmentary and in poor condition; no complete skeleton was recovered. Osteoarchaeological analysis of the remains determined that the burial ground was not segregated in any way, but used for the burial of a general population, male and female. It was possible to estimate the age at death of nine of the adult burials; none was over 40 years of age. A limited range of pathologies were noted, including degenerative joint disease, healed fracture and muscle strains, iron deficiency and spina bifida occulta, as well as various dental conditions, such as abscesses and caries.
Relikoran may have been established as a satellite burial ground for laity not long after the monastery (SL001-001001-) was founded on Inishmurray, and continued in use to the mid-17th century. O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin (2008, 293-97) emphasise that it is a unique example of an excavated satellite burial ground with a surviving suite of features that represents a single design of medieval date. Furthermore, its dedication to St. Odrán, a follower of St Columba of Iona, may have conferred a special spiritual benefit to burial at Relickoran. They speculate that ‘it may have been the burial place of an elite group, possibly patrons of the monastery or kin to its abbots, or indeed both.’
(O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 161-169; 251-298)

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 8 March 2018

source_data.original_text:
Located within an enclosure (SL001-004007-), on an eroding cliff face on the SE shoreline of Inishmurray Island.
This leacht is part of a complex of monuments, named ‘Relickoran’ on the 1837 and 1912 OS 6-inch maps, a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership. Subject to severe marine erosion, these monuments were archaeologically excavated (99E0381) over two seasons in 1999 and 2000; the results are described in detail in O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin (2008, 251-298).
Prior to the excavation, the leacht stood only 0.7 m from the eroding cliff-edge. The N half (1.95m E−W; 1.3m N−S) of the original rectangular drystone structure remained, but the S half had collapsed into the sea. It was built of massive stone blocks, well laid to form regular faces on all sides, with a core of small rubble. There were two large, edge-set flat stones at the base of the N side. There was a plain slab erected within the surface of the leacht. This may once have been inscribed, but is not recorded as a cross slab by Wakeman or other authorities.
The excavation revealed that the leacht and its enclosure (SL001-004007-), as well as the adjoining enclosure (SL001-004001-), were built sometime between the early 8th century and the 12th century on a pre-existing burial ground (SL001-004003-).
Following excavation, the leacht was reconstructed in by the OPW at a safer distance from the cliff edge. (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 251-298).

source_data.original_text:
Located on an eroding cliff face on the SE shoreline of Inishmurray Island, this small enclosure is conjoined to the E side of a larger enclosure (SL001-004001-), and is part of complex of monuments named ‘Relickoran’ on the 1837 and 1912 OS 6-inch maps. It encloses a leacht (SL001-004006-). It is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.
As it was subject to severe marine erosion, the enclosure was fully excavated (99E0381) over two seasons in 1999 and 2000; the results are described in detail in O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin (2008, 251-298). Following the excavation, the enclosure and its leacht were reconstructed by the OPW using the original rubble masonry, but set back at a safer distance from the eroding cliff edge.
Prior to excavation, this rectangular enclosure (4m E−W; 3m N−S) was defined at N and E by collapsed drystone walls, evident as banks of stone rubble (Wth c. 2.5). At W it shared the E wall of the larger enclosure (SL001-004001-), and a simple stile in this wall allowed access between the two enclosures. The sea had destroyed the enclosing wall on the S side at the cliff edge.
The excavation revealed that the two enclosures, and their respective leachts, were built sometime between the early 8th century and the 12th century. They were built on a pre-existing burial ground (SL001-004003-), and burials continued in the larger enclosure (SL001-004001-) until the early post-medieval period.
The leacht (SL001-004006-) in this, the smaller enclosure overlay two graves. A bone sample from a male skeleton in one of the graves, produced a radiocarbon date to the period between late 9th-century to mid- 12th century, and skull fragments, found scattered among stones at the base of the leacht, were dated to the period between early 11th-century to early 13th century. 
After burials ceased, the enclosures and leachts remained the focus for devotional activity, and there is evidence that the enclosure walls and the leachts were repaired or partly rebuilt on several occasion during the modern period. (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 251-298).

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 8 March 2018

source_data.original_text:
Found in Relickoran cemetery (SL001-004003-) during excavation in August 1999, one of two cross-slabs (see also SL001-004010-) located in superficial rubble spreads on the S side of a leacht (SL001-004002-). Now in the Schoolhouse/OPW conservation store.
Worn, slightly tapering slab fragment (H: 0.285 m, W: 0.165 m, Th: 0.047 m) with incised shafted cross the base of which is missing. At the surviving upper terminal the line bifurcates to encircle a false relief boss. The vertical arms divide again at the crossing to delimit a single element in false relief which forms the horizontal arms. This element features a slight expansion at the crossing decorated with a dimple, and it had slightly bulbous terminals. The quadrants were probably each decorated with an incised cross with modest rounded terminals surrounded by a rectangular frame with rounded corners. In the surviving upper right quadrant the frame respects the horizontal arms of the cross, breaking into two U-shaped elements rather than fusing with the arm terminals. 

The above description is derived from the results of a programme of survey and excavation undertaken in 1997-2000 on Inishmurray and published in:

source_data.original_text:
Located on a low eroding cliff-edge, immediately to NE of Clashymore Harbour, on the S side of Inishmurray Island. This small enclosure (SL001-005001-) encloses a leacht (SL001-005002-), traditionally known as Ollamurray. These monuments were subjected to severe ongoing erosion/storm damage; in 2000 they were fully excavated (00E0484), and then reconstructed in 2001 by the OPW at a safer distance from the cliff-edge (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin  2008, 298-313). 
Prior to excavation, the enclosure was evident as a rectangular area (6.2m E−W; 5.7m N−S) enclosed on the W, N and E sides by a collapsed drystone rubble wall (Wth 1m; H 0.5m). The wall on the S side had largely been destroyed by erosion at the receding cliff edge, and only a small rubble mound remained there (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin  2008, 169-170; 298). Excavation revealed that the upper part of the enclosing wall consisted of roughly mounded angular rubble and represented episodes of rebuilding, the latest incidences of which probably took place in the 19th century or later. However, beneath this, the primary basal level of the wall survived. It consisted of an outer face of edge-set flat angular stones, up to 0.4m high, containing a core of smaller rubble and dark peaty soil. A roughly laid paving of large, irregular flat slabs covered the space between the central leacht (SL001-005002-) and the enclosing walls, but this appears to have been a relatively late feature. (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin  2008, 302-7). Radiocarbon analysis of charcoal, from a layer underlying the enclosure wall and the leacht, produced a calibrated date range of late eighth to late 10th centuries, providing a terminus post quem for the construction of the enclosure (ibid. 312).
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 19 February 2018

source_data.original_text:
Located on a low eroding cliff-edge, immediately to NE of Clashymore Harbour, on the S side of Inishmurray Island. This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.
This leacht is traditionally known as Ollamurray (Ulaidh Mhuire or ‘Mary’s Altar [or Cairn]’). It is centrally located within a small stone-built enclosure (SL001-005001-). These monuments were subjected to severe ongoing erosion/storm damage; in 2000 they were fully excavated (00E0484), and then reconstructed in 2001 by the OPW at a safer distance from the cliff-edge (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin  2008, 298-313). 
Prior to excavation, the leacht appeared as a roughly square drystone structure, with the S side reduced by storm damage to a spread of random rubble (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 170; 298). The excavation revealed the primary basal outline (c. 1.8m E−W; c. 1.4m N−S), which consisted of an outer facing of edge-set stones, which enclosed a core of close-set rounded beach cobbles and angular blocks (ibid, 304). This use of flat, edge-set stones is a notable construction feature of the leacht. The technique was also used in the construction of other Inishmurray leachts (e.g. SL001-001013-; SL001-004002-; SL001-007002-; SL001-013003-). The excavators conclude: ‘An inescapable inference is that all of these leachta were built to a common design, probably at the same time, and under supervision of one individual.’ (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin  2008, 313).
A cross-slab (SL001-005003-) may once have stood on this leacht.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
Located on a low eroding cliff-edge, overlooking the NE end of Clashymore Harbour, on the S side of Inishmurray Island.
An excavation (00E0484) in 2000 at Ollamurray enclosure (SL001-005001-) and leacht (SL001-005002-) uncovered evidence for a phase of prehistoric activity at this location (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin  2008, 298-313). A small assemblage of worked flint/chert was recovered from a soil horizon which pre-dated the construction of the enclosure and leacht. The assemblage included fragments of tools, as well as debitage or waste flakes. A single fragment of a barbed-and-tanged flint arrowhead is probably of Bronze Age date. Also at this level were two pits (Wth c. 0.7m; D c. 0.8m), exposed in section in the eroding cliff face. The excavators concluded that, while these finds 'may simply represent transitory use of the site for fishing or seal hunting, the presence of debitage suggest more than a passing presence and the two pits recorded in the cliff face may be vestiges of a shelter, campsite, house or even enclosure.’ (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 313).

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
This possible promontory fort was first noted by Casey (1999, 90-1) who described it as follows:
‘A previously unnoted promontory fort lies on a narrow west-facing peninsula at the extreme southwestern end of Inishmurray. The surrounding land consists of gently rolling open poor quality pasture and bog, with traces of old cultivation ridges visible nearby. Low but sheer cliffs surround the headland on three sides. Faint traces of two slightly curving earthen banks and two fosses crossing the neck of the headland are visible from the air. The triangular interior measures approximately 20.5m long and 10.5m wide at the bank, reducing to 4m wide at the western extremity. The bank is of earth and stands 20cm high and measures 3.1m wide at the base. A band of darker vegetation running along the outside suggests the former presence of an external fosse, the second bank and fosse cannot be seen on the ground. The interior is flat, level and featureless.’
Following a survey of the archaeology of the island in 1997-99, O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin (2008, 172) recorded this monument as follows: A possible promontory fort is recorded by the SMR files on this narrow, eroding headland. There is a remnant of a low grassy bank (0.3 m high) on the neck of the promontory, but this is a slight feature, demarcating only a small area (c. 40 sq m) and no ditch or occupation strata appear in the eroding cliff section at either side.  No significant evidence of a promontory fort exists on the site. Heraughty (1982, 19) is probably right in ascribing any earthwork remnants on this site to agricultural enclosures.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 18 August 2017

source_data.original_text:
On an eroding cliff edge at the most westerly point on Inishmurray, incorporated into NE angle of a later square, stone-built enclosure (SL001-007007-). 
This small subcircular building or cell (diam. c. 1.8m), with walls (Wth c. 0.8m) of drystone construction, was known traditionally as Trahanareear (Trahan na Righ-fhear or Trahan na Riair or Trahan na Rí-Ghear or Trahan Ó Riain), and also ‘Breadserve’. It has been interpreted as a hermitage, which ‘provided shelter and seclusion for fasting, prayer and penance’ for individual monks at an isolated location away from the bustle of the main monastic complex (SL001-001001-) (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 237).
In the 1990’s it was found to be in a state of collapse -the western part had already succumbed to the eroding cliff- and in 1997 it was fully excavated (licence: 97E0256) in advance of its reconstruction by the OPW at its current location at a safe distance from the cliff edge. The excavators concluded that: ‘in its primary phase, the monument appears to have consisted only of the cell and – immediately before it – a small area of paving which supported an upright timber. Large, undressed stones formed the inner and outer wall faces of the cell. The wall core consisted of medium and large stones in alternating radial and segmental courses (i.e. the stones of each course were all laid either along or across the wall line, so that the wall core formed a compact lattice of large stones). The terminals at either side of an east-facing entrance were formed by small orthostats, which flanked a narrow doorway 0.45 m wide. Most of the primary structure had already fallen into the sea, but the wall remnants could be projected to form a subcircular plan, 1.8 m in diameter, within walls 0.8 m thick. The cell contained deeply stratified layers of mottled sand, but no clearly anthropogenic material (i.e. charcoal, midden material or artefacts) was observed. Unfortunately, from the surviving remnants, one cannot say for certain whether the walls of this building were raised in corbelled courses, like the ‘beehive’ cells within the monastic enclosure (MA001-001001-), or whether it simply consisted of low stone walls with a roof of turf or thatch. The relatively thin walls suggest that the latter is more likely.’ (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 218-219).
The small area of paving (max. dim. c. 2m), located outside the cell, c. 1m E of the entrance, incorporated at its centre a stone-packed post-hole, designed to take an upright timber post (diam. c. 0.2m), most likely a support for a wooden table altar (ibid, 236). At a later date, this was replaced by a stone altar or leacht (SL001-007002-), which was built directly above the stone setting/post hole, and a stone path was laid leading from the N side of the leacht to the doorway of the cell.
Later again, probably in the 17th century, the square enclosure (SL001-007007-) was built to surround the hermitage and the leacht. The excavation found that the hermitage, the leacht and the enclosing wall had all been subjected to successive episodes of rebuilding in the modern period. A cross-slab (SL001-007008-), found in the entrance to the hermitage, appears to have been used to rebuild the doorway in one such reconstruction event (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 227).

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 23 January 2018

source_data.original_text:
Located on a cliff-edge, abutting a hermitage (SL001-007001-), and enclosing a leacht (SL001-007002-), with another possible leacht (SL001-00700) 2m to S. 
This small complex of monuments was subject to erosion and in danger of collapse at the eroding cliff edge; it was fully excavated (licence: 97E0256) in 1997 in advance of reconstruction by the OPW at a safe distance from the cliff-edge (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 216-239).
Prior to excavation, the small square enclosure (4.1m N−S; 4m E−W), defined by a drystone wall (Wth 0.65-1m; H 0.65-0.8m), with an entrance gap (Wth 0.5m) on the S side, was ‘still partly upstanding but with some loss to erosion on the western or seaward side.’ (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 177, 226). The excavation revealed that the enclosure post-dated the hermitage (SL001-007001-) and the leacht (SL001-007002-), and that the enclosing wall had undergone successive episodes of rebuilding, summarised by O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin (2008, 177, 226) as follows: ‘The upper part was of loosely arranged random rubble, but on dismantling the wall, the lower or basal courses were found to consist of more regular stones, laid in even courses, which formed inner and outer faces with a core of small rubble chips and loose sand. A narrow, south-facing opening in the wall was flanked by low orthostats or jambs. A fragment of a small, green glass vessel with everted rim was found within the base of the wall core at the north side; further fragments were found within an adjacent peaty loam deposit at the foot of the inner wall face. The glass bottle fragments are remains of a late 17th-century apothecary’s bottle and attest that the enclosure – and possibly the leacht – was rebuilt in the early modern period.’

Date of upload: 25 January 2018

This inscribed stone was discovered in 1997 during an archaeological excavation at a small complex of monuments, known as Trahanareear, which includes a hermitage (SL001-007001-), leacht (SL001-007002-) and an enclosure (SL001-007007-). The stone was found lying in shallow peat against the base of a possible leacht (SL001-007004-) located 2m S of the enclosure. Following the excavation it was moved to the Schoolhouse/OPW conservation store (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin 2008, 227).
It was described by O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin (ibid. 177) as follows: ‘Roughly dressed rectangular slab (H: 0.732 m, W: 0.405 m, Th: 0.04 m). Positioned in the upper left area appear three capital letters – J A W – and directly above them is a small incised cross. 
The letter forms and context of this stone indicate that it is of fairly recent date. It may commemorate John Andrew Waters, a notable character among Inishmurray's last generation of inhabitants and a brother of Michael Waters, the island's last 'King' (pers. comm. Mr Rodney Lomax, Mullaghmore).’

At its apex the upper arm expands markedly in a semi-circular shape, terminating in three points separated by steep cusps. The other arms have irregular forked terminals with cusped butts. source_data.original_text:
In a low-lying position in a peaty wet flush by the north shore at the NW end of Inishmurray. This leacht is not indicated on the 1837 OS 6-inch map, but is named ‘Laghtnasaggart’ (Leacht na Sagart or ‘The Priests’ Leacht’) on the 1912 edition.
Scarcely anything remains of this obscure site which is almost entirely destroyed by storm damage/marine erosion. Within low moorland grasses, two small orthostatic flags stand 3 m apart and are, respectively, 3 m and 7 m from the shore. Small angular rubble is scattered widely. Some of this is storm rubble; but some of the smaller stones are washing out of meandering rivulets from the peaty flush. The monument was in no better shape when seen by Wakeman (1893, 137), who recorded ‘a little inland from the brink of the cliff, a very slight grassy elevation, through which a few bleached stones appear, is styled by the natives Leacht-na-Sagart.’ Evidently the monument has been denuded for well over a hundred years. A short segment of low drystone walling to the west, immediately on the cliff edge, is probably a kelp-drying wall.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Located on moorland overlooking northerly cliffs on Inishmurray. 
Indicated on the 1837 and 1912 OS 6-inch maps, where it is named ‘Crossmore’ (Leachta Croise Móire or Cros Mhór, ‘Great Cross’). The leacht is a roughly built pile of drystone rubble measuring 2 m (east/west) by 1.8 m by 0.55 m high. Many of the stones are laid flat, as if once laid in even courses, but the whole effect now is uneven and even a little unstable. The leacht stands within a drystone enclosure (SL001-009003-). The roughly coursed stonework, but absence of peripheral rubble, suggests the monument has been intermittently rebuilt.

source_data.original_text:
Located in enclosed pasture overlooking northerly cliffs on Inishmurray. Indicated on the 1837 and 1912 OS 6-inch maps, where it is named ‘Trahanee’. 
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership. The main feature at this site is a small drystone enclosure (SL001-010001-) –this may possibly be the remnants of a cell or clochaun – surrounded by a low circular bank (SL001-010002-). There is a quarry pit (SL001-010004-) adjacent to the monument. This group of features overlooks a holy well (SL001-010004-) that lies below a sharp break in slope defined by outcropping bedrock. There is no associated cross slab.
This small, angular enclosure (SL001-010001-) is of random rubble construction. The wall terminals expand at either side of a narrow entrance break in the south. The corners at north-west and north-east are rounded externally but, overall, the internal plan is angular, almost square. The enclosure is 2 m wide within walls 1.5 m wide at the base and up to 1.2 m high. The loose, vacuous, rubble construction of this enclosure could not have persisted from antiquity; it has probably been repeatedly re-built.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Surrounding an enclosure (SL001-010001-), named Trahanee’ on the on the 1837 and 1912 OS 6-inch maps, in enclosed pasture overlooking northerly cliffs on Inishmurray.
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership. Outwith the drystone wall of an enclosure (SL001-010001-) is a second enclosing element. A low bank – 1.8 m wide and 0.3 m high – surrounds the drystone wall. The overall diameter of the bank is 9 m. There is no visible break, but the bank is more pronounced on the north side. There is a quarry pit (SL001-010005-) immediately to W, and a holy well (SL001-010004-) 15m downslope to N.

Close to Trahanee enclosure (SL001-010001-). Wakeman (1893, 137) recorded this structure, now vanished, as follows: ‘At a short distance from it [i.e. Trahanee] stands an altar ... but the name of the saint to whom it was dedicated has not been retained, and the pile is simply called Altóir, ‘altar’. It is square in plan, seventeen feet eight inches [5.4m] in girth at the ground, and still exhibits a finial, consisting of a rude flagstone devoid of cross or carving on any kind set upright on its summit.’ 
This was not seen by the survey team in 1998. Wakeman may have printed a false account from a misreading of his field notes. It is more likely that this once existed and is now dispersed.

source_data.original_text:
Located 15 m north of an enclosure (SL001-010001-), below a sharp break in slope. This holy well is named ‘Tobernacoragh’ (Tobar na Corach or ‘Well of the Fair Wind’) on the 1837 and 1912 OS 6-inch maps.
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership. A small and rather disorderly heap of stones (2 m east/west by 3 m north/south, overall) surrounds a small wet hollow (no standing water in August 1998) with an irregular, narrow outflow channel winding seaward through long grass and weeds. The mound supports a couple of large slabs which span the wet hollow and are evidently remnants of a lintelled roof.
Wakeman depicted this as a small corbelled structure and his accompanying description indicates that it was once less dilapidated and more free-flowing (1893, 124): ‘It is protected by a building, of the bee-hive class, formed of large stones laid without mortar. From it extends, northward, a kind of stone-lined channel, flagged over at its ends, and having an open space at its centre. This channel, which seems to have been excavated through clay and rock to a depth of about two feet six inches [0.76m] below the natural surface, is twenty feet [6m] in length ... A scarcely-ever-ceasing flow of bright sparkling water passes from the well through the channel.’
The stones no longer comprise an immediately recognisable structure. The well is partly choked with weeds and grass, including dead vegetation. Folk traditions associated with the well are recounted by various authorities and include a ritual to calm stormy seas.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.
