source_data.original_text:
Located at Rue or Rubha point, at the east end of the Inishmurray. Indicated on the OS 6-inch maps as ‘Laghta Patrick’ (Leachta Phádraig). Also known as ‘Leachta Cuimhne’.
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.
Various authorities describe a leacht and cross (SL001-011002-) at this site, but the monument was destroyed by storm damage and the cross is lost or stolen (i.e. it could not be located in the field in 1998–99 or by subsequent inquiry). 
By the time of the survey of 1998, the upstanding part of the structure was entirely dispersed. In the immediate environs, small and medium rubble overspreads a flat grassy expanse of 30 m (north/south) by 16 m (east/west). Much of this is probably storm rubble. Some may be remnants of kelp-drying walls. There was no visible, upstanding feature obviously corresponding to the remains of a leacht and no cross slab. This is in startling contrast to early descriptions and even some more recent ones (following). Compare, for instance, O’Donovan (1836 'Sligo Letters' OS Letters, no. 36. Royal Irish Academy) – ‘The leachta is a square pile of stones, on the top of which an ornamental stone cross stands’ – with Herity (1989a [1995b, 115]) – ‘The base of a very ruined dry-built leacht, roughly rectilinear in plan, about 1.92 m by 2.3 m, with no cross slab’. Thus, while O’Donovan could describe a leacht and cross-slab in the 1830s, the monument had been reduced to a ruinous heap by the 1980s and had disappeared from view entirely by the 1990s. Despite this, it was possible to identify the base of the leacht by means of a very limited archaeological investigation [99E0382] in 1999. The base consisted of a setting (2.6m E−W; 2.4m N−S) of stones, roughly trapezoidal in plan, defined by a rough kerb of large and medium-sized stones (O’Sullivan and Ó Carragáin  2008, 239-241). 
The leacht was reconstructed on site by the excavators in 2006.

The above description is derived from the results of a programme of survey and excavation undertaken in 1997-2000 on Inishmurray and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Date of upload: 23 January 2018

Only a few small cavities or hollows in the turf were found on the alleged site of this well; even these may have been no more than collapsed rabbit holes. Located 270m to SE of an ecclesiastical enclosure/cashel (SL001-001001-), over cliffs.
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership. Drystone rubble walls form an enclosure which measures 4.5 m east/west by 3.5 m north/south within walls up to 1 m thick and 1.4 m high on the south or seaward slope, but 0.8 m high elsewhere. The walls include frequent small flat slabs and are roughly coursed to produce a sound build with a fair-faced finish. There is a narrow entrance on the west side (facing Treenode Beg leacht (SL001-014001-) 0.7 m wide; this is spanned by an edge-set sill at the inner wall face. 
There is a leacht (SL001-013003-), known as Treenode More, and cross slab (SL001-013002-) within this enclosure. Another leacht (SL001-014001-) is located outside the enclosure, a few meters to W.

source_data.original_text:
Erected on a leacht (SL001-013003-), known as Treenode More, within an enclosure (SL001-013001-).
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership. Slab (H: <0.873 m, W: 0.456 m, Th: 0.126 m) whose visible surface is filled with a slightly irregular central cross (0.769 m by 0.366 m) surrounded by four crosslets. The lower two crosslets develop from a horizontal bar that forms the base of the main cross, while the slightly smaller upper crosslets develop from points midway along its horizontal arms. All of the crosses are shafted with flat, or in a few cases slightly cusped-butted, serifs in the upper arms. The crossing of the main cross is decorated with a false relief dimpled boss.

Traditionally known as Treenode More (Tríonóid Mór or ‘Great Trinity [Leacht]’), this leacht stands centrally within the enclosure and is a well-made rectilinear cairn of evenly course flat stones, brought to a fair finish  on all sides and a flat upper surface. Another leacht (SL001-014001-), known as Treenode Beg, is located outside the enclosure, a few meters to W.

source_data.original_text:
At a junction of field dykes on a low hill north-east of the Cashel/ecclesiastical enclosure (SL001-001001-).
The Ordance Survey maps of 1837 and 1912 indicate an ‘altar’ located at the junction of massive drystone field dykes that are now entirely overgrown by tall bracken. Nothing was found by the 1998 survey team or by Markus Casey, for the Archaeological Survey of Ireland, in 1994. The leacht may in fact have been incorporated within the later stone dykes, although it was evidently free-standing when seen by Wakeman (1893, 155): ‘All has been described except one small altar, situated to the north-east of the Cashel, about midway between it and Teernaneane on the brink of the Atlantic. The pile is now nameless, and as the stones of which it composed are much disturbed, further description of the ruin will not be necessary.’ 
Although nothing can now be found, the location is of some interest as it lies on a low inland rise or summit and is, therefore, on a horizon line viewed from the Cashel. Thus, from that viewpoint, it appears to continue the circuit of leachta which otherwise occur nearer the cliff edges.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
Located on a leacht, known as Laghta Columbkille. This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.
Slab (H: 0.915 m, W: 0.416 m, Th: 0.08 m) with rectangular frame defined by an incised line. Rising from its lower edge is an incised cross (0.54 m by 0.262 m) whose upper arms terminate in broad cusped-butted serifs. In each quadrant is a subordinate rectangular border arranged symmetrically so that they double as an outline cross around the main motif. In the lower quadrants these frames terminate short of the baseline with a clubbed serif and each surrounds a smaller version of the main cross motif. The frames in the upper quadrants each contain a smaller rectangle which in turn contains a stepped motif. On the opposite face is an incised cross (0.485 m by 0.28 m) with forked serifs, a false relief boss at the crossing and a small circular pit in each quadrant.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

source_data.original_text:
Located immediately west of Clashymore harbor on the S side of Inishmurray.
Edge-set slabs within a deep grassy hollow probably correspond to the site of a cist found in 1938 and described by Heraughty (1982, 17). The hollow is 2 m deep on the west side, but only 0.6 m on the east, where it overlooks the wave-cut rock terraces of Clashymore. Within the hollow, large, flat, edge-set slabs form the north and east sides of what may once have been a lintelled short cist. The site was examined by E Estyn Evans who was satisfied that it was a later prehistoric funerary cist; the whereabouts of an associated urn or food vessel are now unknown.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1998-2000 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Located in open moorland on the NW side of Inishmurray. An extensive rubble spread or low cairn lies on gently sloping moorland north of the Cashel (SL001-001001-) (the two are intervisible). The rubble spreads over an area of about 15 m east/west by 13 m north/south and is no more than 0.5 m high. On the south and east margin are short lengths of drystone walling, evidently secondary features (possibly remains of livestock pens or shelters). A few small slabs are erected or edge-set within the north-west quadrant and may be remains of an entranceway to a structure. The monument is of unknown date or type, but may be the remains of a medieval structure, a ‘lost’ leacht or even a building.

source_data.original_text:
At the outfall of Inishmurray's only stream, located immediately to E of the Templenaman graveyard (SL001-002007-), and 115m SE of an ecclesiastical enclosure (SL001-001001-).
This is a National Monument (no. 117) in state ownership.
Drystone walls retain the banks of the island’s only watercourse at its outfall to the sea. The walls form three sides of a pit (2.8 m north/south by 2.1 m; 1.3 m high) with a breached, or wave-eroded outer side. Exploratory investigation [099E0381] in 1999 confirmed that the masonry observed in 1998 represents vestigial remains of a mill undercroft but could find no dating evidence or suitable sample for radiocarbon dating. A large land parcel east of this is identified by Heraughty’s (1982, 76) placename map as Fál an Mhuilinn (literally ‘millbank’ or ‘millgreen’). A millstone, possibly from this mill, is now located in Templenatinny church (SL001-001011-) in the ecclesiastical enclosure (SL001-001001-).

The above description is derived from the results of a programme of survey and excavation undertaken in 1997-2000 on Inishmurray and published in:

In cliff face east of Women’s Cemetery (SL001-002007-). At 10 m east of the mill (SL001-022001-), two or three courses of large boulders form an arc of drystone masonry – 3 m wide and less than 1 m high – within steeply banked ground, immediately below the low cliff edge. Above the cliff edge, the ground is uneven and pitted by subsidence or burrowing. When first observed the masonry was thought to represent the remains of a largely eroded kiln, built into the low cliff face, and associated with the adjacent mill (SL001-022001-). Subsequent investigation in 1999 discovered that it was merely part of a low revetment wall retaining cultivated soils (O’Sullivan 2000). A sherd of 17th-century gravel-tempered ware, found during a limited excavation at the site, provides a terminus post quem date for construction of this retaining wall.

The above description is derived from the results of a programme of survey and excavation undertaken in 1997-2000 on Inishmurray and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

source_data.original_text:
In the eastern and southern quadrants of the island, later editions of the Ordnance Survey (e.g. 1912) record drystone walls enclosing a regular system of small rectangular fields. These were evidently a product of the planned re-settlement of the island in the 19th century as it matured and prospered. These new dykes replaced an older field system of irregular land parcels which is recorded by the first edition of the Ordnance Survey (1837) and is also concentrated in the south and east. On the margins of this are relics of other early banks – not recorded by the Ordnance Survey – which meander west and north over the otherwise open moorland. At several intervals the older banks are slighted or traversed by later stone dykes. The older field system is generally represented by low banks, up to 2 m wide but seldom more than 0.3 m high, and occasionally faced with large stones. In some instances, only intermittent lines of large stones survive, with no embanked soil present.

The above description is derived from the results of a survey of the archaeological monuments on Inishmurray undertaken in 1997-1999 and published in:

Jerry O’Sullivan and Tomás Ó Carragáin  2008  Inishmurrary. Monks and pilgrims in an Atlantic landscape. Volume 1: Archaeological Survey and Excavations 1997-2000. Cork. The Collins Press.

Not marked as an antiquity on the 1837 edition of the OS 6-inch map. At the outer lip of the fosse is a second bank (Wth. 3m; H 0.5m). A modern stone wall divides the enclosed area from the banks and fosse. The OS Letters (1837, 174) record that this monument was called 'Dún Balra'.

source_data.original_text:
Located in the interior of an enclosure (SL002-014004-), adjacent to a holy well (SL002-014001-). 
This cross-inscribed pillar consists of a roughly rectangular sandstone block (H 0.85m; Wth 0.28m; T 0.17m at base). The outline of a Latin cross (H 0.46m; Wth across arms 0.18m) is incised on one smooth broad face of the stone, occupying over half the available space on the stone surface. At the junction of the arms and the shaft, there is a central circle (diam. 0.025m) defined by an incised line and enclosed by two outer incised rings (outer diam. 0.075m). The short arms extend 0.05m on either side of the concentric circles, and their engraved outline each encloses a square panel filled with two incised diagonal crossed lines or ‘X’. Each ‘X’ fills the entire available space, from corner to corner of its panel. This ‘X’ motif is also found on the long, lower portion of the shaft (H 0.28m; Wth 0.10-0.12m) which is divided by incised transverse lines into three panels. The uppermost, smallest panel is blank. Below that is a larger, rectangular panel within which there are two incised ‘X’s, one above the other. The upper ‘X’ is larger and more elongated than the lower one. The third and lowermost panel is roughly square and is also filled with an ‘X’. The short portion of the shaft, which extends above the junction with the arms, consists of a roughly square panel (H 0.05m; Wth 0.05m) containing an incised swastika (max. dim. c. 0.035m). An incised line, describing a semicircle (H 0.085m; Wth 0.1m), arcs over the top of the cross shaft. A drawing of the cross published by Wakeman (1880, 376) shows that each terminal of this incised arch curled into a spiral. These spirals are no longer clearly visible. Lichen covers much of the stone surface.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the western outskirts of Cliffony village, located on gently elevated ground. To NNW there is a gradual fall of ground towards a flat expanse of machair. Sand dunes intervene between the machair plain and the sea, which is located c. 1km from the enclosure. This enclosure consists of a circular area (diam. 54m) enclosed by an earthen bank. The bank (Wth c. 5m; int. H 1.35m; ext. H 2m, at NW) is best preserved at WSW–NNW where it consists of a substantial, grass-covered rise, with a broadly slumped inner slope, and a high and rather vertical-faced external slope. Elsewhere around the circuit, the bank is severely degraded, and is evident only as a low earthen rise topped with later drystone walling. The S quarter of the interior is at a slightly higher level with a gently slope down to N. A wall, evident as a grass-covered rise (Wth 1.5-3m; H 0.5m, at NW), curves in an arc from the enclosing bank at NE to the enclosing bank at NNW, partitioning off a semi-circular area (c. 25-30m E-W; 20m N–S) in the N third of the interior. Within this subdivision, there is a holy well (SL002-014001-), dedicated to St. Bridget, and a cross-inscribed pillar (SL002-014003-). A drystone field wall (Wth 0.8m; H 0.6m), bisect the enclosure centrally on a NNW–SSE axis, dividing it into two properties. The holy well (SL002-014001-) is located on the E side of the property division.`

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, at the base of W-facing slope, on the SW side of Dernish Island. The shoreline is c. 20m to W, bordered by a vertical scarp (H 2m) which drops from the land to a stony shore.
This holy well is not shown on the 1837 OS 6-inch map; it is indicated as ‘Tober Patrick’ on the 1912 edition. It consists of a spring well, which rises, at the base of the slope in a small subcircular hollow (diam. c. 1m), amidst a random scatter of large stones and boulders. There is no evidence of walling or a formal structure enclosing the well. It is partly engulfed in overgrowth. From here, the water flows as a stream in a shallow, stony gully towards the shore. At the shoreline, c. 20m SW of the holy well, where the stream crosses the vertical land-edge scarp (H c. 2m), there is a setting of three large upright slabs at the top of the scarp, and at the base of the scarp, on the shoreline, a 2m wide channel is faced with boulders. The purpose of these features is unclear; they appear to be relatively late in date, and it is unclear if they relate in any way to use of the spring as a holy well. There is a fulacht fia (SL002-055----) 8m to WNW of the holy well.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located at the NE end of Conor’s Island, at the NE end of the Streedagh peninsula. The outline of this enclosure is very low profile, and difficult to trace at ground level. Aerial views suggest the remains could be interpreted as a large, D-shaped enclosure (c. 80m NE−SW; c. 55m NW−SE), with an internal division curving through the E half. It is possible, however, that the remains represent multiphase activity. The curving internal division, may represents the E boundary of an early oval enclosure (c. 65-70m E−W; c. 50m N−S) which was extended to NE to create the larger enclosure. At ground level, the large enclosure is defined by a sod-covered stone bank (Wth 1.75-2m; H 0.2-0.3m) which can be traced NNE−W in a broad curve. The NNE and W terminals of the bank end at an eroding earth and stone cliff (H 2.5-3m) which defines the straight NW side of the enclosure. The cliff drops to a boulder beach and a rocky shoreline. At SW−W the enclosing stone bank merges with a relict field wall (Wth c. 1m; H 0.2) which extends to E beyond the enclosure and may represent a later phase of activity at the site. An upright stone (0.54m NNE−SSW; 0.4m WNW−ESE; H 1m) stands c. 3m S of the enclosure, on the line of this relict field boundary. A number of low stony banks intersect with the enclosure at S and SE; it is not clear to what extent they are contemporary with the enclosure. There are four sod-covered mounds (SL002-027002-) located to W of centre in the enclosure. They are most likely field clearance heaps associated with cultivation ridges which traverse the interior of the enclosure on a NW−SE axis. Cultivation ridges are also evident in the surrounding field. In 2012 the section face of the enclosure, exposed in the eroding cliff face, was sampled (12E0256) for environmental and dating analysis. A charcoal sample yielded radiocarbon dates ranging from late 17th to late 19th centuries. These late dates may indicate a later reuse of the site (Read 2012).

raw_items.raw_text: 19th-century field associated with a vernacular farmstead

source_data.original_text:
In lowlying pasture, on the E side of Conor’s Island, at the NE end of the Streedagh peninsula. There is an area of dampish ground fed by a spring to W, and the shoreline is located c. 60m to S. This enclosure is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. It is located in the W half of a rectangular, 19th-century field associated with a vernacular farmstead, the ruined buildings of which lie c. 60m to SE. The remains are evident as a D-shaped area (c. 43.5m NW−SE; 16.5m NW-SE) defined on the curving side by a low, partly levelled sod-covered bank (Wth 2.5-2.8m; H 0.2-0.4m) which describes a shallow arc N−SSE. The straight side at W is formed by the NW−SE drystone field wall which forms the W side of the rectangular field. There is no convincing evidence at ground level of a continuation of the bank to W of the NW−SE field wall. A low irregular rise extends E-W across the N half of the interior.
This monument may represent the E side of a circular enclosure (diam. 45-50m), the W half of which has been destroyed.

Exposed in section in the land-edge scarp on the SE side of a headland, located on the E side of Conor’s Island, at the NE end of the Streedagh peninsula. The headland projects to NE into a sheltered tidal channel between Conor’s Island and the mainland, where sand flats are exposed at low tide.

source_data.original_text:
In rough, pasture, located on a terrace on a SW-facing slope, on the SW side of Dernish Island. Ground falls away at W−SW for c. 15-20m to the shoreline. 
Roughly oval, sunken area (c. 6m E−W; c. 4.5m N−S) enclosed by a sod-covered bank. The interior is sunken to a depth of c. 0.4m below exterior ground level. Stones protrude from the bank in parts. The N arc of the bank (W 1-1.4m, int. H 0.6m; ext. H 0.2m at N) is quite well-defined, but at SE the bank appears more irregular, and varies in width (Wth 1.5-2.5m), with a broadly slumped, possibly disturbed, internal face. At SW the bank takes the form of an inward-facing scarp, which does not have a clearly defined external edge, but appears to merge with the natural slope. There are breaks (Wth 0.4-0.5m) in the bank at W, E and SSE; those at W and E may be the result of erosion by farm stock. The break at SSE may be an entrance feature; the E terminal of this gap has a linear extension (L 2m) to S, mirrored on the W side by a rise from which a large stone protrudes. The remains as a whole are low-profile and rather irregular, and are covered by ferns and brambles. This may be some form of hut, date and exact function uncertain.

source_data.original_text:
In an expanse of undulating grass-covered sand dunes which lie to W of Bunduff Strand, 300m S of Mullaghmore village. Bunduff Lough is 1km to SE. 
The midden is located on a gentle E-facing slope on the W side of a roughly oval, wind-eroded hollow (c. 30-35m N−S; c. 25m E−W) enclosed by higher ridges of sand. It is evident as a concentration (c. 6m N−S; c. 4m E−W) of sea shells exposed on the eroding sand surface. The midden has no depth, consisting merely of a thin surface spread, becoming increasingly thin and diffuse towards its outer limits. 
A higher density of shells occurs roughly in the centre of the spread, covering an area of c. 2m N−S by 2m E−W, and here the shells are mingled with a dark coloured soil and charcoal fragments. A few small stones, some with a heat-shattered appearance, protrude from amongst the shells. 
Periwinkles are the most numerous shell type, followed by limpets. Lesser quantities of mussels and scallops are evident. The majority of periwinkles and many limpets survive intact; all the mussels are fragmentary. Overall there is a high frequency of fragmentary shells. Occasional small fragments of bone (L 2-4 cm) are visible amongst the shells; these are too fragmentary to allow identification, but at least one piece appears to have some from a cow-sized animal, and a single sheep tooth was noted. 
There is another midden (SL002-059002-) 20m to E on the E side of the same dune hollow.

Notified to NMS by Aoife Heguarty

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 18 December 2020

In an expanse of undulating grass-covered sand dunes which lie to W of Bunduff Strand, 300m S of Mullaghmore village. Bunduff Lough is 1km to SE. 
The midden is located on the E side of a roughly oval, wind-eroded hollow (c. 30-35m N−S; c. 25m E−W) enclosed by higher ridges of sand. It is evident as a thin surface scatter (c. 7m N−S; c. 5m E−W) of sea shells exposed on the eroding sand surface. A slightly higher density of shells covers an area of c. 1m N−S by c. 1.5m E−W in the N half of the spread, where a small deposit of dark coloured soil is mingled with the shells, and there are occasional tiny charcoal fragments. 
Limpets and periwinkles are the most numerous shell type; scallop shells are also present. Many periwinkles shells survive intact, but the majority of shells are in a highly fragmented state. There are occasional small fragments of bone (L 2-4 cm), too fragmentary to allow identification, and a single sheep tooth was noted.  
A small cluster of large limpets was evident on the slope c. 1m to E and upslope from the main body of the midden. Towards the S limits of the midden a single large rectangular block of sandstone (L 0.35m; Wth 0.15m; H 0.18m) rests on the sand surface. One end is broken. There is a reddish stain/colour on one side which may be heat-induced.
There is another midden (SL002-059001-) 20m to W on the W slope of the same dune hollow.

source_data.original_text:
Situated in a slight hollow in gently undulating sand dunes which rise to the N to the cliff edge. The monument consists of a pair of fine grained sandstone slabs set on edge and orientated NNW-SSE.. The northernmost stone (average L 1.25m; H 1.05m; T 0.2m) is rectangular in shape and is laid on its long edge. The southernmost stone (L 0.65m; H 0.85m if erect; T 0.24m) is roughly triangular in shape: it is 1.05m SSE of its counterpart and leans markedly to the N. Both stones have rounded corners and very smooth surfaces. There are no visible markings on either stone. Without doubt this is the same monument as that described and illustrated by Wood-Martin (1888, 154-5). His sketch and plan shows a third low stone standing c. 1.4m to the W of and parallel with the northernmost stone (pers. comm. M.A. Timoney): the dimensions of the stone are not recorded and it is no longer visible. A low set stone (SL003-042----) stands 32m W of this monument. The relationship, if any, to this monument is unknown but it may be an outlier. Timoney (2016, 14) suggests that this might be remains of a 'Four-poster' type monument.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Revised date of upload: 23 January 2017

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a slight rise in gently undulating sand dune pasture. Not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. The account of the discovery of this burial is recorded in a letter to the Keeper of Irish Antiquities at the National Museum of Ireland, dated 14 August 1944, from the Garda Superintendent at Sligo. The letters records the following: 'I beg to inform you that while digging trenches in connection with Military exercises near the seashore at Bunduff, Cliffoney, one of the party . . . came upon a human skeleton. It was enclosed in a stone grave, the bottom, sides and top of which was made of 3/4 inch stone slabs, and the head and foot of thick square stones. The stone slabs forming the sides and roof of this grave were broken in places. Nothing was found in the grave except human remains. It was 2 1/2 foot from the surface of the earth. The coroner . . . was informed and he decided not to hold an inquest.' The bones were packed in a wooden box and forwarded to the National Museum. Further correspondence in the National Museum files dated 1948 records that the 'burial consited of an inhumation of a bdy which lay in a contracted positon on it side in the a cist 3 foot x 2 foot x 1 foot deep, lying 2 foot below the surface.' (NMI Topographical files). The exact location of this cist is unknown as the copy of the surviving copy of the map from 1944 on file in the National Museum is not of sufficient scale to enable the precise position to be plotted with an degree of confidence. In consequence, the location recorded for this record must be considered as indicative only. There is no visible evidence of the 'trenches' referred to in the above correspondence. There is a depression (L E-W 3m; Wth top N-S 1.3m; Wth base 0.55m; D 0.7m) in the sand hill near the shore c. 10m S of a vertical 25m high, N-facing, E-W orientated sea cliff which perhaps might be the site of this burial. The current coordinates are for this location.  The grave has been tentatively dated to the early medieval period. (Cahill and Sikora 2011, Vol. 2, 167-8).

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 20 January 2014

source_data.original_text:
Not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. A souterrain was discovered in 1954 at or in proximity to a possible levelled cashel (SL003-019001-). The monument was visited by an OPW fieldworker in the same year (SMR file). His report reads:'Souterrain of gallery type. Drystone walls. Slab roof. Two chambers accessible. At present entered through roof of chamber broken in removing stones by Co. Council workmen. Chamber 1 (that through which it is now entered) measures approximately 10m feet 6 in. [3.2m] in length (probably longer, slightly curved). Upper courses of side walls corbelled. Height about 5 ft. [1.5m] but original floor level probably lower. Small doorway blocked with earth on either side of chamber 1. Chamber 2 lies in a straight line with chamber 1 and is entered from it by a low passage, through which it is possible to crawl by going flat on one's face. Chamber 2 is of similar construction to chamber 1. Its visible length is about 16 ft. [4.9m], but it is half-filled with a mass of earth and stones sloping down in a sort of ramp from the far end, representing a possible former entrance. Chamber 2 is a little less than 6 ft. [1.8m]in width. Maximum height about 5ft [1.5m] at present. Chamber 2 has an air shaft, a little over 1 ft square, slab-lined, leading towards the surface over the roof of chamber 1. The top of another air-shaft, apparently ventilating the sealed chamber on right of chamber 1 from the present entrance, has been exposed.' In a report to the NMI the fieldworker also recorded 'occupation (burned stones, iron slag, charcoal, burnt stone) on the floor of Chamber 1' (NMI topographical file). In 1962 a fragment of a decorated rotary quern (SL003-019003-), now in the National Museum, was recovered from the souterrain (Lucas 1964, 98-100). No trace of the souterrain is now visible at ground level.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

source_data.original_text:
Situated close to the base of a steep SE-facing slope. Not marked on the 1837 edition of the OS 6-inch map. Raised circular area (diam. c.30m) defined from ENE-E-S by a steep scarp (H 1m - 1.4m) which may have had a stone wall at its upper edge. Elsewhere the perimeter and portion of the internal area have been destroyed as a consequence of the construction of modern linear field boundaries. Original entrance not recognisable. Within the internal area at SW, adjacent to a modern field wall, is a circular hole giving access to a souterrain (see SL004-007002-).


Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 17 April 2013

source_data.original_text:
At Doonfore enclosure (see SL004-007001-). Within the internal area at SW, adjacent to a modern field boundary which truncates the site, is a hole (diam. 0.7m) which is now closed with stones and metal sheeting. This gives access to a chamber or passage whose walls are constructed of drystone masonry and which is roofed with large lintels. The chamber/passage extends in a NNW direction.

source_data.original_text:
In a damp, rush-grown meadow, on a slight elevation. A field drain which cuts through the lowlying centre of the field, on a NE–SW axis, lies 3m to NW. A kidney-shaped mound (c. 15m E–W; c. 13m N–S; H c. 0.5m) with a shallow depression (4m E–W; 2m N–S) on the N side indicating the likely location of the trough. A layer of black, charcoal-rich soil, overlying a concentration of stones, is revealed in a small patch where the sod is eroded from the mound surface. The mound is distinguished by a growth of vegetation which is shorter and greener then the pasture elsewhere in the field.

geometric.primary_shape: L 8-10m NW−SE; D 0.2-0.4m (midden); D c. 0.2-0.3m (orange-brown soil layer); D 0.8-1m (boulder clay); depth c. 0.4-0.5m below grass-covered top of cliff

dimensions.raw: L 8-10m NW−SE; D 0.2-0.4m (midden); D c. 0.2-0.3m (orange-brown soil layer); D 0.8-1m (boulder clay); depth c. 0.4-0.5m below grass-covered top of cliff

source_data.original_text:
Located on top of a shoreline cliff, which drops to an expanse of limestone rocks extending into the sea, at the W end of Ballyconnell beach. The midden is exposed in section beneath a layer of sod and dark brown top soil, at a depth of c. 0.4-0.5m below the grass-covered top of the cliff. It is visible as a dense concentration (L 8-10m NW−SE; D 0.2-0.4m) of limpet shell. There appear to be small quantities of periwinkles in dark, pebble-rich soil directly above the limpets. The shell layer overlies a layer (D c. 0.2-0.3m) of orange-brown, relatively stone free soil, which in turn overlies natural orange-brown stony boulder clay (D 0.8-1m). Beneath the latter, are further layers of gravel and stone dropping to the base of the cliff. 
According to local information, the pasture field on top of the cliff was the location for ‘bothies’, temporary huts or shelters erected during the summer season for minding cattle, which were grazing along the shoreline. One possibility is that the midden is related to that activity.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 29 June 2017

Situated on a slight SSW-facing slope on summit of a NNE-SSW orientated ridge, at SSW end, in pasture. Slightly raised D-shaped area (dims. 9m N-S; 8m E-W) enclosed by a bank of earth and stone (Wth 5.95m; int. H 0.85m). There is no fosse visible at ground level. The bank is curved NNW-SW with the straight side SW-NNW. The external base of the straight side is revetted SW-W by a line of limestone slabs (av. dims. L 0.7m; Wth 0.5m; T 0.2m) set on edge. The original entrance is not recognisable.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on level summit of broad E-W orientated ridge. Views are good to excellent in all directions. Raised circular area (diam. 38m) enclosed by the footings of a drystone wall (Wth 2.9m; int. H 0.25m). There is no fosse visible at ground level. From ENE-S the site is enclosed by a low bank of rubble limestone and elsewhere by a scarp. The internal and external basal blocks (av. dims. L 1m; Wth 0.8m; T 0.4m; spaced 1.5m apart) of the wall survive S-SW with the external basal blocks surviving ENE-SE and NE-N. The original entrance is not recognisable. A NNE-SSW orientated drystone field wall extends along the base of the scarped edge SW-NW, turns ESE extending 8m into the interior from the cashel wall at NW, turns at a right angle to cross the cashel wall again at NNE.

source_data.original_text:
A fieldworker who inspected Moneygold cashel (SL005-002001-) in 1991 recorded three holes in the NE sector which he interpreted as a possible souterrain (SL002-002002-). He noted that 'the soil matrix which makes up the sides of the holes have clusters of sea shells, probably midden material.' (SMR file). The latest field report interpreted the possible souterrain as being probably badger setts and makes no mention of the possible midden material.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on level summit of broad E-W orientated ridge in pasture. Circular mound (base diam. 11m; H 1.9m) of earth and stone enclosed by a berm (Wth 2.3m) with an outer stone kerb (ext. H 0.6m). A NE-SW orientated drystone field wall traverses the site slightly to NW of centre. The summit of the central mound has been truncated on either side of the field wall to form a level D-shaped level area (dims. 4.5m NE-SW; 2.8m NW-SE). The straight side of the D-shaped area is defined NE-SE by an inward facing scarped edge (H 0.6m) and the curved portion of the D-shaped area is defined by original slope of the side of the mound NE-SE. The berm encloses the central mound NE-SW is absent elsewhere. The external edge of the berm is defined by an earthen scarped edge that is best preserved NNE-SW where a discontinuous kerb of small limestone slabs and boulders survives.

Located at the base of the N-facing slope of a hill, in the SW corner of a field, with a ruined vernacular cottage 15m to N. This holy well consists of a natural spring contained within a roughly D-shaped cavity (1.4m N–S; 1.4m E–W; D 1m) which is faced with stone. A curving drystone wall defines the E–S side of the well but the N and W walls are straight. The N wall consists of one or possibly two large edge-set slabs. The well is enclosed on all sides by the slumped, grass-covered W-facing slope of a penitential cairn (SL005-004003-). There is a bullaun stone (SL005-004002-) on top of the penitential cairn, a few meters SE of the well. A church and graveyard (SL005-005001-; SL005-005002-) are located c. 100m to ENE. According to local tradition, water from the well was especially valued as a cure for sick cattle.

At a holy well (SL005-004001-), located on top of a penitential station or cairn (SL005-004003-). This bullaun stone consists of a roughly square boulder (0.4m by 0.37m; H 0.3m) with a central, oval depression (0.23m by 0.18m; D 0.1m) in its upper surface. The depression is straight sided with a flat base. A fragment of mortar adhering to one side of the stone suggests that it may once have been affixed to a wall. A church and graveyard (SL005-005001-; SL005-005002-) are located c. 100m to ENE.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, in the SW corner of a field, located at a holy well (SL005-004001-). This penitential station consists of a substantial, compact, grass-covered mound or cairn (10m N–S; 7.7m E–W; max. H 1.8m at S) of small and medium-sized stones in a soilmatrix. It is roughly oval in plan, with a domed profile and a narrow, somewhat flattened top. The cairn encloses the holy well within its W-facing slope. There is bullaun stone (SL005-004002-) on top of the cairn. A row of sycamore trees grow along the E side, and a E–W field wall abuts the S end of the cairn. A church and graveyard (SL005-005001-; SL005-005002-) are located c. 100m to ENE.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located c. 35m W of a graveyard (SL005-005002-), and c. 70m ENE of a holy well (SL005-04001-). The location of the souterrain is marked by a low rise (c. 15m N–S; c. 4-5m E–W) in the surface of the field. The rise is defined at SW-NW by a slight scarp, and is bordering at E by a shallow surface depression (c. 4-5m across). A surface opening (0.4m N–S; 0.3m E–W), created by the removal in the past of a roof lintel, reveals a drystone-built chamber (Wth c. 4m; int. H c. 2.25m). A passage appears to extend to S from the chamber. The surface opening to the chamber is now covered by concrete slabs and a boulder.

source_data.original_text:
Situated in gently undulating deciduous forest and now inaccessible. Recorded by a fieldworker in 1991 as a circular raised area (diam. 16m) enclosed by a fosse (Wth 4m) and an external bank of earth (Wth 5m; int. H 1m). The external bank is absent NW-NE and incorporated into modern field boundaries at E and W. The interior is domed and rises to a maximum height of 2m above the fosse at S. (SMR file). The monument is now densely overgrown with scrub rendering satisfactory inspection impossible.

The bank has been disturbed in all areas having an irregular profile and field clearance earth and stone has been dumped against the external face of the bank N-NE. source_data.original_text:
Situated on the steep, exposed SW-facing slope of a sand dune, overlooking a cobble and sand beach and small bay to SW. The midden is located part-way down the dune slope about 8-10m above the beach. The shifting nature of the dunes exposes and obscures the layer over time, but on various occasion shells, fragments of animal bones and fire cracked stone have been noted extending over an area of 8m by 8m. A hammerstone was recovered from this area in 1962 (NMI 1964, 104). 
Following erosion and collapse of the dune slope in Winter 2020/21, an enlarged section of the midden layer was exposed, with burnt stone, charcoal-enriched soil, shells and bone fragments clearly visible in a dark brown/black soil matrix (pers. comm. Tamlyn Mc Hugh 2021).

source_data.original_text:
Located on a slight elevation surrounded by damp, lowlying coastal pasture, overlooking  a small rocky bay. Inishmurray Island is visible c. 6km offshore to NW. The eroding land-edge cliff face, bordering a cobble beach, is located c. 6-10m N of the church.
This ruined, roofless medieval church is rectangular in plan (12.2m ESE−WNW, 5.1m NNE−SSW) with walls of undressed mortared rubble. The E gable (H c. 4.5m; T c. 1m) stands to full height, and contains a single, narrow light (ext. Wth 0.2m) with a broadly slayed internal embrasure (Wth c. 1m). The other three walls are reduced to a few courses only (max. H c. 1m). There is a record of a recess (Wth c. 0.55; H c. 0.43m; D 0.43m) at the E end of the S wall (Wakeman, 1893; OPW topographical Files). A rubble-filled gap towards the W end of the S wall is a possible location for a doorway. Stone rubble is strewn through the interior and surrounds the exterior. A possible graveyard (SL005-022005-) is located immediately to E of the church, and low banks, c. 30m to E and S of the church, may represent an outer enclosure (SL005-022007-) or boundary to the settlement.
The church is named ‘Staad Abbey’on the 1837 and 1912 OS maps, and is known as ‘Teampull’ in local tradition. It is late medieval in date, but may have been built to replace an earlier church: Gwynn and Hadcock (1970, 405) suggest that there was an early Christian monastic settlement here, its foundation attributed to St. Molaise of Inishmurray. Though no remains of an explicitly ecclesiastical nature have been found to confirm this, the presence of a souterrain (SL005-022002-) a few meters to NW of the church, and the excavated remnants of a house (SL005-022009-) points to a phase of early medieval settlement. A substantial midden (SL005-022004-), located immediately to N of the church, also indicates a long period of settlement at the site. The upper levels of the midden, radiocarbon dated to between the 15th-17th centuries, are likely to be contemporary with the use of the present church. A limekiln (SL005-022008-), located c. 10m to N of the church, may have been used to produce the lime mortar used in the church’s construction (McCormick and O’Sullivan et al. 2000, 27).
A strong link to Inishmurray Island is preserved in local tradition: This sees Staad serving as a staging post for monks, pilgrims and other travellers en route to the monastic settlement (SL001-001001-) on Inishmurray. The church has also been postulated as a candidate for a church at which Captain de Cuellar, a survivor of a Spanish Armada ship wrecked at Streedagh, sought refuge; however, this has not been confirmed.

source_data.original_text:
Located immediately to NW of Staad Abbey (SL005-022001-), in an area of lowlying coastal pasture, bordering a cobble beach. In 1999 this stone-built souterrain was noted eroding out of the section face of the land-edge cliff (H c. 2m) bordering the cobble beach. In 2000 it was recorded and partly excavated (Licence no.: 00E0235) (McCormick et al. 2000, 18-19, 25). The remains consisted of two walls (H 1.8m) of drystone construction set 0.7m apart, defining a passage or chamber that extended roughly NNW−SSE. No roof was evident. An iron blade and a chert flake were found on the compact earthen floor. Layers of redeposited midden material (SL005-022004-) filled the space between the walls. This suggested that the souterrain went out of use and was deliberately backfilled; the roof may have been dismantled at this stage. It is likely that a ‘stone-lined drain’ noted in the eroding cliff face in 1993 was also part of the souterrain, perhaps the remains of a creep, but this was already lost to erosion by the time of the investigations in 2000 (McCormick, F. and Bently, B. 1994, 2; McCormick et al. 2000, 19). A sample of cow bone retrieved from the lowest fill of the souterrain produced a calibrated radiocarbon date of AD 1010-1155 (UB-4575, at one standard deviation) (McCormick and O’Sullivan et al. 2000, 20). 
The souterrain points to a phase of early medieval settlement pre-dating the construction of the present late medieval church (SL005-022001-); McCormick and O’Sullivan et al. (2000, 20) postulate that the deliberate backfilling of the souterrain in the 11th or 12th century may have happened at a time of reorganisation of the site in preparation for the building of the present church. 
Coastal erosion appears to have destroyed the last remnants of the souterrain; a shallow C-shaped indentation in the cliff-edge marks the location.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload:  3 July 2017

source_data.original_text:
Exposed in section in the low, eroding cliff face (H c. 2m), bordering the shoreline, c. 10m N of Staad Abbey church (SL005-022001-).
The midden is visible in the cliff face as a shell-rich layer (H 0.5-0.6m), extending for a length of 40-50m from a point c. 10m E of the church to a point c. 20m W of the church. It appears as a dense concentration of limpet shells, and periwinkles shells, with lesser quantities of cockle, mussel and crab shells, as well as animal, bird and fish bones. This food waste debris is enveloped in a matrix of dark-grey, sandy soil, flecked in parts with charcoal, and mixed with small and medium-sized stones, both rounded and angular in form, and including stones with a heat-shattered appearance.
Although recorded here as a single monument, archaeological recording and sampling of the midden in 1993 and 2000 has shown that the midden is, in fact, a complex series of successive layers, incorporating a suite of features such as pits, possible hearths, walls, a souterrain (SL005-022002-) and a lime kiln (SL005-022008-) (McCormick and Bently 1994; McCormick et al. 2000). Analysis of samples taken from the midden has confirmed that the most common shell fish exploited were limpets and periwinkles, that the animal bones included cattle, sheep/goat, pig, horse and seal, and the fish bones included ballan wrasse, herring, hake and salmon and scad. Barley, oat, wheat and flax seeds, as well as hazel nut shells, were also recovered. (McCormick and Bently 1994, 2-7; McCormick and O’Sullivan et al. 2000, 10-15). The lower levels in the midden appear to be early medieval in date, and contemporary with a souterrain (SL005-022002-), the lowest fill of which produced a radiocarbon date of 11th-12th century AD (McCormick and O'Sullivan et al. 2000, 20). A horse bone, retrieved from an upper layer in the midden, produced a radiocarbon date of AD 1447-1632 (UB-3771) (McCormick and Bently 1994, 2). The midden points to a long period of settlement at Staad, which, according to tradition, was used by pilgrims and other travellers as a staging point en route to the monastic settlement (SL001-001001-) on Inishmurray Island, located c. 6km offshore.

This consists of a rectilinear enclosure (18m E−W; 10m N−S) defined by a low grass-covered bank, which extends ENE from the E gable of the church. source_data.original_text:
Located c. 10m N of Staad Abbey church (SL005-022001-), in an area of lowlying coastal pasture, bordering a cobble beach. This bowl-shaped, stone-lined pit is exposed in section in the land-edge cliff (H c. 2m) bordering the cobble beach. It was record in 2000 during archaeological investigation (licence no. 00E0235) at Staad Abbey, and at that date measured c. 2.5m in diameter and 1-1.5m in depth (McCormick and O’Sullivan et al. 2000, 21-23). The base of the pit contains fire-reddened material overlain by lime residue, which points to its function as a lime roasting clamp for the production of mortar. These basal fills are overlain by redeposited stony soil, used to backfill the pit when it fell out of use. The position of the pit in the stratigraphy of the cliff face suggests that the pit belongs to a late medieval phase of activity at the site, and may be associated with the construction of the church (SL005-022001-) (Ibid., 27). The cliff face continues to recede due to erosion, but remnants of the pit are still visible.

Located immediately to N of Staad Abbey church (SL005-022001-). Excavation (00E0235) in 2001 revealed remnants of paving and two ash spreads or simple hearths, which were interpreted as the remains of an early medieval house floor. It overlay a deep layer of natural sand, and was overlain by layers of midden material (SL005-022004-) (Dunne, McCormick, and O’Sullivan 2001, 1).

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 4 July 2017

In lowlying coastal pasture bordering a cobble beach, in the vicinity of Staad Abbey church (SL005-022001-). Survey and excavation (00E0235) in 2000 and 2001 revealed evidence of an early phase of settlement activity, pre-dating the late medieval church (SL005-022001-) and the early medieval souterrain (SL005-022002-). A horizon of bowl-shaped pits was recorded, dug into deep deposits of wind-blown sand, in the lowest stratigraphic levels in the eroding land-edge cliff face (McCormick et al. 2000, 15-17), and, in a trench excavated in the space between the church and the sea cliff, a wall built of beach cobbles underlay a layer of wind-blown sand, which in turn underlay the foundations of the church (Dunne, McCormick, and O’Sullivan 2001, 1). These features have not been precisely dated, but their position in the stratigraphy of the site suggested that some may be prehistoric in date.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on level ground in gently undulating pasture. 
This holy well is not shown on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, but is shown on the 1912 edition, where it is named ‘St Patrick’s Well’. 
The well consists of a subrectangular pit (2m NW−SE; 0.85m NE-SW) dug to a depth of 1.4m below surface ground level. The vertical sides of the pit are faced with drystone walling. A low wall (Wth 0.45m; H 0.2-0.3m) of mortared limestone blocks rises proud of the well pit on the NE, SE and SW sides; this wall is now partly collapsed on the S and W sides. There is a lintelled rectangular niche (Wth 0.3m; H 0.35m; D 0.35m) in the internal face on the NE side. The well is open on the NW side; there may have been steps here to aid access to the water, but wall collapse/loose rubble now makes this unclear. Rubble also fills the base of the well, where water is still evident.
Traditional devotions which were practiced at the well are recorded in the National Folklore Schools Collection (1937-39): volume 0155, p. 001 (https://www.duchas.ie/): 
"It is said that this well was blessed by St. Patrick when he was passing from Connacht into Ulster. Around the well is a stone wall. In this wall are round holes - fourteen in number; these are called the Stations. Every year on St. Patrick's Day people from the adjoining townlands visit Tobar Phádruig. They make the Stations of the Cross round the well: each hole being used as a station. At the entrance to the well they recite the Rosary or some other prayers. Those who visit the well usually bring with them some flowers, or holy pictures or medals or old crosses: these they leave at the well…It is said that when St. Patrick was blessing this well, he left the mark of his thumb on a stone which is pointed out to the present day. This stone which is round with a flat top and bearing a mark resembling the imprint of a human thumb is placed in the wall at the entrance to the well. People visit the well at other times of the year as well as on St. Patrick's Day for cures for animals…".
There is a rath (SL005-040----) and children’s burial ground (SL005-040001-) 35m to S.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on a terrace on the E bank of the Grange River, overlooking a bend in the river. There is a gently drop from the terrace for c. 10m to the river bank. The terrace continues beyond the rath to NW where it takes the form of a low linear spine of raise ground. The ground rises steeply on the opposite river bank. To E, the ground rises gently to a higher terrace and then levels out. The Dartry Mountains loom in the background to E-SE, with the dramatic profile of Ben Bulben prominent to S.
Circular earthen platform defined on the S arc by a stony bank (Wth 4.5m; int. H 0.6-0.7m; ext. H 1.5m, at S), reduced on the N arc to a scarp (H 1m; Wth slope 3m, at N). The bank has a substantial external slope and a rather slumped internal rim; it is topped by a skim of sod-covered stones. At W the slope of the bank merges with the break of slope at terrace edge. Hawthorn trees grow on the S arc.
The interior is grass-covered; low stones break the surface in parts. The NE quadrant is at a slightly lower level to the rest of the platform. An ENE-WSW drystone field wall (Wth 0.9m; H 0.7m) crosses the rath to S of centre. 
An outer stone bank, of uncertain date, arcs around the E half of the rath, with an intervening gap of c. 14-16m. It is poorly preserved on the NE arc, reduced to a low grass-covered rise with a low stone-faced scarp (H 0.55m) at N; there is a broad gap/levelled section at ENE−E. At E−S it forms a substantial sod-covered bank (Wth 2.8-3m; H 0.5m) of earth and stone, now largely obscured by hawthorn and blackthorn bushes. There is no evidence that this outer bank ever fully encircled the rath; on the contrary, it curves inwards at NE to meet the N side of the rath, and merging at SW with the natural scarp of the terrace. The outer bank, therefore, encloses a broad, roughly D-shaped annex on the E side of the rath. A portion of this space at E is subdivided by low ruined cross walls, marking the location of a children’s burial ground (SL005-040001-).  There is a holy well (Sl005-039----) 35m to NNE.

source_data.original_text:
Located at a ringfort (SL005-040----).
According to local information, burials of unbaptized babies took place in the space intervening between the E side of the rath and the concentric outer bank. The space (7m N-S; 15m E-W) is bounded on the N side by the E-W field wall which crosses the rath and on the S by a low ruined E-W wall (Wth 1m; H 0.3m) that extends between the rath and the outer bank. Short lengths of low ruined walls subdivide the space. The area is grass-covered; with low, moss-covered stones protrude randomly from the grass. No formal grave plots can be discerned. A single upright stone (H 0.53; Wth 0.3m; T 0.18m) stands at the E edge of the space. Three slabs, which may originally have stood upright, lie prostrate at the base of a sycamore tree which is growing on the line of the E-W wall on the S side of the space.
It is possible that burials also took place in the rath interior, but there is no direct evidence.
The burial ground is named ‘Cill Rouderaun’ in one of two accounts which are preserved in the National Folklore Schools Collection (1937-39) (https://www.duchas.ie/):
 
Volume 0155, p. 001: "… an old graveyard called Cill Rouderaun. About a quarter of a mile from the village of Grange, on the south side of the road leading from Grange to Ballintrillick, Cill Roudeaun is situated Around the ‘reilig’ is the remains of an old stone wall. People say that unbaptised children were buried there long ago: but it has not been used as a burial place within the memory of the oldest inhabitant. About 200 yards north of the ‘reilig’ is a holy well called ‘Tobar Pádruig’"

Volume 0155, p. 236-7: "There is an old disused graveyard in the townland of Ardnaglass near Grange, Co Sligo … This graveyard was used only as a burial place for unbaptised children about eighty years ago. There is a large fairy fort in this field and it is said that the children's graves are in and around the fort. There was a flax mill in this field and every morning when the workmen went to work in it they used to see the tracks of little feet in the mill. They thought these were made by the children who had been buried in the fort."

source_data.original_text:
The following description is taken E. Cody’s published account (2015): ‘The central-court tomb at Doonshaskin is sited on a slight ridge in low-lying pasture just over one km from the coast. The outlook from it is now largely restricted by high field hedges. What lay under the bushes there is portrayed in Fig. 3 where stones shown cross-hatched stand upright in the ground in their original positions. Stones shown in outline are either clearly displaced or of uncertain status. Readily apparent are two chambers lying east and west of each other and about 4.5m apart. The western chamber is some 4m long and 2.6m wide. Its northern side is formed by four stones lying end to end. A stone at the inner face of the westernmost of the four sidestones is a jamb-stone; more-or-less opposite it is another jamb-stone and this stone and two other set stones either side of a partly buried stone represent the south side of the chamber. At the east end of the chamber are two opposed jamb stones inside the lines of the chamber sides. These are entrance jambs between which access was gained to the chamber while the two jamb-stones at the west end mark a point of segmentation between the chamber and another no trace of which now remains. The eastern chamber, some 3.5m long and as much as 2.9m wide, is represented by two entrance jamb stones at its front or west end, two sides tones at the north side with a gap between them and three stones at the south side. This chamber, like the western example, is open at the rear and is but the forward example of what was at least a two-chambered gallery. The stone outlined in bold on the drawing is a lintel which originally lay on top of the entrance jambs to the eastern chamber. Between the lintel and the front of the western chamber there are a number of displaced and partly-buried stones. The upright stones of the two chambers range from about 0.25m to 0.7m in exposed height.

The court, little of which survives, is represented by three set stones, 0.25m to 0.4m high, two to the north of the entrance to the western chamber and one to the north of the entrance to the eastern chamber. These are the remains of the northern half of the court. It is expected that there was a matching semi-circular setting of court stones at the south but this is no longer apparent. It may be that some of the displaced and partly-buried stones lying between the two chambers and already referred to may have served as court stones. The gap between the fronts of the opposed chambers is 4.5m east-west and this represents the greatest width of the court. The court length, its north-south dimension, is not now known but may have been a little greater than its width. In addition to the structural stones of the two galleries and the court there are some other securely-set uprights to the north of the eastern chamber, the precise role of all of which is somewhat uncertain. One stands just outside it; three more form a slight arc aligned roughly north-west to south-east to the north of the last and to the north of these there is a line of three tallish stones. These last three are about 4m north of the gallery and like it are aligned east-west They are the tallish stones, 0.45m to 1.1m high, that were visible before the bushes were cleared from the monument. As may be detected from the plan, some of the chamber and court stones have flat inner and rounded outer faces; these were boulders of roughly oval outline that have been split longitudinally by the tomb builders and then set on edge. Such split boulders were frequently used in court tomb construction.

The outer pecked line on the drawing combined with the curving fence line depicts the current outline of the cairn that was heaped up around the tomb structure. Its original outline is not now apparent but the three stones, already mentioned, standing 4m north of the eastern end of the tomb may have formed part of a kerbed perimeter to the cairn. On comparison with other central-court tombs the cairn may have been of double trapezoid form (Ó Nualláin 1976, 105), i.e., broad at mid-length and narrowing to both ends, in this case to east and to west. Originally it would have reached to the height of the galleries which would have been roofed with large slabs and the cairn would have helped stabilize the structure. Though the galleries were encased in the cairn the court area would have remained as an open space where it is presumed people would have gathered to participate in rites and rituals of a varied nature, some of which undoubtedly related to death and burial. The court would have been entered via a narrow passage, probably slab-lined, through the cairn. There is now no surface trace of this entrance but it would have opened from either the north side of the cairn or, on the basis of comparison with other central-court tombs, more likely from the south side.’ (Cody 2015)

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located at the NW end of a low undulating ridge which borders the S side of a river. The enclosure is sited at the N-NE edge of the ridge where the slope falls away in a long steep drop to the river bank. The location provides good views over the surrounding hilly terrain, overshadowed to SE by the looming slopes of Benbulbin. It is indicated on the 1837 OS 6-inch map as a circular enclosure (c. 15-20m), bisected centrally on a roughly N−S axis by a field boundary, and shown on the 1912 edition as a semi-circular hachured arc (diam. c. 15m E−W), curving W−N−E, abutted at SE by field boundaries. It was listed in the SMR (1989) as ‘enclosure’. It was not listed in the RMP (1995) on the basis of a 1991 field report which recorded only a quarry hollow at the location. An inspected in 2016 confirmed that there is evidence of an enclosure. It consists of a circular area (diam. 13m NNE−SSW; 14.5m E−W) defined at SW−NE by a low scarp (Wth 0.5-0.6m), enhanced at N−NE (ext. H 0.7-0.8m; Wth slope 1.3m) by the ridge slope. At N−NE the scarp is topped by a very slight rise or bank (Wth 1m). The scarp is indistinct at NE−E. At ESE−S the circuit is defined by an arc of ruined drystone wall, evident as a tumbled heap (Wth 1.2-1.4m; H 0.3m) of loose stone. The S−SE arc of the enclosure cannot be traced. A roughly circular, now grassed-over, quarry pit (diam. 5.4m; D 0.5-0.8), with a shallower extension (Wth 2m) at SW, has destroyed the centre of the interior.

Situated on a moderate N-facing slope upland pasture. Circular area (diam. 21m) defined by a bank (Wth 4.6m; int. H 1.3m; ext. H 1.1m). No fosse now visible. The site is bisected by a NE-SW orientated relic drystone wall. The inner side of the bank has been rebuilt to form a vertical face ENE-W. Two roughly rectangular sheep pens (dims. c.2m by 4m) have been built in the angle between the re-modelled inner face of the cashel bank and the NW side of the field wall. A relic field wall abuts the external side of the cashel bank at W and W-N. Original entrance not recognisable.

Situated on slight N-facing slope in gently undulating upland pasture. Slightly raised circular area (diam. 33m) enclosed by a bank of rubble limestone (Wth 2.8m; int. H 1.1m). source_data.original_text:
Situated on a slight rise on the summit of a NW-SE orientated ridge in a mature coniferous forest clearing. Raised circular area (dims. 23.5m E-W; 23m N-S) enclosed by an internal rubble limestone wall (Wth 3.6m; int. H 1.75m). Immediately outside the wall is a level berm (Wth 3.25m) and a rubble limestone bank (Wth 3.8m; int. H 0.4m) with an external fosse (Wth 6.3m; D 0.4m). The inner face of the internal wall has been entirely rebuilt and it extends 1-1.2m above the level of the surviving original wall and the original external basal facing of large thick slabs and blocks laid flat survives on all sides. A vertically backed recess (Wth base 1.1m; Wth top 2m; D 0.5m) at ESE in the internal face may be original. From SW-NW the external stone bank and the fosse are absent and the site is defined by a scarped edge (ext. H 1.4m). A break (Wth 1.9m) in the internal wall with a corresponding break (Wth 2m) in the external bank and a stone causeway (Wth 2.3m) across the fosse marks the position of the original entrance. A modern NW-SE orientated field wall lies on the W side of the site crossing the external stone bank at external fosse at SW and at NW. Relic field walls link to the external face of the external stone bank at NNE and at SSE and a relic field wall lies along the SW side of the entrance causeway, extending across the berm and linking to the external face of the internal wall at SE. The remains of a souterrain (SL005-118002-) are located to N and NW of centre in the interior.

raw_items.raw_text: survey of the souterrain undertaken in 2016

source_data.original_text:
This souterrain, of drystone construction, located in a low hillock, in gently undulating pasture. An opening (0.6m wide x 0.4m high) into the souterrain is located within a depression on the summit of the hillock. A vertical drop through the opening provides access into the E end of a passage (10.2m E−W; 1.1m N−S; H 1.2m high) with a clay floor. At the W end of the passage, there is a constriction or creep (1.2m E−W; 0.5m N−S; H 0.7m), which opens onto the NE end of a rectangular chamber (4.4m N−S; 1m E-W; H 1.4m high). The chamber, which extends to the S, lies perpendicular to the passage, giving the souterrain an L-shaped plan. There is a possible vent (c. 1m E-W; Wth 0.3m; H 0.3m) at the N end of the W wall of the chamber, and a recess (c. 1.5m x 0.2m x 0.3m) in the S wall. The S wall appears more crudely constructed that the rest of the chamber, and may have been modified or rebuilt. A number of features post-date the original construction of the souterrain. These include: the neat piling of stone rubble (L 3.6m; Wth 0.5m; H 0.4m) along both the N and S wall of the passage, two shallow pits in the floor of the chamber, one against the W wall and one against the E wall, and a crude hearth in the NW corner of the chamber. These features appear relatively recent in date, and may relate to the local tradition that the souterrain was used as a hideout during the War of Independence. 

The above information is derived from a survey of the souterrain undertaken in 2016 by Dr. Marion Dowd, Sam Moore, Ivan Sullivan and Stewart Sullivan.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Revised upload: 5 December 2016

In pasture, located on a small rounded peak on a narrow NW−SE ridge. There are extensive views encompassing a broad sweep of the surrounding undulating grassland, Donegal Bay and Slieve League to NW, and the corrugated slope of Ben Bulben which dominates landscape to SE. The deep gully of the Grange River cuts through a small valley c. 150m to S. A rectangular-shaped stone slab (L 0.55m NNW−SSE; T 0.16m at base; 0.2m at top; H 1m) set upright in the ground, with long axis aligned roughly N-S. The cross-section is rectangular. The stone expands in thickness at top, and the top of the stone slopes up slightly to S. A natural vertical crack (L 0.3m), which extends through the full thickness of the stone, extends down for c. 0.3m from the top of the stone midway along the broad sides. A second standing stone (SL005-181----), which shares the same alignment, is within sight on another small peak 31m to NW on the same ridge.

source_data.original_text:
Within a peat layer exposed on a beach, on a NW-facing bay. A church (SL005-022001-), known as Staad Abbey, is located c. 25m NE. 
In May 2017 several upright timber stakes and other pieces of timber were noted in a peat layer exposed when a covering layer of loose beach cobbles had been swept away by storm/wave action. A rescue excavation (17E0317) was carried out on behalf of the National Monument Service between 27 June and 3 July 2017 to investigate and record the timber features as they were vulnerable to further erosion and possible destruction (Beglane 2018).
The excavation was limited to the exposed portion (c. 30m E−W; c. 4.6m N−S; max. D 1.59m) of the peat layer. The full extent of the layer along the shoreline is concealed by beach cobbles, and it is likely that it also extends to SE−S beneath the field of damp, rush-grown pasture which borders the beach.
Specialist analysis of a peat core taken during the excavation showed that the peat layer accumulated between the late Mesolithic and the late Iron Age periods in a local environment quite different from that of the present day. The seashore during that period was some distance to NW of its current position, and the peat layer formed in fen-like conditions in what had been a freshwater lake. 
The excavation revealed activity within the peat layer in the Bronze Age. This record refers to the earliest phase of activity which was represented by a horizontal layer of wood. It was partly excavated. Only one piece of worked wood was recovered -a piece of willow brushwood with a long, shallow chisel point -nevertheless, the layer of wood appeared to have been deliberately laid, and may have served as a trackway, platform or surface. Many of the wood pieces were on a roughly NW-SE axis, suggesting that they may have formed a trackway running across the boggy ground. The excavator concluded that ‘they did not seem to be tightly packed across the whole area or regularly aligned so they probably did not form a permanent route-way, but instead might be considered as occasional aids for persons needing to access or to cross this boggy area, or may only have been placed over the wettest portions of the peat surface’ (Beglane 2018, 40). The wood was mainly willow, reflecting the local wet environment. A wood sample returned a radiocarbon dated of 2285-2044 cal BC, indicating activity during the Early Bronze Age. (Beglan 2018). 
This structure is overlain at a higher level in the peat layer by other structures (SL0005-193----) dating to the Middle Bronze Age.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 19 December 2018

source_data.original_text:
This midden is exposed in section in the eroding land-edge on a small headland, which is located on the SE side of Conor’s Island, at the NE end of the Streedagh peninsula. The headland projects to SSE into a sheltered tidal channel between Conor’s Island and the mainland, where sand flats are exposed at low tide. 
This midden is evident as a layer (D 0.2-0.25m) of fragmentary cockle, oyster and periwinkle shells in a matrix of pale grey sand. It is located at a height of c. 0.8m above the base of the section face, overlying a sterile layer of boulder clay incorporating large stones and boulders. Above the midden layer, the section face rises (H 1-2m) in a number of sandy layers which are slumped and eroded. The section face is partly concealed by vegetation, and the full extent of the midden is unclear, but intermittent evidence of the layer can be traced for 10-12m NE-SW. 
This midden was sampled in 2009 for scientific and dating purposes, and a charcoal sample submitted for radiocarbon dating produced a late Mesolithic date (Kytamnov et al, 2010, 11).

In the garden of a private house. This bullaun stone consists of a sandstone boulder (0.68m by 0.66m; H 0.35m), rather rounded or subcircular in shape and profile, with a rough, pitted surface. There is a circular hollow (diam. 0.24m; D 0.15m) off-centre in the upper surface. The sides of the hollow appear to be relatively vertical towards the top, but incline gently inwards to merge seamlessly with a gently rounded base.
According to local information, this bullaun stone came from Doonowney townland. It was found amongst stone rubble in the garden of a 19th-century vernacular stone cottage, while the cottage was being demolished. The exact origin of the stone, however, is uncertain (pers. comm. Leo Leydon, 2019).

source_data.original_text:
Located on the S margins of an expanse of damp, rush-grown boggy pasture, on the W bank of a small, shallow N-flowing stream. The stream rises 6m to SE of the fulacht fia, at the interface of the wet ground with gently rising drier ground.
This fulacht fia is evident as a low, roughly crescent-shaped, grass-covered mound (c. 9m NW–SE; c. 4m NE–SW; H 0.3m) composed of a concentration of angular stone fragments in black, charcoal-rich soil. The mound may have been disturbed in the past, and its exact original extent is uncertain. A slight boggy depression on the E side, intervening between the mound and the stream probably marks the trough area.
There is a possible burnt mound (SL005-198----) 15m to SW, and a burnt mound (SL005-196----) 120m to NE. A church (SL005-061001-) and graveyard (SL005-061002-) are located 125m to ENE.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
In an E–W field ditch on the N boundary of a pasture field in an area of undulating boggy terrain. Ground rises gently for 50m to S where a cashel (SL005-016----) is sited on the crest of the elevation.
This fulacht fia is not visible at surface ground level. It has been bisected by an E–W field ditch (Wth 2m at top, 0.5-0.6m at base; D 1.4-1.5m). The mound (L 9m E–W; H 1.4m) is clearly visible in both section faces as a gently domed, dense concentration of angular, heat-shattered stone fragments in black charcoal-rich soil. The top of the mound underlies a layer (D 0.3-0.4m) of peat and sod, and the mound extends to the full depth of the field drain. A piece of timber protrudes slightly from the E edge of the mound at the base of the field ditch in the S section face, but it is impossible to determine if this is related structurally in any way to the fulacht fia. To the N of the field ditch there is an area of rough boggy, scrub-covered ground, and here the field ditch is bordered by heaps of field clearance debris, and soil upcast from the digging of the ditch. These heaps are now largely scrub-covered, but displaced burnt mound material is visible in parts, and two timber planks -possibly originally derived from a trough -protrude from one of the spoil heaps.

Notified to NMS by Leo Leydon.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
In the NW corner of a pasture field, located in damp, level rush-grown ground, bordered to E by a low natural rise.
This burnt mound, probably a levelled fulacht fia, is not visible at ground surface level, but is exposed in section in two intersecting field field drains. A dense layer (L 15m; D 0.23-0.3m) of burnt stones in black, charcoal-rich soil is exposed in section in both the E and W sides of a roughly N−S field drain (Wth 1.2m at top, 0.6m base; D 0.4-0.5m), which cuts through the wet NW corner of the field. The burnt layer is directly overlain by topsoil/sod (D 0.15-0.2m), and overlies a peat layer. The drain intersects at its N end with an E−W field drain on the N boundary of the field. The burnt stone layer is also visible in the E−W drain, extending to E for c. 5m from the point of intersection with the N−S drain.

raw_items.raw_text: early nineteenth-century two-storey square-plan signal tower
constructed by the British Board of Ordnance in the first decade of the 19th century
abandoned by the mid-1810s when the threat of a French invasion diminished

source_data.original_text:
Situated towards the N tip of a flat coastal plain (15m OD), c. 80m W from the coastline to its nearest point, with a small modern housing development located c. 420m to the SSE, and an area of sand dunes c. 900m to the S. The surrounding area consists of unenclosed machair pasture, with a small area of enclosed pasture surrounding the housing development. The site has unobstructed views in all directions. The adjacent signal tower at Knocklane Hill (SL007-057----), located c. 9.6kms to the SW, now survives as a low ruin, and can no longer be seen from this site; the signal tower at Killcologue Point (SL002-062----), located c. 8.25kms to the NE, has been largely demolished, and can no longer be seen from the site. Signal tower site located c. 892m NNE of a wedge tomb (SL005-017----).

An early nineteenth-century two-storey square-plan signal tower, built with roughly coursed rubble masonry (int. dims. 4.25m NE-SW x 4.25m NW-SE). The signal tower consists of the semi-basement level of a signal tower that survives as a shallow square hole\cut lined with rubble stone walls, and a ragged survival of the first few courses (in places) of the former ground floor walls, which retain traces of lime mortar render to the internal faces. Only the internal wall faces and the tops of the surviving walls are now visible. The external wall faces are concealed by the sides of the cut into which the semi-basement level was built, and by a low bank of sand and rubble that surrounds the structure. The corners of the signal tower are aligned to the cardinal directions, with the walls facing NE, SE, SW and NW. The bottom of a square-sectioned vertical drainage channel is present at the N corner of the building. This is believed to have brought rainwater from the roof to storage barrels in the semi-basement.

The signal tower was part of a system of over 80 signal stations constructed by the British Board of Ordnance in the first decade of the 19th century to warn of the approach of a French invasion fleet. Signalling between sites was accomplished using a naval signal post. The system formed a continuous chain from Dublin Bay running clockwise all the way around the coast to Malin Head in County Donegal. It was abandoned by the mid-1810s when the threat of a French invasion diminished (Kerrigan 1995, 157-66).

Compiled by: Stuart Rathbone

Uploaded on 02\11\21

Listed in the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified 'Enclosure' in both. On a SE-facing slope within a dense plantation of coniferous and deciduous trees. It is shown on the 1913 edition of the OS 6-inch map as a subrectangular-shaped hachured feature. It's depiction on this map resembles that of a quarry rather than of an archaeological monument. There were no upstanding remains visible when visited in 1991 or in the course of the latest inspection in 2012. However a feature resembling the plan of the feature depicted on the map is visible from aerial photography coverage (OSi Orthophoto).

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a small platform on a north facing slope near the foot of Tievebaun Mountain within a an area of dense scrub and hazel. The entrance to the souterrain is located within the forecourt area of the court tomb (SL006-025001-) and is exposed at the northern end of a rectangular pit-like depression. The souterrain passage extends for at least 2.5m in a northerly direction. The walls are composed of dry-stone walling and it is roofed by lintels. The entrance opening measures 0.85m wide and is 0.4m high. It was recorded in 1943 as having 'two entrances, each about 2 ft. [0.64m] square. Local accounts say there are three chambers. Only one is no accessible. It measures approx. 20 ft. [6.4m] long by 6ft. [1.92m] wide. From it there is the usual creep-hole into a second chamber which is at present under water but seems to have the same dimensions as the former. A second entrance leads apparently from the outside to the chamber which is now flooded.' (Irish Tourist Association Survey). A second entrance was not located and the souterrain was not explored.

SL006-025002-_01.jpg. The entrance to the souterrain passage.
SL006-025002-_01.jpg. The east wall of the souterrain passage just inside the entrance.
