source_data.original_text:
Listed in the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified 'Sweathouse Possible' in both publications. Not marked on any edition of the OS 6-inch map. On a steep NNE-facing slope immediately above an area of scrub and loose stones. Small rectangular building (int. dims. 1.55m NNE-SSW; 0.85m WNW-ESE) whose SSW side, and the SSW half of the WNW and ESE sides are built into the hillside. The structure is defined by a well-constructed drystone walls (Wth. 0.56m) on the SSW, WNW and ESE sides. That at SSW side is the highest (H 1.4m). Although lower, those at the WNW and ESE sides are still substantial (H 0.85m). The NNE wall, where the entrance must have been, has collapsed and is marked now only by a few stones strewn on the ground. At least three flat, narrow stones at a slight upward angle are visible at the top of the SSW wall which may be the springing for a corbelled roof. The floor level is now comprised of earth and grass. Superficially this resembles an infilled well. There is a local tradition that this is the remains of a sweathouse. The composition of the walls strongly suggest that this structure is post-1700 AD in date.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 21 August 2012

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, in a lowlying area bordered immediately to E by the rising slope of a small hill, and c. 15m to SW by gently rising ground. Shown on the 1837 OS 6-inch map, but not on 1913 edition. Raised trapezoidal area (30m NNE–SSW; 22.5m WNW–ESE at NNE end, 19m at SSW end) defined by an earthen bank. On the E side, the bank cuts across the base of the hill slope so that on this side it is steeper internally and lower externally than elsewhere. The bank (Wth 5-6m) is gently flattened on top (Wth top c. 1m) with a generally low internal slump (int. H 0.4m at WNW, 0.7m at ESE) and a pronounced, broadly slumped external slope (ext. H 1.6m at WNW, 1m at ESE). The bank at the SW angle of the enclosure appear to be more substantial and to project (L c. 6.5m) outward further than the three other corners of the enclosure. The interior is divided in two, slightly NE of center, by a low, broadly slumped bank (Wth c. 3m; H 0.45-5m) on a WNW–ESE axis. The interior is at slightly lower level to S of the dividing bank. There is a low area (Wth c. 3m) in the center of the bank on the NNE side of the enclosure which appears to represent the original entrance.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a slight rise on level, elevated ground. Ground falls away c. 40m to S in a long, broad slope to a lowlying basin of reed-covered, marshy ground. There is a possible barrow (SL007-050----) c. 90m to NE, and a moated site (SL007-015----) c. 230m to NW. The cross-inscribed pillar, which formerly stood upright, lies propped against a rounded boulder. It consists of a rectangular sandstone block (L 1.18m; Wth 0.35m; T 0.15m), on one broad face of which there is a Latin cross (Total H 0.76m; Total Wth 0.32m across arms) with four branching crosslets. The cross is carved to a depth of c. 0.01m below the surface of the stone and fills much of the available space on the stone face. The terminals of the vertical cross shaft and the horizontal arms expand to a slightly concave splay. The base of the vertical shaft does not splay, but rests on a small incised circle (diam. 0.06m) which has a central boss (diam. 0.03m) in false relief. There is a similar central boss within an incised circle (diam. 0.05m) at the junction of the vertical shaft and the horizontal arms of the cross. Two small Latin crosses or crosslets (H 0.16m; Wth 0.09m) rise from the arms, one from the midpoint of each arm. A horizontal bar (L 0.2m) extends across the lower part of the vertical shaft of the main cross, with a crosslet (H 0.13m; Wth 0.09m) rising from each end, mirroring the crosslets on the main arms of the cross. The terminals of the four crosslets appear to be slightly splayed. The cross-inscribed pillar and the townland name suggest that there was an ecclesiastical site here; however, no convincing evidence of this is visible at ground level. 
The unusual branching cross design on this pillar links it with the monastic settlement on Inishmurray Island, c. 9.5km to NW, where there is a collection of cross slabs (SL001-001054-; SL001-001078-; SL001-004005-; SL001-013002-; SL001-016002-) bearing almost identical designs.

source_data.original_text:
In a cashel (SL007-020001-). A souterrain, indicated as ‘Cave’, is shown in the NW quadrant of the cashel on the 1913 OS 6-inch map. A 19th-century account (Milligan 1890-1, 576), however, describes ‘two pairs of crypts or souterrains each pair being detached from its neighbour.’ This suggests that there may be two souterrain here. Describing one pair of chambers (SL007-020002-), Milligan records that a narrow surface opening drops into a ‘passage which is about 12 feet [3.6m] in slant length. The first chamber is about 15 feet long [4.5m], 6 feet broad [1.8m], and 5 feet 9 inches high [1.75m]’. From this chamber, a sloping passage c. 2.4m long drops into the second chamber which is set at a lower level than the first. The second chamber measures ’16 feet long [4.9m], 9 feet broad [2.7m], and 6 feet high [1.8m]; the end of the chamber is curved and the roof arched’ and there is a ‘small funnel’, possibly a ventilation shaft. The chambers are of drystone construction. According to Milligan (ibid.), a second surface opening, some distance from the first, gives access to the second pair of chambers (SL007-020003-), which are almost identical in construction and layout to the other pair, but apparently not connected to them. The cashel was inspected in 1991, but dense overgrowth impeded access to the interior, and the souterrains could not be examined.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on the broad, level top of a ridge on the fertile Maugherow peninsula, with panoramic views, encompassing sea, mountains and undulating hills. At E−S the tomb overlooks the broad sweep of Drumcliff Bay, backed by a dramatic line of mountains: Benbulbin, King’s Mountain and Cope’s mountain at E−ESE, the Ballygawley Mountains at SE, the long undulating spine of the Ox Mountain’s at SE−SW, and the squat bulk of Knocknarae at S. The low outline of the Belmullet Peninsula, Co. Mayo is visible across the sea to W, and the Donegal Mountains, Slieve League and the Blue Stacks are visible in the far distance at N−NNE.
This portal tomb, named ‘Druid’s Altar’ on the OS 6-inch maps, is ruined, but remains an impressive monument. A special and unusual feature of the tomb is that one of its stones bears rock art (SL007-026001-). 
The tomb is of relatively simple design. A single large portal slab defines the E side. The W side is formed of three stones, the portal stone and two much smaller stones, one of which appears to be displaced. The capstone has collapsed and overlies a prostrate slab which bears the rock art. The long axis of the tomb is oriented NNE−SSW, with the entrance at NNE marked by the two portal-stones.

The two massive upright portal-stones each have a roughly lozenge-shaped cross-section and a sloping top, and are well matched in bulk and height. They are notably different, however, in surface appearance. The E portal-stone (H 2.4m; L 2.5m; T 0.9-1.1m) is a heavily quartzite-bearing, white-speckled gneiss, with a rough, seamed surface; its top comes to a peak at the NE end and slopes markedly down from there towards the back of the tomb. The W portal-stone (H 2.6m; L 1-1.1m: T 1.1.) appears to have been deliberately split, giving it relatively smooth, flat angular surfaces. 
The positioning of the portal-stones is such that the gap between them narrows from the exterior (Wth 1.3m) to the interior (Wth 0.6m), creating a funnel-like access to the tomb interior.
The long E portal is the only stone on the E side of the tomb. The W side, however, is defined by the tall portal-stone and a squat, upright boulder (H 0.7m; L 0.7m; T 0.5m) which abuts its S side, with another stone (L 0.9m; Wth 0.55m; T 0.2), probably displaced, immediately to S. The latter underlies a large prostrate slab (L c. 1.7m E−W; c. 1.3m; T 0.5-0.55m), which bears rock art (SL007-026001-) in the form of a series of cupmarks on its NE side. The original position of this stone is uncertain. It now underlies the massive capstone, and one possibility is that it originally served as a back stone to support the capstone. The capstone (L 3.4m NE-SW) is an angular sandstone slab, with a rough, corroded surface. It narrows markedly from its NE end (Wth 0.85m) towards a broad mid-section and SW end (Wth 2m). It has slipped from its original position and tilts to W, with its SW end slumped heavily onto the ground. 
Ground surface in the tomb interior forms a low earth and stone mound, rising 0.3-0.5m above surrounding field level. Two loose boulders at the SW end of the tomb appear to be field clearance stones.

The entrance of the tomb faces NE, where the sun can be seen rising above low hills on the Summer solstice. Across the Bay, directly E of the tomb, the deep glacial valley of Glencar dips between King’s Mountain and Cope’s Mountain; viewed from the tomb, sunrise at the spring and autumn equinoxes emerges at the base of the silhouetted valley, and golden light fills the valley bowl from base to top (pers. comm. Leo Leydon).

source_data.original_text:
At Cloghcor portal tomb (SL007-026----).
This very rare example of rock art found at a portal tomb consists of a series of cupmarks on the surface of one of the stones that form the tomb.
The stone bearing the cupmarks is a large, subrectangular-shaped slab (c. 1.8m E−W; c. 1.3m N−S; T 0.35-0.5m) which lies prostrate and partly embedded in the ground towards the rear (SW end) of the tomb. It is now overlain by the collapsed capstone, and it is possible that it originally served as an end stone to support the capstone. The cupmarks occur on one of the narrower sides of the stone, which presents a relatively flat, smooth surface (L 1.3m E−W; D 0.5m at W end, 0.57m at W end) and currently faces NE toward the entrance of the tomb.
The cupmarks are evident as small, shallow circular dimples (max. diam. 0.04m; D 0.01m) in the stone surface. They are not sharply defined and are barely discernible in normal light conditions. Photographic images taken at night under strong artificial illumination reveal two clusters, each of about 8-10 cupmarks, with a shallow linear feature/motif (L c. 0.1m) merging with the W cluster (see: SL007-026001-_01.JPG; SL007-026002-_01.JPG, provided courtesy of Ciaran McHugh). A shallow, natural ‘step’ or change of level in the surface of the stone divides the two clusters. More cupmarks may be concealed at the E end of the panel, where the stone is embedded in the ground. A 3-D photogrammetry image also highlights these details (courtesy of Martin Duffy).
The purpose and meaning of the cupmarks remain enigmatic. The original position of the decorated stone within the tomb is uncertain, and therefore so too are the original orientation of the decorated panel and how visible it would have been in the past to visitors to the tomb. It is also uncertain whether the rock art is contemporary with the construction of the tomb or was added at a later date in prehistory.

Notified to the National Monuments Service by Tamlyn McHugh.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located in the NE quadrant of a modern rectilinear field. Ground falls gradually to S, towards the N shoreline of Drumcliff Bay. There is a portal tomb (MA007-026----) 200m to NE.
This standing stone is not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. A squat, flat-topped six-sided granite boulder (1.05m E−W; 0.85m N−S; H 1.4m) set upright in the ground. There is no evidence that the stone is shaped or worked; the hexagonal shape is natural, and the angular sides vary in width (Wth 0.45-0.65m). The top is relatively flat but with an uneven surface. The date and function of the stone is uncertain. It is known locally as the ‘Fairy stone’ (SMR file). The stone is used as a scratching post by farm stock and as a result some of the angles are rubbed smooth. A number of small and medium-sized field stones are piled on top of the stone.

source_data.original_text:
On Ardtermon Strand, located in a S-facing sand dune immediately above a shingle beach. In May 1994 this cist was exposed in section as a result of coastal erosion. In October 1994 it was reported to and recorded by the ASI. The structure was of drystone corbelled construction, capped with lintels, and consisted of two compartments, built side by side, each measuring c. 1.7m wide at the base, and 0.7-1m in height. The internal area of both compartments was entirely filled with dark yellow sand. Surrounding the structure was a matrix of small stones, some burnt, with a few shells and animal bones, which extends for c. 10m E–W. Human bone, identified as the left upper arm of a young adult male, was retrieved from the fill of the W compartment (SMR file). An inspection in January 2014 found that the dune face is grass-covered and only one of the two compartments is visible. The remains appear as a shallow C-shaped drystone structure (1.7m E–W; H 0.8m; D 0.9m) set into the dune face, and open to S. The side walls reveal four or five roughly built courses which support an upper course of larger capping stones. The sand which infilled the compartment in 1994 has been eroded away. A few large stones, protruding randomly from the grass, 0.6m to W, may be remnants of the second compartment.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a lawn in the rear garden of a dwelling. Four upright and three prostrate stones appear to represent the last vestiges of a megalithic tomb. The stone to the S is 0.7m long, 0.5m thick and 1.15m high. A pair of stones, probably originally one stone, stand 2.2m to the N of this. The taller stone is 0.95m long, 0.25m thick and 0.90m high and at its N base is a smaller piece, 0.3m long by 0.18m thick and 0.45m high. Beside these to the N is a prostrate stone, 1.25m long by 0.9m wide and 0.4m thick. It is possible that this represents part of the previous stone that has been broken off. Some 0.4m W of this slab is another upright, 1.05m long, 0.55m thick and 0.8m high. A prostrate slab (0.95m by 0.80m and 0.2m thick) lies c. 3.8m to the NNW. Another prostrate slab (1.5m by 0.85m and at least 0.22m thick) lies 1.2m E of the S upright. The relationship of these to the structure is unclear and they clearly are displaced. Inasmuch as the garden has been landscaped there is no evidence of any surviving mound around the structure. The monument appears to be the last vestiges of a megalithic tomb, though in view of the scantiness of the remains some caution is necessary. The orientation of the three principal uprights would support interpretation as the remains of a gallery aligned E-W with possible affinities to those of the wedge-tomb class. However, elucidation of the full design of the monument must await excavation. Immediately E of the monument is a ring-barrow (SL007-040002-) the outline of which is visible as slight circular undulations (diam. 6.5-7m) in the ground surface.

This is one of three middens (SL007-045----; SL007-046----; SL007-047----) exposed in section on the shoreline of Horse Island. A sampling strategy (09E0174) was undertaken in 2009 as part of a radio-carbon dating programme (Sherlock et al. 2009). This large midden which extends around the E tip of the island produced cattle, sheep and pig bones, as well as fish bone and evidence of cereals (Kytmannow et al. 2009, 16). Radiocarbon analysis of a charcoal sample returned an Early Christian date. Sampling at SL007-047---- also returned a date (from charcoal) in the Early Christian period. It is suggested that these middens may be part of a more extensive system along this stretch of the island shoreline (pers. comm. T. Kytmannow 2012).

source_data.original_text:
Located on the narrow summit of a steep-sided hill which rises on the S side of a promontory jutting into the Atlantic. The hill provides extensive views, including Ben Bulbin and the Dartry Mountains at ENE-E, and Knocknarae and the Ox Mountains at SE–S. To W and NW there are views out to sea. Sod-covered, circular mound (overall diam. 7-8m) with a flat top (diam. 2-2.5m) and broadly sloping side (H c. 1-1.2m). An E-W earth and stone field bank (Wth 1-1.2m; H 0.5m), topped with post and wire fencing, overlies the mound to S of centre. There is an upright, concrete trigonometrical station on a concrete base on the flat top of the mound, immediately to N of the field fence. A slight depression is evident at the base of the mound at SE and also at W. The mound barrow is not shown on the 1837 and 1913 OS 6-inch maps, but the location is marked on both maps as a trigonometrical station. There is a promontory fort (SL007-001001-) c. 400m to NW.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

On the N shore of the island-like peninsula of Raghly this midden was discovered in 2014. The remains consist of a deposit of shell material visible in the exposed cliff face below the turf line. Measuring c. 1m by 0.25m thick, it includes periwinkles and limpets with occasional mussel and razor-fish shells (pers. comm. Ciarán Davis, 14 October 2014). The compact and exposed limited extent of the midden suggests that the material may be contained within a pit-like feature.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, in undulating terrain, located at the NW end of a narrow, elongated NW–SE ridge. Ground falls away c. 60m to S into an area of lowlying marshy ground. 
This consists of a circular mound (diam. 5m) with gently domed profile, slightly flattened on top (diam. c. 2m), with low, broadly sloping sides (Wth slope c. 1.5-2m; H 0.3m at NW; 0.6m at SE) that grade into the slope of the ridge on which it is located. The mound is grass-covered. The S side has been partly eroded away, revealing the largely stone-free, earthen core of the mound. According local information, this location was traditionally known as ‘Sheeaun’.

The ridge, on which the barrow is located, consists of an elongated, grass-covered mound (L c. 70m; Wth c. 15m; H c. 2m) orientated NW–SE axis. It has a narrow, flattened top (Wth 3-4m NE–SW) and steep, broadly sloping sides. At both the NW and SE ends, the mound tapers off in a long, gentle slope that grades into the surrounding field surface at SE, and at NW terminates at, or is slightly truncated by, a N-S field fence. The SW side of the ridge appears to have been partly dug away or scarped back in the past. Close to the SE end, there is a shallow, square or rectangular depression (3m NW–SE; c. 3-5m NW-SE) which also appears to be the result of past disturbance. The nature of the ridge as a whole is uncertain. It may be a glacial deposit but, in this locality, its size and form are unusual. The possibility that it was artificially created cannot be ruled out entirely but, on the present evidence, it is taken to be a natural feature.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located at Raghly Point on the SE tip of Raghly peninsula, utilising a low, natural elevation rising above the rocky shore. There are panoramic views over Sligo Bay, with Ben Bulben and the Dartry Mountains to E, Knocknarae to SSE, the Ox Mountains on the S–SW horizon, and distant views of the Donegal Mountains to N. This mound (overall diam. c. 15m E–W) is evident as a low, D-shaped grass-covered platform. It appears to have been circular in plan originally but the S–SSW side, where it borders the shore, has been eroded by the sea to create a straight edge, which drops vertically c. 3.5-4m to the cobble beach below. The flat top of the mound (7m NW–SE; 7m NE–SW) is defined on its perimeter at SW–SE by a low scarp which is highest and most broadly slumped on the W (H 0.75-0.8m; Wth slope 3m) and E (H 0.9m; Wth slope 4.5-5m) where it merges with the slope of the natural rise which the mound overlies. The scarp is lower (H 0.5-0.6m) at NNW-NNE. Stones, which barely protrude from the sod, are evident in parts along the top edge of the scarp at W-NW and at NE, and a few stones break the surface on the top of the platform. In the exposed section face on the S side of the mound, a thin covering of humic soil and sod overlies a layer of relatively stone-free, orange-brown boulder clay (D c. 0.4m). This appears to represent the body of the mound. The boulder clay layer overlies a natural concentration of gravel, rounded stones and boulders, probably a glacial or alluvial deposit, which drops c. 3m to the base of the section face. Though the mound is low profile and not sharply defined when viewed in close proximity, it is clearly visible, silhouetted against the backdrop of the mountains that border Sligo Bay, as one approaches Raghly point from the landward side to N.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the N side of Drumcliffe Bay, located on dry, elevated ground with a S-facing slope. The slope ends at a rocky cliff dropping to the seashore. The location provides excellent views over Drumcliff Bay in the foreground, and of the mouth of Sligo Bay further to S. This possible bastioned fort is not shown on 1837 OS 6-inch map but is indicated on the 1913 edition as a rectilinear enclosure. It was levelled during land reclamation in the early 1970’s, and its outline is now best seen as a cropmark in aerial views (See 'Digital Globe' in Basemap gallery). The cropmark shows a trapezoidal area (c. 38m N–S; c. 40m E-W at N, c. 50m E-W at S) defined on the W, N and E sides by a levelled bank with projections (max. dim. 6-7m) at the NE and NW corners. Outside the bank is an infilled fosse (Wth c. 3-3.5m). There is a hint of a break or possible entrance in the middle of the N side. At ground level, the outline of the enclosure is barely discernible. The interior slopes to S, mirroring the natural fall of ground, and the corner projections are located at the highest point of the slope providing good views along the coast and out to sea. No enclosing element is apparent on the S side where the enclosure is bordered by an eroding cliff face (H 5-6m) which drops to a rocky shoreline and a cobble and sand beach. According to local information, this enclosure was intact in the late 1960’s when it was defined by an substantial earthen bank on the W, N and E sides, with raised rounded projections at the NE and NW corners, and a deep external fosse, all largely engulfed in overgrowth (pers. comm. 2016: Leo Leyden, Maugherow, Co. Sligo). In 2016 magnetic gradiometer and earth resistance surveys (Licence no. 16R0006) were carried out (Siggins 2016). Magnetic anomalies detected in the interior of the fort were interpreted as pits/postholes, with linear features possibly indicating buildings. High earth resistance readings in the centre may indicate a demolished stone building. The data provides tentative evidence for timber and stone buildings erected to accommodate troops and artillery at the fort (Siggins 2016, 12).

In the land-edge scarp on the N shoreline of Drumcliff Bay.
A thin layer (L 1.15m; D 0.05m) of sea shells –cockles, periwinkles, razor shells –is exposed in section at a height of c. 1.3m above the beach cobbles that have accumulated at the scarp base. The shells are visible at the base of a layer (D 0.2m) of brown soil, which underlies a grass/overgrowth-covered overhang (H 1.5-2m) that slumps from field level at the top of the scarp.
The midden overlies stony orange-coloured boulder clay, which in turn overlies a gravelly layer which drops to beach level. The full extent and date of the midden are unknown. Two other middens (SL007-054----; and SL007-055----) are located 195m and 245m to E, respectively.

In the land-edge cliff on the N shoreline of Drumcliff Bay. ITM 560533 843513
A thin layer (L 1.3m; D 0.03m) of fragmentary oyster shells is exposed in section close to the top of the cliff face, at a height of 3-4m above beach level. It is located at a part of the cliff face which projects outward slightly from the E−W line of the cliff.

The quantity of visible oyster shell is meagre, and the full extent and date of the midden are unknown. Two other middens (SL007-053----; and SL007-055----) are located 195m to W and 40m to E, respectively.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on the top of a ridge. Ground falls away in a steep slope to E and more gradually to SE−S. Ground rises again further S to a ridge top on which a portal tomb (SL007-026----) is located 275m to SSW. Views are good to N over undulating terrain, and extensive to E, where a rath (SL007-021001-) is visible on a ridge c. 600m to E, with Drumcliff Bay beyond. Gently rising ground restricts views to W. There is a farmyard at the base of the slope immediately to S.
According to local information, this is the site of an enclosure, and the location was traditionally known as the ‘fort field’. It is not indicated on OS 6-inch maps.
Little remains of the enclosure. A shallow arc of field fence/bank is extant, merging at its SW and NE ends with straight field fences, and coinciding with the boundary between Cloghcor and Cloghboley townlands. It may preserve the W half of a roughly circular enclosure (diam. 15-20m). It is engulfed in overgrowth and difficult to examine. It appears to consist of a curving bank (Wth c. 2-3m; int. H c. 1m; ext. H 1.6m) of earth and stone with a broad slump on the W side. The E face is cut to the vertical and faced with stones. Although clearly been modified to serve as a boundary fence, it is noticeably more substantial than the adjoining straight field fences. The E half of the enclosure probably coincided with the natural coutour/break of slope of the hill, but no trace of an enclosing element is now visible on that side. 
In the early 1990’s, a rectangular hearth-like feature (L c 2m; Wth c.1m) was exposed in the interior area of the enclosure during ground works to create a farm track. It was defined by a setting of low rectilinear stones, and containing black soil. Three fragments representing approximately three-quarters of a rotary quern stone were found in the hearth-like feature. One fragment had a small, rough cross incised on it. The whereabouts of the quern fragments are now unknown (pers. comm. Leo Leydon).

Notified to NMS by Leo Leydon.

Situated in low-lying level pasture within a small copse of coniferous trees. The well has been modernised and is enclosed by a circular concrete wall (int. diam. 2m; T 0.2m; H 1.25m) with access via steps on the S side. The well is located at the centre of a circular paved area (diam. c.17m) enclosed by a wire and post fence. Access to the paved area is via a gate at N. The Stations of the Cross extend around the edge of the paved area NE-SE and SW-NW. The outflow from the well extends beneath the paving and emerges at the S edge of the area where it flows into a drain. A modern stone altar and a N-facing statue of the Virgin Mary are located immediately to the W of the well.

Drystone walling of random rubble limestone was added to the external face of the bank/scarp to form a vertical façade. This walling has largely collapsed where it defines the external face of the bank NW-NE and is better preserved where the bank is absent NE-NW. The original entrance is not recognisable. Mature ash trees grow along the perimeter and across the interior.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a slight rise, in gently undulating pasture, on a slight S-facing slope. An enclosure (SL008-181---* / SL005-114---) is located 60m to the NE. Slightly raised oval area (dims. 33m N-S; 38m E-W) enclosed by a substantial bank of earth and stone (Wth 4.5m; int. H 1m; ext. H 2.5m). At the external foot of the bank is a broad flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 5.2m; D 0.9m). The bank and is best preserved NNE-ENE. From E-ESE the external face of the bank has been quarried out almost entirely removing the bank. The external face of the bank has been cut back and is now almost vertical ESE-S. A now relic modern drystone wall lies along the inner base of the bank S ? W. The fosse is best preserved NNE-E. A drystone wall has been built across the fosse at E and the fosse is infilled and barely visible E-SE. From SE-WSW the fosse is absent and a now disused track lies along the line of the fosse. A modern N-S orientated drain has been cut along the line of the fosse WSW-NW with spoil from the cutting of the drain has been used to infill the fosse NW-NNW. There are two breaks in the bank, at NW (Wth 2m) and at SE (Wth 2m), either of which could mark the position of an original entrance. Dumps of field clearance rocks are located at the centre of the interior.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 21 April 2011

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a slight SSW-facing slope in gently undulating pasture. Roughly circular area (diam. 26m) enclosed by the footings of a drystone wall (Wth 2.3m; H 0.3m). There is no fosse visible at ground level. From N-SE the footings consist of two rows of limestone slabs and blocks (av. dims. L 1-1.6m; T 0.3-0.8m; H 0.3m) with a fill of small rubble between. From SSE-SE the basal external blocks are visible only as this area is now a stockpile (H 1.8m) of rubble stone where three field walls meet. The footings are absent elsewhere and the edge of the site is defined by a slight sod-covered rise. The original entrance may have been at N where there is a slab across the end of the footings. A souterrain (SL008-042002-) is located on the W side of the interior.

The cashel consists of a circular area (diam. 26m) enclosed by a low bank of rubble limestone (Wth 4-5.25m; int. H 0.3-0.45m). There is no fosse visible at ground level. The original entrance is not recognisable. A possible enclosure (SL008-043001-) is located on the W side of the interior.

source_data.original_text:
Situated in level wet upland pasture at the S base of Benbulbin. Oval-shaped area (dims. 31m N-S; 25m E-W) enclosed by a collapsed rubble drystone field wall (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 1.1m). There is no fosse visible at ground level. The facing, of un-coursed random rubble, survives best on the external side of the wall at SW and is very patchy and inconsistent elsewhere. The wall appears to have been entirely rebuilt as part of a field wall NNW-NE (Wth 1.2m; H 1.4). A roughly rectangular sheep pen (dims. 5m NE-SW; 2m NW-SE) extends into the interior at NW. Two other sheep pens have been built against the external face of the cashel wall at SSE. The original entrance is not recognisable. The SE quadrant of the interior is enclosed by a gently curving collapsed drystone wall (Wth 3.4m; H 0.4) that links to the interior of the cashel wall at ENE and at S. A collapsed drystone wall (Wth 3.1m; H 0.3) extends W from the internal side of the cashel wall at NE and ends to N of centre.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 21 April 2011

Situated on a steep SW-facing slope in gently undulating upland pasture. Raised circular area (diam. 21m) enclosed by a substantial flat-topped bank of earth and stone (Wth 4.85m; int. H 1.4m; ext. H 1.8m). At the external foot of the bank is a fosse (Wth 4.65m; D 1-1.6m). The bank is low, denuded and barely visible SSE-W. The fosse encloses the site N-SE and is absent elsewhere. A break (Wth 2m) in the bank at SSE marks the position of the original entrance. To compensate for the underlying slope, the interior is divided into two terraces by a SW facing scarp (H 1.4m) that links to the internal face of the bank at NNW and at ESE. A roughly circular relic quarry (diam. 6m; D 0.4m) is located on the ESE side of the interior against the inner side of the bank. A NE-SW orientated drystone field wall crosses the interior to NW of centre intersecting with the bank at WSW and at NE.

source_data.original_text:
On the S bank of the Drumcliff River, c. 500m E of the mouth of the river where it opens into Drumcliff Bay.
Listed as 'Church' in the SMR (1989) and as 'Church site' in the RMP (1995), this record refers to medieval churches known to have existed at Drumcliff, but which have left no trace at ground level.
A monastery was founded by St Colmcille at Drumcliff in 574 (Gwynn and Hadcock (1970, 34). Early sources suggest that there was more than one church here. The Annals of Connacht record that in the year in 1267 'Drumcliff was completely burned, with its churches'. An entry in the Annals of Lough Cé records that in 1315 the wife of Aodh O Domhnaill, King of Tir-Connaill brought gallowglasses and members of the Clann Muirchertaigh to attack ‘the churches of Druim-Cliabh, and several of the clerics and comarbs of Druim-Cliabh were plundered by her.’  The Down Survey barony and parish maps (1655-6) show two churches at Drumcliff; one of the churches appears to stand more or less at the location of the early 19th-century Church of Ireland church, which now stands in the N half of the graveyard (SL008-084002-), and a second church is shown a short distance to the E. A hint that the current church, which was built in 1809, may indeed overlie the site of an early church is offered by O'Donovan in the 1836 OS Letters: 'There is a tradition that an old church stood where the Protestant church of Drumcliffe now stands, which was called Teampull Buide.' (O'Flanagan 1933, 83 (31)).

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
Located in an area of lowling, damp grassland in the shadow of Ben Bulben, just SE of the mouth of the Drumcliff River, where it flows into Drumcliff Bay.
This graveyard encompasses a roughly L-shaped area, enclosed by a mortared stone wall and bordered at W by the main Sligo-Donegal road (N 15). St. Columba’s Church of Ireland church (see NIAH record no. 32305001), an elegant limestone building, constructed between 1805-09, stands in the tree-shaded NE section of the graveyard, surrounded by a high density of formal inscribed graveslabs, headstones, box tombs and table tombs dating variously from the early 1800’s to the 2000’s. In the SE section of the graveyard, a few informal, uninscribed stone gravemarkers, some set in N-S rows, can be seen amidst the formal grave plots.
Several 20th-century headstones, especially evident in the W section of the graveyard, are in the form of ‘Celtic crosses’, in imitation of the medieval high cross (SL008-084004-) which stands on the NW boundary wall. The high cross is one of the most visually engaging of several monuments which serve to remind the visitor that the graveyard is on the site of an early medieval monastery: a plain cross (SL008-084005-) stands on the line of the boundary wall to W of the high cross; an early medieval cross-slab (SL008-084010-) has been reused as a gravemarker; a high cross base (SL008-084008-) is located immediately S of the church, and two high cross shaft fragments (SL008-084015-) are within the church, and 40m to NW of the graveyard there is a round tower (SL008-084003-).
The graveyard is also celebrated for the grave of the poet William Butler Yeats, the unadorned headstone engraved simply with the poet’s own famous injunction: 'Cast a cold Eye on Life on Death, Horseman, pass by.'

source_data.original_text:
Located 40m NW of Drumcliff graveyard (DG008-084002-), in the shadow of Ben Bulben, and less than a kilometre from the mouth of the Drumcliff River, on the E side of Drumcliff Bay. It stands within a small walled enclosure, bordered on the E side by a road (N15), which intervenes between the tower and the graveyard.
This round tower is a National Monument (no. 119) in state ownership. It consists of a plain, circular tower (diam. c. 5m; current H c. 9m) of coursed, mortared stone rubble, which no longer stands to its full height. At its base there is a low, narrow plinth or offset (W 0.04-0.1m; H c. 0.5m). The rectangular, flat-headed doorway (Wth 0.54m base, 0.53m top) is located on the ESE side, at a height of 1.78m above the offset. There is a square-headed window at SSW, c. 2m below the current top of the tower. (Barrow 1979, 181). 
The 1836 OS Letters record that ‘The name of the tower is ‘Claictheach Dhruim Shliabh’; a great part of it was demolished for the erection of a bridge [SL008-072001-] in the neighbourhood…’ (O’Flanagan 1933, 83-5 (31-2)).
There is a high cross (SL008-084004-) c. 50m to ESE and remains of a plain cross (SL008-084005-) c. 40m to SE, both incorporated into the N boundary wall of the graveyard. The round tower and the crosses are the only visible remains of an important monastery, which St Columcille is said to have founded here c. 574 AD on a site granted by Aed son of Ainmire, King of Ireland. He appointed St Thorian (Mothorain) to be the first abbot (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 34). The annals make several mentions of the monastery between the late 10th to the early 16th century, recording the deaths of various abbots, and also repeated occasions when the monastery was attacked and plundered: For instance, the Annals of Connaught notes that in the year 1416 the abbey was attacked and set on fire, and the abbot Maurice O’Coincoil perished in the flames. The Annals of the Four Masters specifically mention the round tower, recording that it was struck by lightning in the year 1396.

source_data.original_text:
Located on the N edge of Drumcliff graveyard (SL014-084002-), incorporated into the 19th-century mortared stone wall which encloses the graveyard.
This early medieval high cross -an ornately sculpted freestanding stone cross- is a National Monument in state ownership (no. 119). It is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as ‘Stone cross’ and on the 1940-41 edition as ‘Celtic cross’.
 
The cross consists of three separate elements: base block, shaft and ringed head. The base block is devoid of decoration, but the shaft and ringed head are richly ornamented with a harmonious scheme of geometric motifs and figurative biblical scenes, and notable also for a number of intriguing animal figures carved in eye-catching high relief.
The base block of the cross rests on a large flat limestone slab (c. 1.05m N−S; 1.4m E−W), the N end of which is incorporated into the graveyard wall. It consists of a massive block of worked stone (1.2m N−S; 0.97m E−W; H 0.84m), rectangular in basal cross-section, with sides tapering towards a flat top edged with a low step. In the centre of the top is a rectangular mortise or socket which holds the cross shaft (0.45m N−S; 0.3m E−W).
The sandstone cross shaft, with its ringed head, rises to a height of just over 3m above the base. The join between the shaft and the ringed head is clearly visible. Harbison (1992, 70-73) has suggested, based on discontinuities in the decorative scheme, that the current ringed head may not be the original head planned for the cross: either the plan changed during the making of the cross or the original head was replaced at a later date. The uppermost section of the head is damaged, and the cap, usual in high crosses, is missing. There are pronounced semicircular arcs at the junction of the arms, on the inner edge of each of which is a roundel or cylinder, a common feature of high crosses, but, unusually, here the outer ends exhibit decoration, now partly eroded. The ring or wheel is slightly offset from the arms and shaft, which serves to emphasise the arms of the cross. The outer edges of the shaft, arms and ring are defined by roll moulding, which forms a frame for the decorated panels. 
In the following description, the decorative scheme on each of the four faces of the cross will be outlined in sequence from base to top. The meaning of individual figurative scenes cannot always be deciphered with certainty, either because the symbolic intentions of the carvers are now obscure, or simply because weathering over time has abraded detail. In some instances competing interpretations of individual scenes have been offered by scholars.

N AND S FACES:
The decorative schemes on the narrow N and S faces of the cross are almost mirror images of each other. The shaft bears abstract decoration enclosed within a frame of two close-set parallel grooves. The lowest section of the shaft is blank on both faces. Above this on the S face is a panel of gracefully flowing, interlocking spirals, and on the N face, a panel of interlace. Above this on each side, is a small rectangular mortise or socket (H 0.06-0.07m; Wth 0.05-0.06m; D 0.05-0.07m) in the centre of a blank panel. Above this, the S side features a panel of stylized animals intertwined in intricate interlace, with a blank panel intervening between this and the head of the cross; on the N side a panel of interlace rises to the join with the cross head. Just above the join, on both the N and S sides, is a high relief carving of a four-legged beast, rearing up in profile. Immediately above this, on the underside of the ring, is a startling carving of a muscular beast, presented as if viewed from above and facing down the cross. Its four legs are splayed and it appears to crouch or crawl menacingly. The beast on the underside of the N arm of cross is framed by a  double grooved ornamentation. Another downward-facing, crouched beast is carved on the vertical end of the N arm. An image of the Virgin and Child fills the vertical end of the S arm.
 
THE E AND W FACES:
The broad E and W faces of the cross mirror each other in the number and arrangement of their carved panels, which are framed by a decorative border of small raised beads. The ornamentation is symmetrically arranged, with the elements on the E face of the shaft occurring in pairs and those on the W face in threes. Figurative scriptural scenes predominate. Old Testament events that prefigure the coming of Christ are found on the E face; New Testament events feature on the W face. On each face the scenes, reading from base to top, culminate at the junction of the arms of the cross in a scene fundamental to the Christian faith, emphasising Christ’s role as Saviour or Redeemer.
E FACE:
The lowest decorated panel is filled with interlace of four circular elements arranged in pairs. Above this is an elegant rendering of the Fall of Man. The double-stemmed Tree of Knowledge grows directly from the interlace pattern beneath, and Stokes (18, 558) has proposed that the interlace represents the roots of the tree. The canopy of the tree is similarly stylized as four circular spiralling, interlaced motifs arranged in pairs, mirroring the symmetry of the lowermost panel. The sinuous body of the snake wraps itself around the tree, whispering temptation into the ear of Eve, who has already eaten of the forbidden fruit she holds in her hand, and both she and Adam cover their nakedness. 
Directly above this scene is a large, impressive beast, possibly a lion, viewed in animated profile, with its long tail curled upward in a tight spiral. It is carved in markedly higher relief and larger scale than any other image on this side of the cross; indeed, it breaks the frame, protruding onto the angle moulding.
Directly above are two human figures, the one at left is wielding a weapon, striking the figure on the right. This may depict Cain killing his brother Abel (Stokes 1896-1901, 556), or David and Goliath, because the figure at right appears to hold a shield (Harbison 1992, 70-73).
Above this, a human figure, flanked by rearing beasts, represents Daniel in the Lions’ Den.
Centrally placed at the junction of the arms of the cross is the figure of Christ, holding a cross-staff at his shoulder. This signifies Christ in Glory or the Last Judgement. The flanking arms of the cross each bear five simplified disembodied heads. Heads are also depicted on the uppermost section of the cross, but this is now incomplete. The ring is decorated with interlace.
W FACE:
The lowermost decorated panel features six circular, intricately interlaced motifs arranged in pairs. Three upright human figures fill the panel above, the central figure holding a child; suggested interpretations include the Presentation of Christ in the Temple (Stokes, ibid.) or the Presentation of John the Baptist in the Temple (Harbison, ibid.). 
Directly above, is a curious, large four-legged beast, with a deeply sinuous back and a long tail; Harbison(ibid.) suggests it may depict a camel. As with the beast on the opposite side, this is carved in dramatic high relief, with its head breaking through the outer decorative frame of the shaft.
There are three human figures in the scene above; the raised arms of the central figure are held by the two flanking figures. Possible interpretations include the Arrest of Christ, the Smiting of Christ (Stokes, ibid.) or the Mocking of Christ (Harbison, ibid.).
Above this, there are two figures of uncertain identity; Stokes suggests Mary and John; Harbison posits Mary and Joseph returning from Egypt.
Centrally placed at the junction of the arms is the Crucified Christ. The detail here is now quite eroded, but Stokes (ibid.) identified the lance and sponge bearers on either side of Christ. The flanking arms each have a single disembodied head enclosed in interlace. The broken top of the cross also bears interlace.

This is the only high cross to survive intact at Drumcliff, but other high crosses once graced the monastic precincts he

Located on the NW edge of Drumcliff graveyard (SL014-084002-), incorporated into the 19th-century mortared stone wall which encloses the graveyard.
This medieval plain stone cross is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as ‘Ancient stone’ on the 1940-41 OS 6-inch map. It consists of the cross shaft set in a stone base block. The head of the cross is missing.
The base block consist of a large, worked boulder, rectangular in plan (c. 1m NNE−SSW; c. 0.8m WNW−ESE; H 0.5m) which tapers towards a flat top with a central mortise, in which the cross shaft is set. The shaft is fashioned from rough-textured, brown sandstone. It is rectangular in cross-section (Wth 0.58m; T 0.26m), and tapers gently from base to top, rising to a height of 2.86m above the base block.  Both the base block and shaft are devoid of decoration. There is a high cross (SL008-084004-) 30 m to E.

source_data.original_text:
This record refers to a carved stone known as the ‘Angel stone’. It was listed in the RMP (1995) as 'Cross fragment', based on Wood-Martin’s (1882, 303-304; fig. 19) interpretation of the stone as being ‘a portion of the shaft and one arm' of a cross. Wood-Martin’s published illustration shows the stone lying on its side and partly embedded in the ground; a carved human figure or angel extends the length of the stone, with a long wing-like element visible along one side of the body, the other side of the body being concealed below ground level. He does not record the dimensions of the stone. Stokes (1901, 555, note) recorded that this 'piece of medieval sculpture called the Angel Stone was found near the round tower, and is now built into the bottom of the wall on the road side. The image of an angel with outspread wings, much mutilated, is carved upon it.' The stone was noted in the fabric of the roadside wall in 1980 (pers. comm. P. Walsh & M.A. Timoney), but was not located during an inspection in 2005. 
A free-standing subrectangular block of worked sandstone (L 1m; Wth 0.55m; H 0.6m) is currently located adjacent to the round tower. The two vertical long sides and one short end of the stone have rough, uneven surfaces. The horizontal upper surface of the stone has a lower ‘shelf’ along one long side, which exhibits a punch-dressed band (Wth 0.12m), with three small notches (each Wth 0.05m; D 0.04m), spaced 0.15-0.17m apart, cut into its outer edge. The other vertical short end of the stone exhibits a carved figure in very low relief on a dressed surface. The figure (H 0.44m; Wth 0.17m) is located at one edge of the stone and extends almost the full height of the surface. The outline is simple, consisting of a head with a pointed chin resting directly on the shoulders of a rectangular body. No facial features are evident, the body is plain, and nothing resembling wings is evident. The provenance of this stone is unknown. Its original form and purpose is uncertain, but it was clearly worked to allow its incorporation into a structure or building. It is possible that it Wood-Martin’s ‘Angel stone’.

source_data.original_text:
This record refers to two separate components of a high cross, first recorded and illustrated by Wood-Martin (1882, 305-306): a broken cross shaft (see DU018-181----) now in the National Museum of Ireland and the base block of the cross (SL008-084008-) located in Drumcliff graveyard (SL008-084002-). 
The cross shaft (see DU018-181----), represented by two fragments, one from the base of the shaft and one from a section of the shaft just below the ring, is described in detail by Harbison (1992, 73). The fragments have roll moulding on their outer edges. The lower fragment has on one face an intact panel of four paired spirals, the interlace interlocking at centre to create a small cruciform design. Above this is a carving of an animal; only its legs are intact, the upper section of the scene is broken off, but Harbison suggests that it depicts David slaying the Lion. The opposite face also has a panel of interlaced spirals. Above this are three human figures, each dressed in long robe, standing side by side; their upper bodies are broken off, and the meaning of the scene is unknown.
The upper fragment of the shaft features two intact biblical scenes on each face. One face depicts Old Testaments events: Abraham sacrificing Isaac, and above that Daniel in the Lions’ Den. Two New Testament scenes on the other face are interpreted by Harbison as the Resurrection, with the central figure of Christ flanked by two angels and at his feet two sleeping soldiers; and above that, the Mocking of Christ, which shows a central figure flanked by two figures, each wielding a stick or weapon. (Harbison 1992, 73).
The cross base (SL008-084008-) remains in the graveyard, 18m S of the SE corner of the church. It consists of a rectangular block of worked stone (base 0.90m x 0.65m; H 0.28m) which tapers towards the top (0.73m x 0.40m). The socket (0.47m x 0.32m; D 0.05m deep) is broken on its two longer sides. It is devoid of decoration.

source_data.original_text:
Located in a grassy space amidst 19th- and 20th-century grave plots in the E half of Druncliff graveyard (SL008-084002-). This cross-slab is listed in the RMP (1995) as ‘graveslab’. It consists of an roughly rectangular stone slab (L 0.46m; T 0.09m; H above ground 0.4m) embedded upright in the ground, with the long axis aligned N−S. A simple cross-in-circle is incised on the broad, smooth W face of the stone. The circle (diam. 0. 23-0.25m) is outlined by a shallow groove (Wth c. 0.02m; D c. 0.01m). Each limb of the cross is outlined by a groove of similar dimensions to that of the circle. The limbs of the cross extend across the full diameter of the circle; the horizontal limb cuts through the groove of the circle and extend beyond it by c. 1cm on each side, but the vertical limb ends at the inner rim of the circle. Though clearly intended to represent an equal-armed cross, the design is somewhat asymmetrical in execution: the circle is imperfect, being slightly wider than it is high, and the vertical limb of the cross is slightly off centre. 
The cross-slab is deeply embedded in the ground; the incised cross is visible 0.18m below the top of the stone, with the base of the circle just skimming current ground level.  The stone tilts gently to W. The W face is partly covered in white lichen, the E face in moss.

source_data.original_text:
In St Columba's Church of Ireland church in Drumcliffe graveyard (SL008-084002-).
This rectangular limestone graveslab (1.74m x 0.73m) is located in the south interior wall of the porch of the church (built 1809). It is a memorial to Thomas Soden of Grange who died aged 109. He may be the Thomas Soden of Grange, who was appointed High Sheriff of Sligo in 1674.The date of death on the slab is illegible, but it is likely to date to c. 1700. A companion graveslab (SL008-084014-) located in the opposite wall, also dedicated to a member of the Soden family, is dated 1704 and is carved in a similar style. Both graveslabs were moved from Ahamlish Church of Ireland church to their present location. 
The decorative motifs on the upper third of the slab, and the inscription, which extends over the lower two thirds, are raised/carved in false relief. The decorative scheme features a central diamond-shaped frame enclosing a rosette surrounded by four geometric motifs, each composed of five small squares, and flanked by two hearts; beneath the rosette is a small winged skull. At the top of the diamond is a harp, and above this is a crown flanked by a unicorn and a horse. The space to right of the diamond is filled with three plants, two birds and a fleur-de-lis; the space at left features an arm wielding a sword, beside which is a heart. The significance of these motifs is uncertain; some may be heraldic symbols associated with the Soden family; some are likely to have religious significance. The inscription is in English and reads: 
Here lyes waiting
for the resurrecti
on of the just the
body of Tho
Soden of Grange
esqr who die
Ye 3d of March
17 [?]   and the 
109th of his age

source_data.original_text:
In St Columba's Church of Ireland church in Drumcliffe graveyard (SL008-084002-).
This rectangular limestone graveslab (1.70m x 0.75m) is located in the north interior wall of the porch of the church. It is dedicated to the memory of Elizabeth Soden who died in 1704, aged 58. James Soden of Grange, her husband, was appointed High Sheriff of Sligo in 1706. 
This slab, with its companion graveslab (SL008-084013-) located in the opposite wall, which is dedicated to Thomas Soden, possibly Elizabeth Soden's father-in-law, was moved from Ahamlish Church of Ireland church to its present location.
The ornamentation, on the upper third of the slab, and the inscription, which extends over the lower two thirds, are raised or carved in false relief. The decorative scene features a central tree or plant with graceful branches, at the top of which a bird sits; swirling around the tree, are two other birds, a stag, a smaller four-legged animal, two hearts and a fleur-de-lis, the whole carved in a pleasing, naïve style. The inscription is in English and reads: 

Here lyes waiting
for the resurrecti
on of the just the
body of Elliza.th
Soden al.s Steephe
ns wife of James
Soden of Grange esq.r
who died the 6th March
1704 and the 58th of her life.

source_data.original_text:
In St Columba’s church in Drumcliff graveyard (SL008-084002-). The remains comprise two fragments. The first is built into the north interior wall of the porch of the Church of Ireland church (built 1809) beside a graveslab (SL008-084013-) to Elizabeth Soden (dated 1704). The exposed face (L 1m; T 0.30m) is decorated with a series of interlace designs similar to those on the high cross (SL008-08404-) in the graveyard (SL008-084002-). The second fragment is set into the west wall of the nave and forms part of the quoin of the S ingoing for the west door. The stone measures 1.05m along its exposed E face and 0.68m along the ingoing; it is 0.30m thick. The E face is decorated with similar ornament to the other fragment described above and has a small socket (L 0.14m; Wth 0.08m; D 0.07 ) at its N end. It seems likely that these two fragments formed part of the shaft of a high cross.

This midden was found in August 2018 during archaeological monitoring (Licence no. E005004) of the digging of a service trench (L 2.5m E−W; Wth 1.15m; D 0.8m) to repair a leaking water pipe (McHugh 2018). The midden was exposed at a depth of 0.5m below the surface in the N section face of the trench. It consisted of a layer (L 1m E−W; D 0.2m) of oyster, periwinkle and limpet shells in a matrix of dark-brown, friable clayey silt. The midden was recorded, and is preserved in situ. The trench was backfilled with gravel. (McHugh 2018, 31-34).

source_data.original_text:
Located beneath the tarmac access road to a public car park, bordering the N side of Drumcliff graveyard (SL008-084002-). 
This midden was found in June 2020 during archaeological monitoring of works on a water service pipe. A narrow trench (L 140m E-W; Wth 0.25-0.5m N-S; D 0.45m) was opened on or close to the line of the existing water pipe in order to install new piping (McHugh 2020, 1-49; Licence no. E005004X extension). 
A midden was exposed at a depth of 0.35m below the road surface at the W end of the trench. It was visible as a shell and charcoal enriched deposit (1.80m N-S and 0.50m E-W) in the base of the trench. The remains were recorded but were not excavated and they remain in situ. The water pipe was laid 0.10m above the midden layer and the trench was backfilled (McHugh 2020, 37). Another midden (SL008-084016-) is located c. 15m to E. There is a round tower (SL008-082004-) 25m to NW, a cross (SL008-084005-) 10m to SSE and a high cross (SL008-084004-) 25m to E.

A slightly raised rectangular area (dims. 17m NW-SE; 15m NE-SW) defined by an irregular scarp (H 0.3m) lies on the NE side of the interior in the angle between the river and the drain.

Situated on a slight rise in gently undulating wet pasture. Raised roughly circular area (dims. 24m N-S; 25m E-W) enclosed by a narrow bank of earth and stone (Wth 5.1m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 3.15m). At the external foot of the bank are a fosse (Wth 6.15m) and an external bank of earth and stone (Wth 6.95; int. H 1.2m). A roughly rectangular, now disused, quarry (dims. 12m NW-SE; 10m NE-SW; D 3m) abuts the external face of the inner bank and has been cut into the base of the fosse and through the external bank at NE. From E-WNW the external bank is absent but the outer edge of the fosse is still visible. A break (Wth 4m) in the internal bank with a causeway across the fosse at WNW marks the position of the original entrance. There is a modern break (Wth 5m) in the internal bank at WSW.

source_data.original_text:
Located on a high ridge bordered on it S side by a rocky ledge, with sandhills to N and NW. A rectangular shaded feature (c. 15-17m N-S; c. 9-10m E−W) with ‘Church’ in gothic script written beside it, is shown on the 1836-7 OS 6-inch map; the location is annotated ‘Church (Site of)’ on the 1840-1 edition. In the OS Letters, O’Donovan recorded ‘an old edifice, in ruins, at which there was formerly a burial [SL008-096002-] as tradition says.’ He theorised that it might be the ‘Creadran Cille, which is mentioned in the annals at the year 1257’ as the site ‘in Ros Cede’ of a battle between Godfrey O’Donnell, Lord of Tirconnell and Maurice Fitzgerald, Lord Chief Justice of Ireland (O’Flanagan 1928, 133-4 (53)). There are no visible remains of a church or graveyard (SL008-096002-) at the location.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 14 December 2016

source_data.original_text:
Spanning level summit of narrow E-W ridge in undulating rocky pasture. Natural ground level slopes down steeply immediately to the N and S of the site. Slightly raised circular area (diam. c.22m) enclosed by a narrow bank of earth and stone (Wth 4m; int. H 0.3m). At the external base of the bank is a berm (max. Wth 4m) and an external broad flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 4-5.5m; D 1-1.4m). The internal and external sides of the bank appear to have been revetted with limestone slabs laid on edge. The berm and the fosse are present from SW-NW and NE-SE. The steeply sloping sides of the ridge slope down from the external base of the bank from SE-SW and from NW-NE. A break (Wth c.3m) in the bank at ESE marks the position of the original entrance. There is an annex located immediately to the W of the rath. This consists of a roughly rectangular area (dims. 22m N-S; 14m E-W) enclosed by a narrow bank of earth and stone (Wth 1.4m; int. H 0.4m). At the external base of the bank is a fosse (Wth 1.15; D 0.2m). The bank of the annex extends in an E-W direction from the NW side of the bank of the rath. The W side of the annex is defined by a bank with an external fosse that lies 4m from and parallel to the fosse of the rath. The S side of the annex is defined by a 7m length of bank linking at a right angle to the bank defining the W side and by the steep S-facing natural slope of the ridge.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 21 April 2011

source_data.original_text:
Located at the NE end of Coney Island, in Sligo Bay. This midden was included in the RMP (1995) on the basis of a small scale map published by Synge (1985, 128) which showed the approximate location of two middens (SL008-099----; SL014-003----) on the NE shoreline of Coney Island. Based on Synge’s map, this midden was listed in the RMP (1995) at IG coordinates 16229 33940 (roughly ITM 562246 839407). No trace of a midden was found at this location during field inspections; it may have been destroyed by erosion. Alternatively, given the approximate nature of the location recorded on Synge’s map, it is possible that the midden noted by Synge is the same as a midden (SL008-204----) which was exposed in the intertidal zone on the adjacent beach by the eroding action of a high tide in 2015.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 29 September 2016

Situated on a slight rise in undulating rocky pasture immediately to S of steep NE facing slope overlooking Doonweelin Lough to NE. Oval raised area (dims. 24m NW-SE; 18m NE-SW) enclosed by a substantial bank of earth and stone (Wth 4m; int. H 0.6m; ext. H 4m). At the external base of the bank are a broad flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 6.5m) and an external broad flat-topped bank of earth and stone (Wth 3.6m; int. H 1.3m). From NW-E the fosse and external bank are absent where a very steep 4m high natural NE facing slope breaks immediately outside the base of the internal bank. A break (Wth 4m) in the internal bank, a causeway across the fosse and a corresponding break in the external bank at SE marks the position of the original entrance. A second entrance appears to have been located at NW where there is a causeway (Wth 2-3m) across the fosse but no break is visible in the internal bank. There is a modern break (Wth 4m) in the external bank at SW. The remains of an enclosure (SL008-104002-) and a hut site (SL008-104003-) are located on the S side of the interior against the inner face of the bank.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a slight NE-facing slope in gently undulating pasture. A steep natural N-NE facing slope defines the edge of the site NW-SE. Oval raised area (dims. 33m WNW-ESE; 26m NNE-SSW) enclosed an internal bank of earth and stone (Wth 4.7m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 3.25m). At the external foot of the internal bank is the first fosse (Wth 6.5m). Immediately outside the first fosse is an intermediate bank of earth (Wth 5.7m; H 0.8m). At the external foot of the intermediate bank is a second fosse (Wth 3.2m). Immediately outside the second fosse is an external bank of earth (Wth 3.4m; H 0.7m). At the external foot of the external bank is a third fosse (Wth 3.1m; D 1m). From NW-NE the internal bank is absent and the internal enclosing element is a slight broad scarp (H 0.4m) that merges with the steep NE-facing slope. A modern drystone field wall and post-and-wire fence extends along the top of the internal bank WSW-NW. The first fosse, intermediate bank and second fosse are absent NW-E and the external bank and the third fosse are absent NW-SE due to the steep NE-facing slope that abuts the NE side of the site. A modern drain has been cut along the base of the external fosse SE-SSE and the external side of the external fosse has been re-cut and lined with modern drystone walling SSE-SW. A break (Wth 2.5m) in the internal, with a corresponding break in the intermediate bank, and a causeway (Wth 2.5-4m) across the first and second fosses marks the position of the original entrance.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 21 April 2011

raw_items.raw_text: OS Name Books (OSNB Co. Sligo, vol. 1, 293)

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on the brow of a low rise on an E-W ridge, which borders the N side of Drumcliff Bay. Ground falls away gradually for 150m to the stony shoreline.
A souterrain in Finned townland was known about in the early 19th century when it was noted in the OS Name Books (OSNB Co. Sligo, vol. 1, 293), however, its exact location was not recorded, and it was, therefore, not listed in the RMP (1995). It was rediscovered in the early 21st century (pers. comm. Leo Leyden, 2019). 
A subcircular opening (max. dim. c. 1m) is visible at surface ground level. It opens into a stone-lined subterranean cavity (D c. 1m), part of a drystone-built chamber or passage. The surface opening is not an original entrance, but most likely resulted from the collapse of a roof lintel. The chamber/passage is now partly infilled with loose soil, and its original form is difficult to determine; drystone walling is evident at S-SW, possibly a side or end wall, and the chamber/passage appears to continue to NNW or N.

Attached images:
SL008-157----_01 Surface collapse/current opening to souterrain
SL008-157----_02 Drystone chamber/passage, viewed from SE

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 19 February 2019

source_data.original_text:
Situated in gently undulating pasture 100m to N of foreshore at W end of Rosses Point. There are excellent views over Oyster Island, Coney Island and the mouth of Sligo Harbour. This enclosure is not depicted on any edition of the OS 6-inch map, but is recorded on an aerial photograph (OS 3 0337-8, roll 158, pr. 24). A field inspection in 1994 found that the enclosure had been leveled, but a faint outline could still be traced. It consisted of a circular area (diam. 9.5m N−S) defined by a fosse, evident as a shallow depression (Wth 2-2.3m; D 0.2m). Outside the fosse, an outer bank could be traced at NE−W as a very low rise (Wth c. 2m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.1m). The overall diameter from mid bank to mid bank was 16m N−S. The interior sloped gently down from N to S. When inspected in 2004, there was no visible surface trace at ground level.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 21 April 2011

source_data.original_text:
Eight architectural fragments set into the wall of a cottage. 1) A slender six-sided, champfered pillar stone fragment (L 38cm, W 27cm). 2) A crude block of stone, cut edged on three sides with two incised panels cut into one of the edges. 3) A block of cut stone (L 30cm, W 20cm). 4) Worked stone (L 93cm, W 34cm), possibly part of a window, T-shaped head with champfered sides. The raised area has two small square indentations with a projecting edge between. The left soffit of the head of the stone has a simple roll moulding. 5) Irregular block with well worked chamfers giving a roll moulding effect in profile (dims. 38cm by 28cm). 6) Irregular block of stone (L 84cm, W 10cm) one face pocked and small cut incision. 7) Block of stone (L 1.12m) deep well at edges. 8) Corner or impost stone (L 28cm) with triangular incised area with triglyph design.

source_data.original_text:
This record was listed in the SMR(1989) as 'routeway' based on  a reference in O'Rorke (1890, 45-8). It is listed in the RMP (1995) as 'road'. It appears to refer to a routeway, indicated by dashed lines on the 1836-7 OS 6-inch map, which extends for c. 1.4km across the sand flats in Druncliffe Bay between Doonierin townland on the S shore and Coolbeg townland on the N shore. It was used at low tide to cross the bay, and joins paved roads on dryland on both the N and S shores. On the N shore a castle (SL008-069----) and salt pans (SL008-068----) are located on the shoreline flanking the dryland road. No trace of any man-made structure is apparent across the sandflats on the line of the route.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
Built into E-W orientated N-facing near vertical scarp overlooking foreshore on N side of Oyster Island. Rectangular structure (Max. ext. dims. 4.2m E-W; 3.2m N-S), with the vertical front (Wth 4.2m; H 2.9m) facing N constructed of roughly quarried sandstone and limestone blocks bonded with a rough lime mortar. The bowl is infilled (int. dims. 3m E-W; 2.6m N-S) with rubble stone and earth and only the E wall (T 0.6m; H 0.6m) is intact as the W and S walls have collapsed. A large recess is located centrally at the base of the N side with a vaulted roof and a segmental arch (Wth 2.15m; H 1.3m) with well cut voussoirs of limestone and sandstone supporting the front wall of the kiln. The side walls of the recess are splayed inwards and the roof slopes down toward the rear of the recess where a raking hole (H 0.2m; Wth 0.25m) is located. Immediately above the keystone of the arch supporting the recess is a stoking hole (H 0.15m; Wth 0.1m) that slopes upwards into the bowl of the kiln. A midden (SL 008-101---) is located 250m to the W and a mound (SL008-100----) 200m to the SE.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 21 April 2011

source_data.original_text:
In the base of a broad valley of flat, damp pasture, stretching c. 800m to W to the E shoreline of Drumcliff Bay, and overlooked to N by the looming bulk of Ben Bulben. The valley is now criss-crossed by a network of drainage ditches. There is a field ditch/canalised stream, on roughly E−W axis, 8m to S of the enclosure, and to S of that, the flat land extends for a further c. 100m before meeting rising slopes. Approximately 50m to N of the enclosure, ground rises in a gradual slope.
This enclosure is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch mapping. It was first identified on Lidar imagery (pers. comm. Dr Steve Davis, UCD School of Archaeology), and is also visible in current aerial imagery.
A flat circular area (c. 70m) is defined by low remnants of an earthen bank (Wth 3-4m; H 0.1-0.2m). The bank has been levelled in the past and its outline is now barely discernible at ground level: It can be traced at WNW−E as a very low profile, broad grass-covered rise; there is a large break (Wth 18m) at E−ESE; the bank is visible as barely discernible undulation/cropmark at SE−S, and cannot be traced at S−W.
The interior is not raised, and is wet and soggy underfoot, especially so in the W half. A later field ditch (Wth c. 2m) on a NNE−SSW axis cuts through the centre of the enclosure.

Not indicated on any edition of the OS maps, this possible barrow was discovered in 2013 in the course of a review of LiDAR data where it is visible as a bi-vallate enclosure-like feature (diam. c. 45m). Although the remains bear a superficial resemblance to monuments of the ringfort class, it is to be noted that the inner enclosed area is almost 1m lower than the exterior ground level (pers. comm. Dr Steve Davis, UCD). In consequence, some caution is necessary in regard to classification and the remains could be interpreted as possibly falling within the pond-barrow or embanked barrow traditions. source_data.original_text:
In pasture, in the NW corner of a field of flat, damp ground. There is a spring well/holy well (SL008-202002-) immediately to NE. A low, grass-covered roughly D-shaped mound (c. 15m N–S; c. 10m E–W) defined by a curving scarp at NNW–S. The scarp is more pronounced (H 0.6m) at NNW–NE but peters out to a barely discernible rise toward the S. The straight side of the mound at W is created by a N–S land drain (Wth top 2.5-3m, Wth base 0.8-1m; D 1.2m) which truncates the SW quadrant of the mound. Angular, heat-shattered stones in a black, charcoal-rich matrix are visible in section in the side of the drain for almost its full depth. It is probable that the burnt mound extends to W beneath a N–S farm road which borders the W side of the drain. Fencing and a small concrete pump house at the spring well appear to truncate the N-NE edge of the mound.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the NW side of a field of flat, damp ground. According to local information, this well is associated with St. Columcille and is visited annually on the saint’s feast day, the 9th of June. It consists of a natural spring enclosed by a rectangular surround (1m NNW–SSE; 0.7m ESE–WSW; D 0.2m) of concrete and stones. A stream flows N from the well for a few meters and then turns to W. There is a concrete pump house immediately to S of the well. The well is located in the SE corner of a square fenced enclosure (c. 8m N–S; c. 8m E–W), with a wooden gate giving access at the W. The enclosure is thickly ringed with willow scrub and brambles, with an ash tree and a hawthorn bush close to the well at SW. There is a burnt mound (SL008-202001-) immediately to SW.

source_data.original_text:
This midden is located at the N end of the S or smaller beach at Rosses Point, exposed in section on the N side of a U-shaped indentation at the base of the eroding W-face of the dunes. It is overlain by the pale-coloured sands of the dunes which form a layer 0.9-1.6m high above the midden, but which rise to several meters in height as they extend to E in undulating, marram grass-covered hills. The midden overlies a layer (0.45-0.5m) of orange-brown stony subsoil which rests on bedrock. As a result of differential erosion, a narrow shelf (L c. 8m NW-SE; max. Wth 1.4m NE–SW) of the more weather-resistant stony subsoil protrudes from beneath the dune face. The midden is exposed on the surface of this shelf. The midden is evident as a dense, compact layer (L 6.5m NW–SE; max. D 0.1m) of oyster shells, which also incorporates a small quantity of periwinkles, stones and charcoal fragments. Due to age/weathering, the oyster shells are in a friable and shattered condition. The shell layer is more fully exposed in plan, and is thickest in depth, at its NW end (Wth 1.2m NE–SW; D 0.1m), but towards the SE the shell layer is visible only in section as a thin lens (D 0.002-0.004m). At its SE end, it is overlain by, or incorporated into, a layer (D c. 0.05-0.07m) of rusty orange-coloured sand exhibiting moderate charcoal flecking, with the pale coloured dune sand overlying this. However, at its NW end the pale-coloured dune sands appear to directly overlie the midden. The exposure of the midden appears to have occurred during the period 2014-2015 as a result of high tide and storm action (pers. comm. 18th May 2015: Dr. J. Bonsall, Sligo IT/Masc Project (Monitoring the Archaeology of Sligo's Coastline)).

source_data.original_text:
In Sligo Bay on Oyster Island, located on the S shoreline at the W end of the island.
This midden was discovered in 2009 during a survey undertaken for the Heritage Council (Kytmannow et al. 2009, 7-9). The midden is visible as a layer (max. D 0.6m) of densely concentrated oyster shells, which is exposed in section along the shoreline. It has been traced intermittently for a length of c. 50m. A single lithic, a bi-polar core, was recovered. The midden was sampled for environmental and dating analyses, and produced a C14 date indicating use in the Iron Age (2nd Cent AD), (Kytmannow, et al,  2009, 27; Kytmannow et al. 2010, 6). There is an enclosure (SL208----) dated to the 13th century AD immediately adjacent.

Compiled by: Jane O’ Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 22 January 2018

source_data.original_text:
Located on the S shoreline at the W end of Oyster Island, in Sligo Bay. 
Not indicated on OS 6-inch maps, this enclosure was first recorded using Low Altitude Aerial Photography in 2009 (Kytmannow et al, 2009, 29 (Pl. 33), 30 (Pl. 34)). It is evident at ground level as a subrectangular or roughly D-shaped area (c. 100m E−W; c. 35m N−S) defined in a shallow and irregular curve on the W, N and E sides by a low-profile, sod-covered bank, and on the straight S side by an eroding scarp, which defines the shoreline and borders a stony beach. A break in the bank towards the E end of the N side may represent an entrance feature. A circular feature in the E half of the interior may be a hut site (SL008-208001-). 
In 2012 a portion of the enclosing bank at its eroding E terminal was archaeologically sampled (licence: 12E0255) for the purposes of environmental and dating analysis. A shell retrieved from one of the samples produced a calibrated radiocarbon date of 1264-1297 AD (Read 2012).
There is a shell midden (SL008-207----) dated to the Iron Age on the shoreline immediately to S of the enclosure.

Compiled by: Jane O’ Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 24 January 2016

Located within an enclosure (SL008-208----). This possible hut site is evident as a clearly defined circular feature (diam. c. 4m). It is located in the E half of the large subrectangular enclosure, which has been dated to the 13th century AD (Read, www.excavations.ie 2012:537). There is a shell midden (SL008-207----) dated to the Iron Age on the shoreline immediately to S of the enclosure.

Compiled by: Jane O’ Shaughnessy
