source_data.original_text:
This massive circular, limestone cairn (diam. c. 60m; H c. 10m), named ‘Miosgan Meva’ (Maeve’s Cairn) on the OS 6-inch maps, crowns the summit of Knocknarae Mountain. Its flat-topped silhouette is a miniature version of the squat bulk of the mountain itself, which rises abruptly from the fertile coastal grasslands of the Cúil Irra peninsula, flanked by Ballysadare Bay to S and Sligo Bay to N. It is one of the most iconic archaeological monuments and landmarks in NW Ireland, its importance, past and present, manifest in the enduring folk tradition which identifies it as the burial site of the legendary Queen Maeve of Connacht.
The pale-grey cairn, rising above the dark heather-covered plateau and light-reflecting limestone escarpments of the mountain, is visible and instantly recognisable from many widespread points in the surrounding landscape. The location of the cairn itself affords panoramic views, encompassing extensive areas of county Sligo, and stretching far into counties Mayo and Donegal. Important distant landmarks which tie the cairn into an ancient network of routeways and a wider ritual and mythological landscape, include Benbulben, the cairn-topped peaks of the Ballygawley Mountains (SL020-128----; SL020-129----; SL021-007----) and the Ox Mountains (SL019-174001; SL019-174002-; SL019-177----), Cairns Hill (SL014-231001-; SL014-232----), Carrowkeel Megalithic cemetery (MA040-086---- to MA040-105----) and Kesh Corann (SL040-008----). 
In its more immediate vicinity, the cairn is the dominant visual focus of a remarkably dense concentration of prehistoric ritual and settlement monuments. It is flanked on the summit by a roughly N-S linear cluster of smaller satellite tombs, cairns and mounds (SL014-076001- to SL014-076009-; SL014-076019-); the descending terraces of the mountain host huts sites (SL014-076047- to SL014-076050-), and field walls (SL014-076011-), and two caves (SL014-288----; SL014-290----) on the W flank of the mountain have produced evidence of Neolithic burials. At the foot of the mountain, the numerous passage tombs of Carrowmore megalithic cemetery (SL014-209001- , etc.), and associated monuments, spread eastwards across the undulating lowlands of Cúil Irra.
Flat-topped, with broadly sloping sides, the cairn presents a deceptively simple outline. Closer examination reveals more complexity (Berg 1995, 238-239). Although the body of the cairn is primarily limestone, a number of large gneiss boulders protrude from the perimeter at N−NE, and may be part of a kerb. Five small, low subcircular or D-shaped cairn-like concentrations of stone (diam. 8-11m; H 0.5-1m) abut the base of the cairn at E, S and W. Two large stones, a prostrate limestone slab 2m to N of the cairn, and a gneiss erratic 5.5m to S of the cairn, appear to represent deliberately placed markers on a N−S alignment. A low, inconspicuous earthen bank (Wth c. 3m; H 0.3m) encircles the cairn at a distance of 1-6m; it respects the five small cairns and the marker stones, kinking outwards to include them within its circuit (Berg 1995, 238-239). 
The cairn is intact; it escaped the depredations of 18th- and 19th-century treasure hunters, and it has not been excavated. Its internal structures, therefore, remain a mystery. It is likely to be about 5000 year old, the same age as its eastern counterparts, the excavated Neolithic passage tombs at Newgrange (ME019-045----) and Knowth (ME019-030001-). 

Maeve’s Cairn is a National Monument (No. 153) in state ownership.

source_data.original_text:
On the summit of Knocknarae Mountain, located 35m S of a large passage tomb, known as Maeve’s Cairn (MA014-076003-), and 7m to SW of a mound (MA014-076004-).
 ‘Stone circles (site of)’ is marked at roughly this location on the OS 6-inch map. There are scant remains of this possible passage tomb. An arc of eleven low gneiss stones (H 0.1-0.3m) appears to define the S perimeter of a stone circle (diam. c. 12m) (Bergh 1995, 240), or possibly a kerb (Ó Nuallain 1989), although no trace of a cairn is evident. To N of the arc, a single set boulder may be the in situ back stone of a chamber that opened to the SE. Three displaced boulders lie to E of it. It is likely that this is one of the monuments on Knocknarae, which were disturbed in the early 1800’s by Richard Chamber Walker, a local landowner and antiquarian. (Bergh 1995, 240, site 5). This is a national monument (No. 153) in state care.

On the summit of Knocknarae Mountain, located 60m S of a large passage tomb, known as Maeve’s Cairn (MA014-076003-), and 18m to S of a possible passage tomb (MA014-076005-). There are two cairns (MA014-076008-; MA014-076008-) located 8m to SSW and 30m to SE respectively.
There are scant remains of this possible passage tomb. It was described by Wood-Martin (1888, 111) as ‘…a ruined circle, of which eight stones only, and four of the cist, now remain…’. It is evident now as a loose, irregular cluster of twelve gneiss boulders, with only one boulder set upright (H 0.7m). It may have been disturbed in the early 1800’s by Richard Chamber Walker, a local landowner and antiquarian. (Bergh 1995, 241). This is a National Monument (No. 153) in state ownership.

On the summit of Knocknarae Mountain, located 26m SE of a cairn (MA014-076008-), and 90m SSE of a large passage tomb, known as Maeve’s Cairn (MA014-076003-). It is located towards the S edge of the summit plateau, with a 2m drop in ground level immediately to E.

(Bergh 1995, 241, site 9). This is a National Monument (No. 153) in state ownership.

source_data.original_text:
On a broad terrace below and to SE of the summit of Knocknarae Mountain, 325m SSE of the large passage tomb, known as Maeve’s Cairn (MA014-076003-). It is located 15m from the edge of the terrace, where there is a steep fall of ground to SE. 
This passage tomb consists of a circular cairn (diam. 13.5m) which encloses a central cruciform chamber and passage (L 5.5m), opening to SE. The chamber and passage, constructed of upright stones or orthostats (H 0.3-0.7m), are  now roofless, and the passage is greatly ruined. The cairn is low with a flat profile, and does not rise above the top of the orthostats. It is defined on its perimeter by a kerb of set stones (av. L 0.5-0.7m; H 0.4m). Interestingly, all the visible kerb stones and orthostats are of gneiss, bar one limestone orthostat in the back recess of the chamber. The tomb is largely concealed by heather. (Bergh 1995, 241-242, site 10).

source_data.original_text:
One of four buildings (SL014-076044-; SL014-076045-; SL014-076046-; SL014-076052-) located on a narrow ledge on the N side of Knocknarea Mountain, it consists of the foundations of a building represented by two rectangular room-like spaces set at right angles to each other. The N room (outer dims. 5.5m x 4m) is set perpendicular to, and with its short wall abutting the long side of the S room (outer dims. 6m x 3m). No formal entrance or doorway was noted. From their location on the isolated and limited ledge it is suggested that these buildings may have been used in one and the same context. What that context was, and especially its date, remains unknown (pers. comm. Stefan Bergh, 14 August 2014).

Compiled by: Paul Walsh based on details kindly provided by Dr. Stefan Bergh (NUI Galway).

Date of upload: 12 November 2014

source_data.original_text:
In damp, pasture, in the SW corner of a field, at the junction of two field drains, and close to the junction of four townlands.  Indicated on the 1940 OS 6-inch map as  ‘Holed Stone’.  Upright slab (max. H 2.15m; Wth 2.65m; T 0.2m), with long axis E-W.  The narrow W side of the stone is vertical, grading into the gently arching top, but the E side is broken by a marked step or indentation. There is a perforation (0.86m E-W), off-centre to the E, through the broad face of the stone. According to local tradition, a sick person who passed through the perforation would be cured. 

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Located at the NE end of a hedgerow-lined lane, border by pasture fields. Spring well confined to a square pool (0.9m NNE-SSW; 1m WNW-ESE) by a modern concrete wall (H 0.9m) on three sides, and by a low concrete step on the open side to WSW. The spring exits the well through an outflow hole at the base of the NNE wall, and is channelled from there as a shallow surface stream into a field drain. A burnt mound (SL014-279----) lies 45m to NNW and a second burnt mound (SL014-278---- ) is c. 75m to NNW. There is a standing stone (SL014-105----) c. 200m to NNW.

dimensions.raw: total diameter 16.30 m; circular mound 5.50m in diameter and 40cm high; fosse 1.50m wide and 30cm deep; bank 2m wide and 60cm high; forty feet in diameter

source_data.original_text:
Timoney (1984, 323, no. 12) describes this as follows: ‘The total diameter of this ring-barrow, sited on low ground, is 16.30 m. It consists of a circular mound, 5.50m in diameter and 40cm high, surrounded by a "U"-bottomed fosse, 1.50m wide and 30cm deep, and by a bank, 2m wide and 60cm high. Petrie (1837; Stokes 1868, 245) in dealing with the megalithic remains at Carrowmore refers to this as follows: "This circle which is situated near the road, and eastnortheast of no. 9, is composed of small stones mixed with earth and is forty feet in diameter. There is a stone sepulchre in the center but no cromlcach". Since then it has consistently been classified as a megalithic tomb. Wood-Martin (1888, p. 15, fig. 1) marked this monument on his map as no. 12 and restated Petrie's description of it. Following them Borlase (1897, 151), who completely misinterprets Wood-Martin's plan of the monument, Herity (1974. 266) and Kitchen (1983, 161) all have sought to explain this monument as the remains of a megalithic tomb. If Pertie's no. 12 be equatable with the monument described above, and there seems to be no cartographic or literary reason to do otherwise, then the interpretation of this monument as being the remains of a megalithic tomb are unwarranted. Burenhult (1980:1, 93) lists this not as a megalith, but as Structure 3, Carrowmore.’ (Bergh 1995, 186, Carrowmore 12)

This is a National Monument in State care (No. 153).

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 12 February 2014

raw_items.raw_text: This rath is a National Monument (No. 153)

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, straddling a rise in undulating terrain. Knocknarae Mountain looms to NW, and Benbulbin and the Dartry Mountains dominate the horizon at N−NE. There is a passage tomb (SL014-115----) 100m to N and another (SL014-209007-) 200 m to SW.
This rath is a National Monument (No. 153) in state ownership. It consists of a raised circular platform (diam. 29.6m N−S; 31m E−W) defined by an earth and stone bank. The bank (Wth 3m at S, 4m at N; int. H 0.9m at S, o.3m at N; ext. H 1.2m at S, 1.75m at N) is intact at S−NE, with a relatively low but compact internal slope and a broad external slump. Stones protrude randomly along the top and external slope, suggesting that it may have been topped or faced with stone walling in the past. This is most evident on the W arc, where low, moss-covered stones on the top of the bank resemble rough wall footings (Wth 0.8m). At NE−SE the raised internal lip of the bank does not survive, and here the rath platform is defined only by a steep external scarp (H c. 2m at E), which is enhanced by the natural fall of ground.
There is a poorly defined gap (Wth c. 2m) in the bank at NE; this may be the location of an original entrance. At ESE there is a broad, slightly sunken break (Wth 5.5m) at the top edge of the platform, which extends down the slope, narrowing toward the base of the slope; it is possible that this represents a steep, entrance ramp, but it seems more likely to be the result of disturbance in the modern era.
The W two third of the interior are level; the E third slopes down gently toward the perimeter. Two shallow circular hollows (diam. 1.8-2m) in the N half of the interior may be the remains of hut sites (SL014-0116002-; SL014-0116003-). 
The interior of the rath is grassy. A number of hawthorn bushes and clumps of brambles grow on the perimeter at W; on the E arc the external slope of the rath platform is obscured by a dense thicket of brambles and hawthorn bushes. On the S arc, the bank has been adapted to serve as a field boundary and is topped by a post and wire fence, and a hawthorn hedgerow; here the external face of the bank drops to a grassed-over farm track which skirts the rath.

raw_items.raw_text: Thomas O'Conor recorded the following about the well in 1836

source_data.original_text:
This well is first recorded as an antiquity on the 1st ed. OS 6-inch map where it is named ‘Tobernashelmida’. Thomas O’Conor recorded the following about the well in 1836 (OSL, 211): ‘There is a well in the Town of Sligo called Tobar na Seilmide, Snail’s Well, which, prophetic tradition says, will in time to come overwhelm by its waters the whole town. The reason why it is called Tobar na Selmide is, a snail is seen coming out of the well every seventh year, which is thought to be an enchanted and metamorphosed being, possessing the power of affecting in some time future an overflowing well, which will have the narrated effect.’ There is no local tradition of it being a ‘holy well’ nor is it listed as such in the published historical or antiquarian literature (pers. comm. M.A. Timoney).

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 5 November 2013

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, at the NW corner of a field. A circular area (diam. 22.2m) is defined by a bank (int. H 0.69m; ext. H 0.81m; Wth 1.4m), which is reduced to a scarp from NW to NE, and an external fosse (Wth 5.5m). The entrance to the site is at the S (Wth 2m).

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 21 April 2011

condition.preservation_state: overgrowth impedes examination; internal slope broadly slumped

dimensions.raw: diam. c. 30m; bank Wth c. 5.5m; int. H 1.2m; ext. H 1.6m, at N; fosse Wth 5-6m

phi_data.condition: overgrowth impedes examination; internal slope broadly slumped

raw_items.basis: artefact typology - rath is a characteristic Early Medieval Irish ringfort
document - upload date to Irish NMS

source_data.original_text:
Crowning a low but prominent elevation, with a gradual fall of ground for c. 500m to E to the banks of the Garvoge River. Formerly the demesne land of Cleveragh Estate, the location is now a public park, on the SE edge of Sligo Town. There are excellent views N to the Dartry Mountains.
Slightly raised circular area (diam. c. 30m) defined by a broad earthen bank, with an external fosse evident on the N arc. The rath is largely engulfed in overgrowth, which impedes examination. Beech and chestnut trees were planted in the interior, and sycamores and hawthorn trees ringing the perimeter. The enclosing bank appears as a broad earthen rise (Wth c. 5.5m; int. H 1.2m; ext. H 1.6m, at N), with a pronounced external slope, and a low, broadly slumped internal slope, merging seamlessly with the interior to give the rath a saucer-like profile. Outside the bank on the N arc, there is a fosse, evident as a broad, shallow depression (Wth 5-6m).

dimensions.raw: 19m NW-SE by 5m E-W and up to 5m deep

raw_items.raw_text: Part of this wall and the upper 1m of the midden was leveled in 1991

source_data.original_text:
Situated on cliff-edge slope on E side of Ballysadare Bay, on inspection in 1991, this was found to consist of a compacted shell-midden consisting mainly of oysters but with a mixture of other shells (19m NW-SE by 5m E-W and up to 5m deep). At the E the midden was covered by the modern road and was formerly covered by a stone-built retaining wall. Part of this wall and the upper 1m of the midden was leveled in 1991. The exposed section of the midden contained two thin lenses of charcoal (c. 1m long), the probable remnants of hearths. These lenses were covered by 0.5m of shells suggesting that they were in use during the formation of the midden.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 5 August 2015

Compiled by: Geraldine Stout

Date of upload: 21 November 2013

This tomb was excavated between 1996 and 1998 as part of the Swedish Archaeological Excavations campaign at Carrowmore. The excavations have shown that 'that the tomb was in use at the same time as the Carrowmore cemetery. An intact deposition layer inside the chamber, excavated during 1997, has produced a date of around 4000 BC . . .' The tomb has produced large quantities of unburned human bones, as well as stone and bone artefacts. All the burials found in tomb were inhumations. The finds included extraordinary pieces of chert artefacts, mainly leaf-shaped or pointed arrow-heads. (Burenhult 1998)

See linked document with details from Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume V. County Sligo. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1989)

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
Timoney (1984, 322, no. 3) describes this as follows: ‘This ring-barrow on flat ground has been ploughed down to a considerable extent and is perceptible only under a low setting sun. The total diameter appears to be in the region of 18.50 m. On the southwest side the bank remains to a height of only 13 cm. This is surrounded by a 3 m wide by 15 cm deep fosse and a bank, 3.50 m wide which averages 20 cm in height but is at most 30 cm high. Burenhult (1980:1, 93, 107) includes this within Strutture 13, Knocknahur North, recte Seafield, a group of five structures, all of which registered very low phosphate values. This would appear to be one of the structures included in map 26 (Burenhult 1980:1, 109), the other being unknown to the writer. However recent ploughing for the development of this field for sports has destroyed all of the surface except for the two Seafield barrows listed herein (3).’

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 28 January 2014

raw_items.raw_text: boulder circle with a central structure

source_data.original_text:
At Carrowmore passage tomb cemetery, on the line of a field boundary. This boulder circle with a central structure was damaged prior to 1837. In 1837 Petrie recorded it (No. 53) as follows: 'A few stones only of this circle remain. It was destroyed a few years ago…as usual it had a cromlech within it.’ (Stokes 1868, 181). Nine displaced gneiss boulders survive W of a field boundary with six more incorporated into the field boundary (Bergh 1995, 199-200, Carrowmore 53).

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 2 November 2020

source_data.original_text:
At Carrowmore passage tomb cemetery. This boulder circle with central structure was destroyed in the 19th century. Indicated on the 1837 OS 6-inch maps as a circle of dots, it was already partly destroyed when visited by Petrie who described it as follows: ‘The remains of this circle, which was destroyed with its cromleac about three years since, consist of 24 large stones.' (Stokes 1868, 250; No. 50) There is now no trace of the monument at ground level.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
Timoney (1984, 323-4, no. 13) describes this as follows: ‘The total diameter of this badly mutilated barrow is 19.30 m. The central area is 13m in diameter. An irregular bank, varying in width between 2.50m and 4m and reaching 60cm in height surrounds an irregular depression, averaging 7m in diameter. There is a "U"-bottomed fosse, 3m in width and 60cm deep around the central area. On the west side of the  monument there is evidence of an enclosing bank for about 10m of the circuit. It averages 2.40m wide and is at most 50cm high. This monument lies on flat ground between nos 27, 48 and 51. It is marked on the current, 1940, Ordnance Survey map as "Stone Circle, site of" but not at all on the original, 1837, map. It has not been referred to by any previous writer. The map designation was probably due to its location among the Carrowmore tombs, many of which are marked as "Stone Circle" on the maps, rather than to any proper archaeological reasons. However classification is not possible due to its disturbed nature. Perhaps it was a ring-barrow but with only the short length of bank on the west side surviving or a bowl-barrow of the ditched variety. Burenhult (1980:1, 93) lists this as Structure 8, Carrowmore.’

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 28 January 2014

At Carrowmore passage tomb cemetery. This megalithic structure was destroyed in the 19th century. When inspected by Petrie in 1837 it consisted only of a large stone, possibly 'the table stone of a cromleac’, and a few stones of an enclosing boulder circle (Stokes 1868, 246; No. 21). A single large gneiss boulder is now visible at the location, but it is uncertain if this formed part of the megalithic structure (Bergh 1995, 189, Carrowmore 21).

source_data.original_text:
At Carrowmore passage tomb cemetery. This megalithic structure is indicated on the 1837 OS6-inch map as circle of dots, but is not shown on later map editions. It consisted of a boulder circle with a central construction. All above ground remains were destroyed in the early 19th century; Petrie recorded ‘this circle…has been recently destroyed with its fine and perfect cromleac’ (Notebook,  p. 68, no. 30. Royal Irish Academy Ms. 23, L44).  Wood-Martin (1888, 60-1) noted 'one large stone, standing solitary like a sentinel, marks the site of the monument'. The location is now occupied by a quarry, and there are no visible remains of the monument. (Bergh 1995, 193, Carrowmore 30).  

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
In gently undulating pasture, on the estate/farm of the former Oakfield House. The house is shown on the 1837 OS 6-inch map, but is no longer extant, although part of the associated range of farm buildings survives. Little is known about Oakfield House. The Landed Estates databases records the following: ‘Oakfield (Sligo). In 1786 Wilson notes a house close to Cloverhill House as the seat of Mr. Deboots [?]. This may be Oakfield House. At the time of Griffith's Valuation [1848-64], this property was leased from Captain Richard Gethin by Joseph Holmes. It is described as a herd's house and was valued at £3 10s at the time. An extensive farm is still extant at the site.’ (http://landedestates.nuigalway.ie/LandedEstates; accessed 24/5/2018)
This record was included in the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) as 'earthworks' on the basis of features visible in a black and white aerial photograph (OS 1 3309-10, Roll 160, Pr. 29) (SMR file). In current aerial views, the area encompasses a number of large open fields of pastureland, extending across an area of c. 550m E-W x c. 450m N-S.
The features visible in the photo include a regular grid of large rectilinear fields. Several are shown on the 1837 OS 6-inch map, defined by tree-lined field boundaries, which radiate out from Oakfield House. A tree-lined avenue gives access to the house. A number of field fences/walls are extant, still functioning as field boundaries, and are lined by mature beech trees. Many of the smaller sub-divisions visible in aerial view represent field drains, a series of which cut across the relatively lowlying, damper ground in the E half of the area. They are visible now at ground level as shallow grassed-over linear depressions (Wth c. 2m), most barely discernible. 
It is likely that this field layout, and associated system of field drains, dates to the establishment of the Oakfield House estate, probably to the 18th century. In the SW part of the property, in an area of gently elevated dry ground, a tight arrangement of 4-5 contiguous rectangular field plots, bordered at their SW side by a road, is evident in the aerial photograph; they are not shown on the 1837 and 1940 OS 6-inch maps. They differ from the larger fields in being smaller and narrower (L c. 50-60m NE−SW; Wth 25-30m), and are aligned on a slightly different axis. These field plots have been levelled, but low, grassed-over banks can still be traced at ground level. They appears to represent a small settlement, possibly pre-dating or independent of Oakfield estate, but possibly that of tenants or farmworkers associated with the estate.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 29 May 2018

source_data.original_text:
Located in a low-lying drumlin valley with views onto the Ox Mountains in the S and Knocknarea in the W. Comprises a circular area (diam. 45m) enclosed by two banks and intervening fosse. The entrance (Wth 8.2m) is located in the E. Excavations in advance of road construction revealed a cremation at the base of the fosse and features in the interior that included a pit (diam. 1.3m; D 0.70m) and a number of cut features. Lithics that included scrapers, flakes, a chalk ball and a sherd of plain coarseware were also retrieved from the fosse. Radio-carbon dates obtained from charcoal samples produced a date of 2460-2140 cal. BC which is thought to date from the primary phase of the site (Danaher, E. 2007, 43-59).

Compiled by: Geraldine Stout

raw_items.raw_text: Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume V. County Sligo. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1989)

source_data.original_text:
This large cairn, a possible passage tomb, is a National Monument in State ownership (no. 568). The following description of the monument has been published by Bergh (1995, 232): ‘The site is the easternmost of the two [see SL014-231----] and overlooks the Garavogue River, 700m to the east. The site consists of a large, flat-topped cairn with a diameter of 53-58m, and a height of c. 7.5m. The cairn is placed at the northern end of a ridge that forms the summit. The hillside declines close to the cairn on all sides except to the S where the ground is level. Immediately to the W of the cairn there is a fairly steep, but short slope of only c. 3m, and the cairn has evidently on purpose been placed along this edge. The site is situated in a deciduous forest and is not visible until one is nearly at it. It is today wholly covered by a rich vegetation of bushes and smaller trees. This thick vegetation is probably the reason why the plan of the cairn never has been recorded before, and it definitely was the reason to why it was not measured by Wood-Martin according to the following: “Its circumference at base could not be ascertained, owing both to the uneven nature of the ground and to its being surrounded by trees, and a close undergrowth of briars, furze, & c.” (Wood-Martin 1888, p. 123). Minor quarrying seems to have taken place in the SE part of the cairn, and on the flat top there are several hollows and depressions which are the remains of earlier diggings into the cairn. A number of small semi-circular stone walls are present within the site, and are most likely of modem date.
Dimensions: Diameter, 53m (present minimum diameter/original maximum diameter). Height, 7.5m (present and original). Diameter of top, 23m (present maximum diameter).
The diameter of the cairn is 53m in N-S, but 58m in E-W. The slip of the cairn seems to vary, and has probably been greatest towards the W due to the short but steep slope here. The E and S sides of the cairn are the best 
preserved, and the diameter of 53m is considered as being a maximum for the original diameter The flat and slightly hollowed top has a maximum diameter of 23m. The ground level outside the cairn is 2m higher on the S and E, than on the N and W sides of the cairn. The absolute height of the cairn is c. 7.5m.’ (Bergh 1995, 232, Fig. 30).
Another cairn/possible passage tomb, very similar in size and construction, is located on a hilltop c. 400m to SW.

See linked document with details from Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume V. County Sligo. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1989)

Revised by: Paul Walsh

Date of Revised upload: 2 October 2018

source_data.original_text:
In a wooded area, beside a N-S flowing stream, on the S side of a steep wooded hill.This holy well is called 'Tobernalt'. It is enclosed within a circular setting (diam. 2.15) defined by a stone wall (H 2.27m; wall T 0.5m), which has an entrance to the SE (Wth 0.63m). The surrounding area has been landscaped. There is what is known locally as a 'Mass Rock' or altar (SL014-238002-) 5.5m to the SE of the well. Among plaques of modern date, affixed to the internal walls of the holy well, is a sandstone cross (H 0.43m; W 0.19m; T 0.06m), with a circular head. The site also contains statues and stations of the cross of modern date. A holly tree hung with votive offerings and rags stands on high ground to the NW of the holy well. Locally it is said that the mass rock was used to say mass in penal times and there has been a revival in recent years, with an annual mass being said by the Bishop of Elphin at 6am on Garland Sunday (last Sunday in July). Though no cures were recorded, it is locally believed that the waters of the stream cure blindness. The holy well is very well attended at all times.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 21 April 2011

source_data.original_text:
This souterrain, of drystone construction with lintel roofing, was recorded in 2005 during a pre-development archaeological assessment. The inspection revealed that the souterrain had been accessed previously in the modern era, and had been modified. Current access is through an opening (0.6m by 0.65m) at ground level. The opening is not original, but was the result of the collapse of two stone roofing lintels into the passage beneath. The passage (Wth 0.55m; H 0.8m), oriented NE−SW, could not be explored along its SW extent as it is blocked by a metal grate 2.7m to SW of the opening. The passage extends 2.4m to NE of the opening, where it intersects with a N−S passage (Wth 0.5m; H 0.6m). The N−S passage ends 1.65m to S of the junction; it was not possible to investigate how far it extended to N of the junction. Evidence of relatively recent modification of the souterrain included the metal grate blocking the NE−SW passage, cement coursing on the wall adjacent to the current opening, and the replacement of original stone lintels with concrete slabs along a section of the passage immediately to SW of the opening.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

raw_items.basis: artefact typology (concave scrapers) and archaeological interpretation

source_data.original_text:
Following on from the discovery of numerous lithics a survey was commissioned of c.72 acres of a clear-felled irregularly-shaped area in Rathcarrick townland (Hammar and Bergh cited in Coyne 2010, 15).  The purpose of the survey was to determine the occurrence of prehistoric lithics exposed by the clear-felling, to record the locations and to indicate the areas of archaeological significance. A certain amount of ground damage had been caused by machinery during the felling process although this varied throughout the area surveyed. The visibility of artefacts was also impacted by the growth of brushwood and scrub. 

A total number of 3,600 worked lithics was recorded, at 1,035 find spots. Concentrations of finds were influenced by the degree of visibility. It was noted that areas where few finds were recorded should not be seen as indicative of low activity, as this may simply be the result of low visibility. The lithics recovered from the steeper slopes frequently consisted of chunks of chert, cores and flakes and contained very few formal tools. It was also noted that there was a close spatial relationship between high intensity find spots and exposed outcrops. In some cases these exposed outcrops where a high number of lithics were recovered are located just above terraces: these were interpreted as functioning either as possible processing or habitation areas. Most of the formal tools recorded were associated with these areas.

A number of depressions or "scoops" were also identified and these were interpreted as possibly indicating prehistoric settlement. Subsequent excavation (licence no. 07E0803) of a sample indicated that the ‘features are unlikely to be the result of anthropogenic activity and are of no archaeological significance.’ (Brady 2010, 423). It has been suggested that the extensive quarrying may be related to the evidence for a lithic industry identified on the eastern side of the summit of Knocknarea, where tool production (notably concave scrapers) was a central part of Neolithic activity on the mountain (Coyne 2010, 15).

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 11 March 2014

In Sligo County Museum is a stone with a Latin inscription recording the building of a bridge (SL020-230001-) over the river at Ballsadare Bay by Maria, wife of the soldier Roger Jones, in the year 1628 (Sligo Field Club files). The inscription reads 'Maria Jones, Rogeri Militus Uxor hunc pontem struxit. Anno 1628. Pons Fabricatricis menorat sua facta; superstat marmore qua viva posteritatis inops dumque lapis superest crit indelible nomen, dinque viatores, munera tanta beant.' There are no visible remains of the 17th-century bridge (SL020-230001-). The present bridge is a disused causeway bridge of 19th-century appearance between a railway line and the modern N4 road. raw_items.basis: radiocarbon or artefactual evidence from related site
raw_items.raw_text: Human remains of Neolithic date have also been recovered from Cave C

source_data.original_text:
This cave (Cave K), one of 26 small caves on Knocknarae, is located on a short, steep slope at the NE extent of the massive cliffs that form the W flank of Knocknarea mountain. The cave entrance is small and low. A narrow squeeze leads into a long, low passage (Wth 0.8-1m; H 0.5-1.5m). The passage ends in a calcite choke 26m from the entrance. At a point 16m from the entrance, a narrow aperture connects this cave with a parallel cave (Cave J). In 2013, fragments of human bone were discovered scattered over a 2m stretch of the passage, c. 3.5m from its entrance. A two day rescue excavation (Licence no. 13E0427) was carried out in November 2013 (Dowd and Kahlert 2014). The excavation focussed on the survey and retrieval of the bone remains, both animal and human, which were exposed on the cave floor. No excavation of cave sediments was undertaken. The human bone assemblage consists of 13 bones. Only small skeletal elements were found, the majority of them fragmentary. The bones represented at least one adult (30-39 years old) and one child (4-6 years old). It was not possible to determine the gender of the individuals. Three bones were submitted for radiocarbon analysis and produced Neolithic dates. The majority of the animal bones (213 in total) recovered represent recent intrusions (probably fox prey) into the cave, but it is possible that a few of the animal bones are older and related to human activity in the cave. No artefacts were recovered. The excavators conclude that the patterning of the human bones indicate Neolithic funerary/ritual activity in the cave. They suggest the possibility that the cave was used as a site of natural excarnation, following which bones were retrieved for final burial elsewhere (Dowd and Kahlert 2014, 17-18). Human remains of Neolithic date have also been recovered from Cave C (SL014-290----) which is located c. 50m to SE.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shuaghnessy

source_data.original_text:
This cave (Cave C) is one of 26 small, inconspicuous caves on the steep NW and N slopes of Knocknarea Mountain. It comprises a long, narrow cruciform passage (L 14.5m; Wth 1m; H 1.2m). In 2002 Stefan Bergh discovered a fragment of the occipital bone from the skull of an adult human in the cave. The bone was lying on the cave floor, approximately 8m from the entrance. It returned a radiocarbon date of 4740± 50BP, placing it in the Neolithic period (Dowd 2008). Human remains of Neolithic date have also been recovered from Cave K (SL014-288----) which is located c. 50m to NW (Dowd and Kahlert 2014).

source_data.original_text:
This rectangular panel (0.60m x 0.52m) comprises the lower portion of a much larger memorial 
The triangular inscribed fragment (0.72m wide and 0.41m high) was found in a deep well at the east end of Quay Street, Sligo, in 1989. It is the upper apex of a much larger memorial or wall monument that was commissioned by Eleanor Butler, Countess of Desmond in 1624. The lower portion of the memorial was taken from Sligo in the mid-19th century and eventually found its way to Braganstown House in or after 1877 (Timoney 2013, 113) (see LH015-045---- for its present location).  When grouped together (see Timoney 2013, 112) the inscription would have read: ELINORA/ BVTLER COM/ITISSA DESMOND / IN MEMORIAM / [P]ASSIONIS CHRISTI ET / SVI MARITI DONATI CON/OR MILITIS COMITATUS /  SLIGO  DOMINI MOR/TVI ANO DNI 1609 ET SUAE/ FILIAE DOMINAE ELISAB/ETHAE GERALD SEPULTAE / IN MONASTERIO DE / SLIGO CVM PREDICTO / DONATO / AN 1623 / ME FIERI FECIT AN / DNI 1624. This may be translated as: Eleanor Butler Countess of Desmond in memory of the Passion of Christ, and of her husband Donagh O’Conor, Knight, Lord of the County of Sligo, who died the year of Our Lord 1609, and of her daughter Lady Elizabeth Gerald, who was buried in the monastery of Sligo, with the aforesaid Donagh in the year 1623, caused me to be erected in the year of Our Lord 1624. The original location of this memorial is unknown but it has been suggested that it may have been inserted in the wall of a chapel in the castle of Sligo (Timoney 2013).

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
Located on the N-facing slope of a ridge overlooking Cummeen Strand and Sligo Bay. The slope drops steeply for several meters to a strip of salt marsh which gives way to the mud and sand flats of Cummeen Strand. To S, the slope rises c. 0.5m and then levels out to a broad natural terrace before rising again to the summit of the ridge. The slope is thickly cloaked in hawthorn, blackthorn and bramble scrub. This midden was discovered in October 2015 by the MASC Project, Sligo IT. The midden can be traced intermittently over a distance of c. 25-30m between ITM 564350 836890 at the WSW and 564384 836909 at its ENE end. It is visible as a dense layer of oyster shells, mixed with occasional periwinkle shells and charcoal flecks. At its SW end the layer (L 1.4m; D 0.3m) is exposed in the sides of a deep rut (Wth 0.5-0.8; D 0.5-0.7m) eroded into the slope by farm stock. Another relatively substantial section (L 3m; D 0.4-0.5m) is visible 3m to E of this. To E of these two sections, the midden is glimpsed in patches where the moss and overgrowth has been eroded from a scarp. The scarp appears to be the remnant of a man-made boundary or path, possibly 19th century in date, which extends roughly E–W along a contour of the ridge. A depth of c. 0.4-0.6m of soil overlies the midden. This suggests that the midden accumulated originally on the natural terrace of the ridge slope but has been buried over time by soil build-up. The exact nature and date of the midden is unknown. It has been recorded as a single feature but there may be more than one midden here.

raw_items.raw_text: Identified in 2009 from low altitude aerial photographs

source_data.original_text:
Located in pasture, on Coney Island in Sligo Bay, the enclosure straddles the break of slope on the steep NW edge of a low ridge which extends NE−SW across the centre of the island. The NW-facing slope drops 4-6m to an expanse of flat, marshy ground cut off from the sea c. 250m to W by sand dunes. To SE the ground falls away in a broad gentle slope. The location provides excellent views across the island, and beyond to the mountains of Donegal on the far horizon to N, Ben Bulbin at NNE, and Knocknarea which dominates the view at ESE.
Identified in 2009 from low altitude aerial photographs (Kytmannow et al. 2009, 24, plate 25), this monument was levelled in the past, and the remains are poorly defined at ground level. It consists of a circular or possibly oval area (diam. c. 20-25m) located to NW of centre within a broadly oval area (c. 52m NE−SW; c. 47m NW−SE) defined by a bank. There is a broad intervening gap between the inner enclosure and the outer bank, except at NW where the two are close-set and coincide with the contours of the ridge slope. 
At ground level, the outer bank can be traced in an arc at NW−NNE as a low scrap (H 0.5m; Wth 1m), following the natural contour along the top of the ridge slope, and is incorporated into a later field boundary. Remnants of stone facing along the scarp may relate to the later field boundary. Elsewhere, the outer bank is evident as a barely discernible undulation at NE and SW−W; it is no longer visible at E−SSW. The original form and size of the inner enclosure is unclear –only the NW portion is upstanding; the SE portion is levelled and cannot be traced with certainty at ground level. The NW portion is evident as a raised semi-circular area (c. 25m NE−SW; c. 10m NW-SE), curving WNW−NE, and perhaps utilising a small natural rise or peak on the spine of the ridge. It has a gently domed profile with broadly sloping sides (H c. 1m). At NNW−N the outer bank skirts the base of the sloping sides, but at W and NE there is a gap of 12−15m between inner enclosure and the outer enclosing bank. 
The enclosure as a whole mirrors the natural terrain, sloping gently from higher ground at NW down to SE. It is bisected by two modern field walls in a T-shaped arrangement: one wall on a roughly NW-SE axis bisecting the enclosure to NW of centre, and the second wall lying perpendicular to this and extending to SE through the centre of the enclosure. There are also two relict field boundaries; one on a NW−SSE axis cuts across the NW sector of the enclosure, and the other on a roughly NE−SW axis merges with the outer bank at NW−NE.
The asymmetrical position of the inner enclosure and the broad intervening gap between the inner enclosure and the outer bank are unusual features of this monument.  

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 6 March 2017

In parkland on the SE side of Sligo Town, ground falls away steeply to S.
This circular enclosure (int. diam. c. 20m; ext. diam. c. 34m N–S) is not shown on the 1838 and 1940 OS 6-inch maps, but a roughly circular cluster of trees is shown on both map editions. The enclosure was archaeologically tested in 2008 in advance of proposed development works (Hackett 2008). It is defined by low remnants of a partly levelled earthen bank (Wth c. 4m). Three test trenches (Wth 1.9m), opened across the E half of the enclosure, revealed that the bank has both an internal and an external enclosing fosse. The excavated profile of the external fosse (Wth 1.8m; D below topsoil 1.1m) showed it to have a steeply sloping outer side, a U-shaped base and a gradually sloping inner S side. Its basal fill incorporated frequent stones, charcoal inclusions and substantial amounts of iron smelting slag (59.6 grams recovered). The fosse (Wth 1m; D below topsoil 0.3m) on the inner edge of the bank is less substantial; its profile has a gradually sloping sides and a rounded base. A terminus for this fosse was found towards its E end, suggesting a NE entrance to the enclosure. (Hackett 2008). There is a rath (SL014-134----) 230m to NE.

source_data.original_text:
Located on a terrace on a N-facing slope, in parkland formerly part of the Cleveragh Estate, on the SE side of Sligo Town. To S ground rises in a steep, wooded slope; to N-NE there is a gradual fall of ground towards the Garvoge River, through an area that now constitutes a public park. 
This enclosure is not shown on the 1838 and 1940 OS 6-inch maps, but is indicated on the 25-inch plan as a D-shaped hachured area (c. 35m NW–SE; c. 20m NE–SW), bordered on the straight side at SW by a NW–SE field boundary. This boundary is extant, consisting of a high estate wall, which now marks the S limits of the public park. On the ground, there is slight evidence that the enclosure extends to SW of the wall, and may in fact be circular (diam. c. 35m), bisected roughly centrally by the wall.
A low, D-shaped platform (30-35m E–W; c. 20m N-S; H c. 0.8m at NW) is evident, corresponding with the hachured area shown on the 25-inch map. It is almost entirely engulfed in overgrowth, and cannot be fully examined. It is possible that low undulations visible on the NW arc may represent an enclosing fosse (Wth c. 2.5m) with an external bank (Wth 2m). The straight SW side of the D-shaped platform is defined by the high, mortared stone wall (Wth 0.5-0.6m; H 1.7m), corresponding with the NW–SE boundary shown on the 25-inch plan. Immediately to SW of the wall, a roughly semicircular area (c. 30-35m E–W; c. 15m N-S) of differential vegetation growth, with traces of a possible irregular bank on the W arc, may represent the SW half of the originally circular enclosure.

source_data.original_text:
On the S edge of Sligo town, located on level, well drained elevated ground, with commanding views to NW, and N−NE. There is a rath (SL014-125) 145m to NW, and a causewayed enclosure (SL014-282----) c. 400m to NW.
This enclosure was discovered during archaeological testing (licence no. 19E0775) carried out over four weeks in June 2020 in advance of a proposed residential development (Fitch et al. 2020). 
Excavation of seven test trenches at this location produced evidence of a double-ditched, circular enclosure. The outer ditch (Wth c. 0.30m wide; D 0.25m deep) has a diameter of 49m, the inner ditch (Wth 2.50m; D 0.65 - 0.75) a diameter of c. 37m. The outer ditch may cut through earlier post holes or pits on the northern side of the enclosure. Two fragments of cremated bone, two pieces of chert debitage and small amounts of charcoal were recovered. A rounded nodule of granite/quartz was discovered on the surface of the inner ditch, amongst large stones in the centre of the ditch. A number of possible postholes and small pits were noted within and outside the enclosure; these were not excavated. The excavators conclude that the evidence points to extensive prehistoric activity, and posit that the double-ditched enclosure may be Neolithic in date. All archaeological features were surveyed. Following the completion of testing, the trenches were covered with a layer of permeable terram and backfilled. (Fitch et al. 2020).

Situated on a prominent N-facing slope of E-W orientated ridge in pasture. Raised circular area (diam. c.28m) enclosed by a broad flat-topped internal bank of earth and stone (Wth 4-4.15m; int. H 0.3-0.7m). At the external base of the internal bank is a broad flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 4.8m-5.1m). Immediately outside the fosse is a second broad flat-topped bank of earth and stone (Wth 4.35-4.5m; int. H 2.5-2.8m) and an external broad flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 5m; D 1-1.3m). The internal bank is best preserved E-SSE where it contains more rubble stone than elsewhere. The inner side of the internal bank is revetted with limestone slabs laid on edge giving a vertical inner face to the bank E-SE. The external fosse is best preserved SE-NNW and is mostly infilled and barely visible NNW-SE. A break (Wth 4.5m) in the internal bank, with a causeway across the first fosse and a corresponding break (Wth 4.5m) in the second bank and a causeway across the external fosse, marks the position of the original entrance. The N edge of the causeway is revetted with two courses of limestone blocks where it spans the innermost fosse. A very disturbed kerb consisting of a single row of limestone blocks extends from the N side of the entrance break in the internal bank into the interior. A large rectangular conglomerate block (dims L 1.7m; T 0.44m; H 0.45m) lies at a right angle to the W end of the kerb. The remains of a souterrain (SL015-010002-) are located in the internal bank at W.

source_data.original_text:
These burials were found by Wood-Martin (1888, 127-8) in a cist in the southern of the two contiguous stone circles the whole of which is described as follows: 'The stones forming it are small in size, and are paced in two impinging circles, the larger or northern one being about 20 feet in diameter, and the smaller about 10 feet. No remains of an interment were discoverable in the larger enclosure, but traces of a rude cist were apparent in the smaller circle (A) [on his plan], close to where it touches upon the larger one. The osseous remains were submitted to W. Frazer, F.R.C.S.I., who states that there were no evidences of adult interment, save two incisors (large size), and three molars, the rest all belonging to a child; the set of teeth (incisors not been shed) points to an age before seven, and the bones also appeared to belong to that age. There were six molars, three incisors (one canine), twelve uncut tops of teeth, fragments of child's ribs, two vertebrae, parts of the skull, one portion of temporal bone, with auditory process, finger- and toe-bones, forearm and leg, portions of pelvis - all in a fragmentary condition.'

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a moderate S-facing slope, in gently undulating pasture. Natural ground falls away sharply from the site ESE-W. Roughly circular area (dims. 28m N-S; 27m E-W) enclosed by a low broad bank of earth and stone (Wth 4.6m; int. H 0.6m). There is no fosse visible at ground level. The bank encloses the site W-E. From E-W the site is defined by a near vertical scarp (ext. H 1.5-3m) formed by cutting back a natural slope. The unmodified natural slope links to the edge of the rath at E and at W. The original entrance is not recognisable. The drystone footings of a stone structure are located to SE of centre in the interior consisting of an E-W orientated section of drystone wall (L 4m; T 0.6m; H 0.2m) linking at its E end at a right angle to a N-S orientated section of drystone wall (L 2m; T 0.6m; H 0.2m). The remains of a possible souterrain (SL015-035002-) are located to WNW of centre in the interior.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Situated on slight rise on slight S-facing slope 30 to N of N shore of Colgagh Lough, in low-lying gently undulating pasture. Slightly raised roughly circular area (dims. 20m N-S; 19m E-W) enclosed by a low narrow bank of earth and stone (Wth 1.65m; int. H 0.3m). At the external foot of the bank are a fosse (Wth 1.35m) and an external bank of earth and stone (Wth 1m; int. H 0.2m). The internal bank is best preserved NE-SW with only traces visible SW-NNW. From NNW-NE the bank is absent and the edge of the monument is defined by a straight WNW-ESE orientated relic drystone wall. The fosse is best preserved SE-SW with very slight traces only visible NE-SE and SW-NNW. From NNW-NE the fosse is not visible. The external earth and stone bank encloses the site SE-SW with only very slight traces visible NE-SE and SW-NNW. The original entrance is not recognisable. The interior of the site is slightly domed. A hut site (SL015-041002-) is located in the centre of the interior.

Situated on the level summit of a broad N-S orientated ridge with natural ground level sloping down gently from the site NE-NW. Circular area (diam. 25m) defined by a drystone wall of rubble limestone (Wth 4m; int. H 0.6-1m). Immediately outside this wall is a berm (Wth 4m) and an external stone wall (Wth 3.6m; int. L1m; Wth 1m; T 0.4m) survives sporadically on the internal wall and is absent from the external wall. From NE-SE the internal side of the bank has been rebuilt as a drystone field wall. Modern field walls have been built on top of the collapsed outer cashel wall SE-NW. The original entrance is not recognisable.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a slight S-facing slope n gently undulating elevated pasture. Circular area (diam. 23m) defined by a broad internal bank of rubble limestone (Wth 3.8m; int. H 0.8m). At the external foot of the bank is a level berm (Wth 1.45m) and a mostly collapsed drystone wall (Wth 3.35m; int. H 0.8-1.1m). Immediately outside the drystone wall is a berm (Wth 0.8-1.4m) and an irregular outer bank of limestone (Wth 2.5-3.15m; int. H 0.2-0.4m). The outer bank has an irregular profile being very low and broad in many areas may not be original (M. A. Timoney pers. comm.). A narrow poorly defined break (Wth 1.4m) in the inner bank at S marks the position of the original entrance. Aligned with the break in the inner bank is a break (Wth 1.3) in the second wall that is lined on either side with drystone un-coursed walling. A poorly defined break (Wth 0.4m) in the outer bank that is not aligned with the other breaks and is likely to be modern. The W one-third of the interior is raised and the remains of a souterrain (SL015-052002-) are located within this slight rise. (O'Rorke 1890, 466, 1 fig., JRSAI 1890-91, 578-9, ITA Survey, GSI G352-3).

Located within a slightly raised area on the WSW side of Magheraghanrush cashel (SL015-052001-). The souterrain consists of a passage (L 5.3m; Wth 1.1m; H 1.3m) orientated NNE-WSW. The lintels are absent. The walls are of un-coursed rough rubble limestone and the floor of rock and earth slopes gently downwards from NNE-WSW. The entrance appears to have been at the NNE end where the passage turns at a right angle, extending 2m to the E, before vanishing as the floor rises. At the SSW end of the passage is a roughly rectangular drystone walled chamber (dims. L 2m N-S; Wth 1.65m E-W; H 1.35m) offset to the W of the passage. A single rectangular limestone slab lintel survives over the W end wall of the chamber.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a slight SW-facing slope, in undulating upland, in a coniferous forestry. The cashel is overlooked by higher ground on the NE side and overlooks a narrow N-S orientated valley to the W. Oval area (60-65m NW−SE; c. 55m NE−SW) enclosed by a bank of rubble limestone (Wth 4.6m; int. H 0.5m). An E-W orientated field wall extends across the S edge of the cashel intersecting with the bank at SE and at SW. A subrectangular area (c. 15m E−W; c. 17m N−S), partitioned off by a rubble wall, is shown in the S half of the interior on the 1937 OS 6-inch map, and was recorded by Milligan (1890-1, 579) in the late 1800’s. Also shown on the 1937 OS 6-inch edition is a circular feature in the N half of the cashel interior, most likely the circular hut site (SL015-059004-) recorded by Milligan (ibid. 579), who also noted a souterrain (SL015-059002-) in the W half and a bullaun stone (SL015-059003-) in the E half of the interior. No traces of any of these internal features were evident when the cashel was inspected in 2003.

source_data.original_text:
Situated in a hollow at the base of a slight SW-facing slope, on N shore of Lough Gill, in mature deciduous forest. The well consists of a natural spring that has been lined by a roughly rectangular drystone wall (dims. L NW-SE 2m; Wth NE-SW 1.25m; Max Ht 0.6m). An irregular N-S orientated outflow channel (Wth 0.3m; L 2.5m) extends from the S corner of the wall into the lake. The level base of the well is covered with sand, gravel and some rubble rocks. Mature beech trees grow immediately to the E and S of the well with the roots of these trees extending along the SW and SE sides of the wall. Rags tied to these roots indicate that the well is still in use. Wood-Martin (1882, 91-2) attributes the well to St. Connell whose feast day is celebrated on June 2nd.

raw_items.basis: artefact typology - promontory forts are characteristic Early Medieval defensive structures in Ireland

source_data.original_text:
Located on a NW-SE orientated broad peninsula that extends from the N shore of Lough Gill in mature mixed deciduous forestry. The main enclosure of the promontory fort is at the SE end of the peninsula consisting a roughly rectangular flat topped natural rock outcrop (dims. 32m NNW-SSE; 24m WNW-ESE) defined by modified natural scarp (ext. H 2-4m). From NW-NE the scarp takes the form of a near vertical irregular quarried rock face (ext. H 2m). From NE-NW the scarp consists of a near vertical earth and stone scarp (ext. H 2-4m) that increases in height from N-S to compensate for the underlying natural slope. The original entrance (Wth 5m) is at N consisting of a set of roughly quarried steps (Wth 1.5-2m: H 0.2-0.3m) cut from the exposed rock face. The entrance is roughly lined on either side, at the base of the scarp defining the platform, with a single row of irregular quarried blocks (av. dims. L 1m; Wth 0.8m; T 0.4m). A roughly circular flat-topped mound (diam. top 2m) defined by a scarp of earth and stone (ext. H 1.8m) is located slightly to S of centre in the interior. The peninsula is traversed by the ENE-WSW orientated footings (L 40m; T. 0.8m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.7m) of a drystone wall located 8.5m to the N of the main enclosure. There is a fosse (Wth 3.3m; D 0.3m) on the N side of the footings. A break (Wth 2.2m) in the wall, with a causeway across the fosse, marks the position of the original entrance. A feature that may be a boat slip or small harbour is located15m to the N of the W end of the wall footings and fosse. The feature consists of a broad U-shaped depression (dims. L ENE-WSW 12m; Wth NNW-ESE 5m; D 1.3-1.6m) defined by a scarp. A bank of earth and stone (Wth 4.3m; H at N 1.3m; H at S 0.5m) lies on top of the scarped edge on the S side. The depression is open on the W side toward the lake extending to the waters edge. The base slopes slightly toward the lake. Immediately to the E of this depression is a roughly rectangular area (dims. L ENE-WSW 3.2m; Wth NNW-ESE 1.2m) defined by a single row of rubble blocks on all but the E side. The interior of the area is level and appears to be metalled with stone.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 21 April 2011

Situated on NE shore of small lake, at base of slight SW-facing slope, in gently undulating pasture. The SW half of the site extends out into the lake. Slightly raised circular area (diam. 25m) enclosed by a bank of earth and stone (Wth 2.2m; int. H 0.2m). At the external foot of the bank is a fosse (Wth 4.4m; D 1m). The bank is best preserved NNE-E and at WNW. Elsewhere itis visible as a slight rise only. The internal face of the bank is revetted with blocks of rubble stone NNE-E giving a vertical inner profile. The fosse encloses the site NW-SE and is absent elsewhere where the external base of the bank falls directly into the lake water. A break (Wth 2m) in the bank at NE with a causeway across the fosse marks the position of the original entrance. A NE-SW orientated drystone wall crosses the fosse to link to the external face of the bank at NNE.

source_data.original_text:
Situated on slight S-facing slope in gently undulating rocky upland pasture. Circular area (diam. 60m) enclosed by the footings of a drystone wall (Wth .95m; int. H 0.2m). There is no fosse visible at ground level. The footings of the wall enclose the site on all sides but are best preserved NW-NE. Elsewhere only fragmentary are now visible. Where best preserved, the footings are made up of two parallel rows of slabs set on edge (0.8m apart) with a fill of small limestone rubble between. Elsewhere the footings can only be felt beneath the sod. An ENE-WSW orientated wire fence with a closely spaced row of coniferous trees crosses the interior to S of centre intersecting with the wall footings at SW and at SE. The original entrance is not recognisable. The remains of a souterrain (SL015-086002-) are located to W of centre in the interior, 10m within the footings of the cashel wall.

Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Located 10m within the wall footings of Corwillick cashel (SL015-086001-) on the W side of the interior. A slightly curving portion of the passage (L 5m; Wth 1.35m; D 1.1m) extends in a N-S direction. The walls are lined with drystone random rubble walling and the original rounded end wall survives at the S end. The N end is blocked with earth and access to the remainder of the souterrain is impossible. Access to the passage is between gaps in the lintels which consist of long rectangular slabs of limestone (Av. L 1.5m; Wth 0.5m; T 0.2m) laid across the passage. At the S end, the passage is covered by a large roughly rectangular slab (L 1.8m; Wth 1.5m; T 0.25m).

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a level terrace on side of large hill, in deciduous forest. A steep S-facing E-W orientated slope breaks 10m to the S of the site. Raised circular area (diam. 26m) enclosed by a broad bank of rubble limestone (Wth 4.9m; int. H 0.3m). There is no fosse visible at ground level. The bank has a regular profile and encloses the site on all sides. No facing is evident around the perimeter. A break (Wth 2m) in the bank at S marks the position of the original entrance. The interior has been built up on the E side with rubble limestone to form a roughly rectangular platform (dims. 11m N-S; 10m E-W) defined by a stone scarp (H 0.2m) that links to the interior side of the cashel bank NE-SE. The remains of a souterrain (SL015-087002-) are located in the centre of the platform.

source_data.original_text:
In a small bay known as Tobernalt Bay, at the W end of Lough Gill, c. 120m from the shoreline.
This crannog is depicted on the 1912 OS 6-inch map as a circular island (diam. c. 7m) named ‘Crannoge’.  It was inspected in 2000 in the course of the 'Crannog Survey, Co. Sligo' undertaken by Christina Fredengren. 
The crannog appears to consist of a gently domed circular cairn (diam. c. 18m E-W; 18.5m N-S) of firmly-packed angular stones, rising 1.4-1.8m above the lake bed. The exact limits are indistinct. A number of flagstones (max. dim. 0.4-0.5m) were noted on the crannog surface in the NE quadrant.
At the time of visit, the crannog was almost entirely submerged, with a small heap of stones (diam. c. 2m; H 0.4m), holding an upright iron bar, all that was visible above the water surface.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

raw_items.raw_text: founded by St. Loman, son of Dallan, a contemporary of St. Columkille in the 6th century
the current building is much later in date

source_data.original_text:
In woodland, located at the SE end of Church Island, also known as Inish Mór, in the centre of Lough Gill. 
This medieval church is a National Monument (no. 118) in state ownership. Little is known about its history. It is said to have been founded by St. Loman, son of Dallan, a contemporary of St. Columkille in the 6th century (Gwynne and Hadcock 1970, 31), although the current building is much later in date. The Annals of the Four Masters recorded that in the year 1416 manuscripts, including one named book, Leabhar-Gearr [Short Book], and other valuable items were burnt in a fire at the church: ‘The church of Inis Mor, in Lough Gill, was burned; and Sceaptra ui Chuirnin [library or manuscript house], and the Leabhar Gearr of the O’Cuirnins, as well as many other precious articles, were burnt also.’  Gwynne and Hadcock (1970, 31 suggest that the O’ Cuirnins may have been 'erenaghs', hereditary ecclesiastical officials. 
The church was recorded in the late 18th century by Grose (1791, vol. 1, 58), who published a drawing of it done by Bigari. The drawing shows that the church was already roofless and partly ruined at that date. A fuller description was later published by Fennell (1904, 166-169). 
The extant remains consist of a roofless rectangular, stone-built structure (c. 15m E−W; c. 7m N−S). A N−S cross wall divides it into two parts, with the church proper to E and a smaller room (Wth c. 3m E−W) at W, directly above which is another chamber. 
The church is entered through a round-arched doorway located to W of centre in the S wall. The arch features a series of decorative carved cusps. There is an inwardly-splayed window in the centre of the E gable, and a smaller, inwardly-splayed window in the S wall to E of the entrance. An aumbry or wall recess is located at the E end of the N wall.
A plain, round-headed doorway at the S end of the N−S interior dividing wall gives access from the main body of the church into the small chamber at the W end of the building. This room is lit by a small window in the S wall, but also has a double opening or ‘squint’ in the centre of the interior E wall, which gives views into the main body of the church. There is a recess or wall cupboard in the centre of the W wall, and two smaller recesses in the E wall, one at either end. The upper storey was carried on timber flooring, and may have been accessed by a ladder. The layout of the upper chamber is similar to that on the ground floor, with a small window in the S wall, a recess in the W wall, and an opening/window at the N end of the internal dividing wall, which overlooks the main body of the church. These two chambers served as the priest’s quarters; the lower chamber may also have served as a sacristy or, as Fennell (1904, 167) suggests, based on the annalistic reference to the loss of manuscripts in the 1416 fire, a scriptorium or library. 
There is an inscribed stone (SL015-096004-) in the reveal of the church doorway. A graveyard (SL015-096002-) and a saint's stone (SL015-096003-) are associated with the church.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 30 September 2020

Adjacent to a church (SL015-096001-) on Church Island in Lough Gill.
This ritual stone/saint’s stone is not indicated on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. It is traditionally known as ‘Our Lady’s Bed’ and was believed to have specific protective or curative powers, which were first recorded by Grosse (1791, 58) in the late 18th century: ‘In a rock near the door of the church is a cavity, called Our Lady’s Bed, into which pregnant women go, and turning thrice around, which they believe prevents their dying in labour; at the same time they repeat certain prayers.’ 
Writing at the beginning of the 20th-century, Fennel (1906, 169) described it as a ‘rude construction more like a poor attempt to build a cromleac’, and provided additional detail on the ritual undertaken by women ‘who desired the blessings of maternity’. They were required ‘to enter it feet foremost, which was accomplished by wriggling in and turning three times and always to the right, repeating each time “In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost”, and then emerging, and having said three “Our Fathers and three “Hail Mary’s”, the rite was completed.’ The effectiveness of the ritual was recounted to him by a local woman who ‘knew an American woman who, desiring such blessings, came in good faith to “Our Lady’s Bed”, and observed its ancient rite, with the result that the “blessings” came afterwards to her abundantly, and in quick succession.’ (Ibid. 1906, 169).  

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 30 September 2020

raw_items.basis: artefact typology - ogham inscriptions are characteristic of Early Medieval Ireland

source_data.original_text:
Built into the inner frame of the doorway of a church (SL015-096001-). This inscribed stone was first described by Wood-Martin (1882, preface xiv) as follows: ‘The stone, rough and uneven in shape, measures eighteen inches [0.45m] by seven inches [0.17m], and is built into the wall in the inner side of the entrance door of the church.’ He sent a cast of the stone to Sir S. Ferguson who pronounced that inscription was in ogham characters, placed on the flat of the stone rather than as is usual along the edge or angles. Fennell (1904, 169) published a sketch of the inscription, and noted that ‘It has been regarded as an ogham, and again, as Roman numerals written in church text.’ The inscription does not appear to be ogham. Its exact nature, however, has not been established or its meaning deciphered.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
Listed in the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified 'Potential Site - Aerial Photo' and 'House' respectively. House identified from an aerial photograph (ACP V203/39 Roll 174 Pr. 32). This consists of a rectangular structure (Max. ext. dims. L 22m SE-NW; 6m NE-SW) divided into three rooms defined by earth covered drystone footings of rubble limestone (T 1-1.3m; int. H 0.2-0.4m; ext. H 0.2m). The central room (dims. L 8m SE-NW; 5.35m N-S) is entered via a break (Wth 1.4m) in the NE wall at the N corner of the room.  Access to the NW and SE rooms is via breaks (Wth 1m) in the SW end of the NW and SE walls respectively. The W room (dims. L 6.5m SE-NW; 5.35m NE-SW) has a low pile of rubble against the inside of the NW gable wall. The SE room (dims. L 7m SE-NW; 5.35m NE-SW) has a low pile of rubble against the inside of the N corner. The interior of the house is level being slightly lower than external ground level on the NE side while being flush on the SW side.  The site is dry and clear of overgrowth. The house site consists of the footings of what appears to be a house of post-1700 date. 


Compiled by: Patrick F. O'Donovan

Date of upload: 31 July 2012

source_data.original_text:
Situated on a slight rise in gently undulating rocky pasture. Slightly raised roughly circular area (diam. c.30m) enclosed by the footings of a drystone wall of limestone rubble (Wth 1.85m; int. H 0.2m). There is no fosse visible at ground level. The footings of the drystone wall enclose the site NE-NW and consist of two parallel rows of limestone facing slabs with a fill of small rubble between. The inner or outer facing slabs are not continuous around the entire circuit and the footings often take the form of a low bank of rubble stone. At the base of the inner and outer sides of the footings is a spread (Wth 2m; H 0.2m) of rubble stone. The footings are absent NW-NE where a straight E-W orientated lane defines the N limit of the cashel. The original entrance is not recognisable.

Situated on a moderate S-facing slope of hillock in natural ash wood. Oval area (dims. 20m E-W; 18m N-S) enclosed by a drystone wall of random limestone rubble (Wth 0.6-1; int. H 1.3-1.5m; ext. Described by Cahill and Sikora (2011, ii, 512) as follows: 'In 1990 human remains were discovered during underwater surveying work by the Garda Underwater Unit around Cottage Island in Lough Gill. No details are known as to the disposition of the remains. The human remains (NMI No. 1990:95) were located at the SE end of the island. Two wooden boats were also located in a follow up survey of the lake bed around the island. A dug-out canoe was located off the S shore close to where the human remains were found, and a plank-built boat was located off the northern shore. source_data.original_text:
In pasture reclaimed from boggy ground, located on a low elevation, overlooked by gently rising ground to W. To N there is gradual fall of ground into a broad boggy valley bordered on N side by Crockhauns hill and to W by Keelogyboy hill. There are tracts of forestry in adjacent properties to SE, S and SW. Roughly oval or sub-rectangular platform (c. 30m N-S; c. 42m E-W) defined by a partly levelled, broadly sloping scarp (c. 1m at N and S, c. 1.5m at W), which retains a low internal lip (Wth c. 1.5m) on the S side. Discrete remnants of an original bank may also survive beneath the roots of a lone hawthorn bush growing on top of the scarp at N. The scarp is lowest at E, and the original entrance may have been on this side. Immediately outside the scarp at NE there is a hint of an external depression, perhaps indicating the presence of a fosse, but it can not be traced elsewhere. The interior is level and grassy. The top and slopes of the scarp are marked by a dense growth of rushes. According to local tradition, the site is known locally as a 'fort'.

Attached image: SL015-131----_01 viewed from E

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 12 May 2011

source_data.original_text:
Located in flat, damp lowlying rush-grown pasture, c. 570m N of the NW shoreline of Lough Gill.
This burnt mound is evident as a low subcircular rise (15m N−S; 16m E−W; H 0.65m at E, 0.4m at W). The mound is composed of a concentration of angular stone fragments in black soil. It is most clearly defined on the E side, where there is a slight drop in ground level, but elsewhere the mound grades seamlessly into the surrounding field surface. A covering of bright green grass, and an absence of rushes, distinguishes it from the rough, rushy sward of the surrounding field. 
It is more than likely a fulacht fia, which has been partly levelled in the past; no clearly defined trough depression is visible.
There are two burnt mounds (SL015-133----; SL015-134----) in the adjoining field c. 175m to N.

Notified to NMS by Leo Leyden.

Adjacent to a N−S field boundary in the NE corner of a pasture field, located in flat, damp lowlying terrain. Ground rises gently to N. The NE shores of Lough Gill are 580m to S.
This partly levelled burnt mound has been bisected by a N−S field ditch (Wth 1.4m; D 0.6-0.8m)/property boundary. The W half of the mound is still evident as a low D-shaped rise (12m N−S; 6.5m E−W; H 0.3m), bordered on its straight side at E by the field ditch. A low field bank (Wth 0.8-1m; H 0.6m at W) borders the W edge of the field ditch, overlying the burnt mound. The field bank is composed of upcast soil from the ditch, and incorporates burnt stone and black soil. A post and wire fence borders the E side of the field ditch. In the field to E of this, the burnt mound has been levelled, but a difference in grass growth suggests that it extends at least 3m to E of the field ditch.
There is a burnt mound (SL015-134----) 10m to NNW and another (SL015-133----), in an adjoining field, c. 175m to S.

Notified to NMS by Leo Leyden.

source_data.original_text:
In the garden of a modern house. 
A subrectangular boulder (L 0.9m; Wth 0.55m; T 0.3m) with two close-set circular hollows of unequal size in one broad flat surface. The two hollows are bowl-shaped, with sides grading seamlessly to a slightly concave base: larger hollow (diam. 0.29-0.30m; D 0.15m); small hollow (diam. 0.22-0.23m; D 0.1m). The interior surface of the hollows is smooth and even, contrasting with the natural rough surface of the boulder. 
The two hollows, set 3-4cm apart, occupy most of the available space on the relatively flat surface of the boulder. The bullaun stone is currently set upright on edge, with one broad surface (the original base) abutting a garden feature and the broad face with the two hollows facing outwards. According to the local information, the bullaun stone was found on the shoreline of Lough Gill c. 200m to S of its current location.

The source of this record is recorded simply as ‘Burenhult 1980’ (SMR file). It would appear to refer to Structure 24 recorded in Field XIV on Map 3 (Burenholt 1980, 86) as the adjoining Structure 26 corresponds with the ring barrow (SL020-016----). Burenhult refers to these ‘structures’ as an ‘assembly of earthworks’ with ‘little or no relation to each other (functionally or chronologically) but with overall morphological similarities’ (1980, 93). It is listed as ‘Structure 24. Knocknahur North’ in the list (ibid., 94). It is mentioned again with reference to phosphate surveys undertaken in Field XIV but no further details are recorded (ibid., 105). A field inspection in 1991 failed to locate this ‘structure’/’earthwork’. The precise nature of this ‘structure’ is unknown and a proper elucidation of this feature must await further investigation.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 11 March 2014

source_data.original_text:
Timoney (1984, 322, no. 5) describes this as follows: ‘The total diameter of this barrow, sited on the crest of a glacial ridge, is 21m. A central platform, 6.60m in diameter and 70cm high, is surrounded by a fosse, 2.90m wide and 20cm deep and this in turn by a bank 1.70m wide by 25cm high. There is a bank, 2.50m wide and 60cm high, along part of the northern edge of the central platform. Parts of the west and south sides of this monument have been disturbed in antiquity and the break in the outer bank does not appear to be original. Land improvements in 1982 resulted in the destruction of the outer bank. Burenhult (1980, 94) lists this as Structure 26, Knocknahur North, recte Breeoge. It is within Phosphate Field XIV. Only very small increases of phosphate values were recorded (Burenhult 1980:1, 105).’

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on a rise in gently undulating terrain, overlooking Ballysadare Bay, the shoreline of which is c. 300m to S. There is a marshy peninsula c. 100m to S which extends S into the bay. This possible rath was partly levelled in 2006 during ground works. It is evident as a roughly D-shaped, raised area (c. 33m NNE–SSW; c. 26m WSW–ESE) most clearly defined on the SW arc but low and degraded elsewhere, with a poorly defined depression (Wth 2.2m; D 0.1m) at SSW possibly indicating an external fosse. A 1991 report recorded it as a roughly circular, raised area (diam. c. 30m) which was defined by a scarp (H 1m) on its S half. The perimeter at N graded into the surrounding field and was difficult to trace. A shallow depression (Wth 3-4m; D 0.1-0.2m) on the W side indicated a possible external fosse.

source_data.original_text:
Located in the W half of a graveyard (SL020-054002-). Comprises a ruined rectangular church (int. L 21m, int. W 7m) constructed of split stone rubble masonry with extensive use of pinnings. A short section of the N wall survives at the NE angle. The E gable is intact and has a pointed light of sandstone set in an embrasure with a segmented rear arch which has the negative remains of wattles in the plaster on its underside. There is a recess or aumbry at ground level towards the S end of E gable. Projecting from the exterior face of the gable, adjacent to the window, is a carved sandstone human head (max. dim. c. 15cm). The facial features are greatly eroded. The S wall has an embrasure with a partly destroyed light near the E end, with a square recess or aumbry beneath it. There is a large break in the middle of the S wall. A hint of an inward splay at the edge of the break suggests that there was a second window embrasure here. Towards the W end of the wall there is a blocked-up doorway with a pointed arch. The W gable is missing. 

Compiled by : Geraldine Stout

Date of upload: 14 August 2013

source_data.original_text:
Located in a natural depression of lowlying ground, enclosed at N–SE by rising ground; to S and W is a flat expanse of damp pasture. Subrectangular area (c. 75 E–W; c. 55m N–S) enclosed by a mortared stone wall with an entrance gate at the N end of the E wall. The graveyard is on a slight S-facing incline and the level central area appears slightly raised and is defined by a scarp (H c. 0.8m) which extends E–W through the S half of the graveyard. There are a ruined medieval church (SL020-054001-) and a cross-slab (SL020-054005-) in the W half. The greatest density of graves is on the level central area and around and within the ruined church. The majority of the graves are marked by 19th and 20th century headstones, many at the head of rectangular plots enclosed by low concrete surrounds. There are a few table-tombs and chest-tombs. Low, uninscribed stone grave-markers are also evident, with the greatest concentration immediately to N of the church. There are yew trees growing in the centre of the graveyard, and beech trees, planted in the 19th-century, line the perimeter. Two breaks in the W wall lead into a later rectangular walled extension (c. 70m E–W; c. 45m N–S) which extends to W incorporating gently rising ground. A saint’s stone (SL020-054003-) and a holy well (SL020-054004-) are located c. 30m to N of the NE end of the graveyard.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 23 July 2014

According to tradition, the stone bears ‘the impression of St. Patrick’s knee’ and acquired a reddish hue from the Saint's blood. (OS Letters 1836, 64 (22-3)).
