In pasture, located in a damp hollow with rising ground to N and W, c. 30m NE of the NE corner of a graveyard (SL020-054002-). The well, named ‘Tober Padraig’ on the 1837 and 1913 OS 6-inch maps, consists of a rectangular, vertical-sided depression (1.2m NW–SE; 1m NE–SW; D 0.5m), with sides faced with rough drystone walling. It is enclosed at top on the SE, SW and NW sides by a low wall of jumbled stones and boulders. At SE the boulder wall extends beyond the well pit to enclose a small space (c. 2m E–W) at E which defines the access route to the well. A shallow overflow channel extends to SE from the well, bordered on the E side, for some of its extent, by remnants of a field wall and a line of hawthorn bushes. The well was dry at the time of inspection, and engulfed in overgrowth. There is a holy stone (SL020-054003-) located c. 15m to SW. 

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 24 July 2014

source_data.original_text:
In the W of W of Cloverhill Lough, close to the marshy shoreline. Not indicated on the 1837 and 1913 OS 6-inch maps.  Inspected in 2000, this crannog appears to consists of a low cairn (15m N–S; 12m E–W) of stones capped with grass-covered peat. It reaches a height of c. 1.45m above the peaty base of the lake, and rises to a height of c. 0.45m above the lake surface. Three distinct levels are evident: roughly in the centre on top of the crannog is a small cairn or concentration (3.6m N–S; 3.6m E–W) of subangular stones (limestone) (average dims. 0.3-0.4m) most of which are firmly set in the ground. This protrudes from a plateau of soft peat, which may cover a stone floor, and stretches W for 6m to the lake shore. The perimeter of the crannog is at a level c. 0.2m lower than the peat plateau and forms an encircling berm (Wth 0.4-0.8m). Reeds grow on the perimeter of the crannog, and the centre is covered in overgrowth. A band (Wth 4-7m) of dense wetland vegetation and very soft peat surrounds the crannog.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 17 July 2015

source_data.original_text:
Comprises an irregularly shaped enclosure defined by an earthen bank, on top of which a stone bank has been constructed (Max. Diam. 34m). There were no surface indications of an outer ditch prior to excavation. The proposed Ballysadare-Collooney Bypass clipped the E edge of the ringfort and it was this area that was excavated in 1995 (95E105). Excavations of the E edge produced evidence of a univallate ringfort with an earthen bank and an roughly V-shaped outer ditch (Wth 3.5m, D 2m) cut into the subsoil and bedrock.   This gave a total height/depth from bank top to ditch base of approximately 3.5m. Finds of animal bone were recovered from the ditch. An entranceway was uncovered to the SE (Wth 3.2m). Here the two ditch termini became shallower and narrower before terminating altogether. This consisted of a platform of bedrock and subsoil, sloping upwards from the exterior to the interior. The bank also decreased in height and width at this point (Opie H. 1995).


Compiled by: Geraldine Stout

Date of upload: 16 August 2013

In pasture, on gently elevated ground, in undulating terrain. Raised, roughly circular area (26m E–W; 23.5m N–S) defined by a scarp (ext. H 1.2m at W; ext. H 1.6m at E). At SE–SW the scarp is incorporated into a field fence/property boundary which respects the curve of the rath. At W the scarp is topped with a low stony rim (Wth 1m), possibly wall footings. Elsewhere along the top of the scarp, a few stones are visible, barely protruding above the sod. Stones also protrude randomly in parts on the external slope of the scarp. The SW quadrant of the interior is slightly raised above the rest of the interior. In the E half of the interior, there is a slight slope down to E mirroring the contours of the low rise on which the rath is sited. There is a low stony rise (max. dim. c. 1.3m) slightly NE of centre in the interior.

source_data.original_text:
On a former island (c. 250m N–S; c. 60-70m E–W), named ‘Inishbeg’ on the 1837 OS 6-inch map and ‘Inishcullion’ on the 1913 edition, now connected to the mainland at N by an expanse of flat salt-marsh /grassland. Listed in the RMP as ‘enclosure’ based on a reference in Wood-Martin (1887-8, 255): 'a small circle composed of earth and stones was pointed out on the island of Inishhullion on the opposite, that is to say, the Cuil-irra side of Ballysadare bay…the monument in question is of mean workmanship, and small size, measuring only 21 feet [6.4m] in over-all diameter…’ Wood-martin recorded this in relation to a legend that a fallen warrior was buried in this area following the second Battle of Moytirra. An inspection in 2014 found a small circular feature on level ground, roughly centrally located in the S half of the island. It consist of a flat circular area (3m N–S; 2.8m E–W) enclosed by a narrow, shallow fosse (Wth 0.8m; D 0.1-0.15m). Several stones (max. dim. 0.4-0.8m) are set against the outer perimeter of the fosse. Outside the fosse there is a slight rise or cropmark of shorter grass (Wth 0.8m) which hints at a possible outer bank/wall. The function of this small enclosure is unclear and it is uncertain if it is the feature noted by Wood-Martin.

source_data.original_text:
Straddling the narrow top of a ridge in undulating pasture with views onto Knocknarea, the Dartry Plateau and the Ox Mountains.
A circular area (int. diam. 20.50m) enclosed by a wall (Wth c. 1.8m; H 0.4-0.6m) with a rubble core and remnants inner and outer facing. On the W side the enclosing wall has been incorporated into a later N–S field boundary, and a field wall also merges with the S edge of the enclosure. The entrance may have been in the SE, but is not clearly defined. A slightly sunken trackway (Wth 1.4m) flanked by walls (Wth 0.7m; H 0.55m), now ruined, cuts through the centre of interior on a N-S axis. Hazel and holly trees ring the perimeter, and hazel trees grow in the interior.
